content: Herein lies the *Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Hopes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* (Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom) that clarifies the suchness of dependent origination.May the holy guru, who is the embodiment of the wisdom and compassion of the peerless guides of the fortunate realms, the treasury of the light of elegant sayings, and who causes the white lotus grove of the holy Dharma of scripture and realization to flourish, grant auspicious excellence.May the incomparable Śākyasiṃha, the omniscient God of gods, who has perfected the power of the ten strengths, who has bared the fangs of the four fearlessnesses, who waves the eyes of great love and compassion, who shakes the mane of omniscience, and who loudly proclaims the roar of the melody of emptiness and dependent origination, thereby instantly shattering the skull-vases of the hundred thousand elephants of the false-speaking opponents—may he grant all auspicious glory here and now.I bow my head to the great Maitreya, the regent of the Victor and the guru of gods, whose golden lotus-like feet are adorned upon the crest-jewel crown of a hundred gods.May the constant wheel of stability protect us, he who is the essence of the stainless crystal of the wisdom of all the omniscient ones, the deity who rides the moon, beautiful with the sixteen-year-old youth of the major and minor marks, who removes all the torments of existence and peace with the nectar rays of his pure white enlightened activity, and who causes the hundred petals of the white lotus of intellect to bloom.May the Goddess of the Ocean, who was born from the ocean of the secret speech of all the Victors, who has a white smile like a swaying white lotus creeper, and who grants all desires through the melody of her poetic words, make the ocean of my mind beautiful.I bow with my head to the feet of Nāgārjuna and Asaṅga, the ornaments of the beauty of the world who made the teachings of the Sage clear, having fully opened the grove of the two truths—the hundred-petaled lotus and the white lotus—with the light of the sun and moon of scripture and reasoning.He who is the second Victor, the lord of accomplishment Lobsang, who vowed to spread the most profound view in the presence of the crown of the lords of the Victors, and who accomplished his excellent prayers just as he had made them; whose great fame, like the sun, pervades the three realms with the roar of the melody of his renown; who is the most learned, the crest-jewel among all supreme scholars—may that one, who rests like a jewel, be victorious.I bow to the ornaments of the beauty of the Yellow Hat teachings, such as the Dharma regent Dharmarinchen, the sun of speech Khedrup, and the manifestation of Mañjuśrī, Chökyi Gyaltsen.I respectfully bow to the holy gurus who, having grasped all the pith instructions of the Victor’s treasury of Dharma, remove the poverty of the mind with the jewels of profound and vast elegant instructions, and grant the supreme benefit and happiness.How could the wing-flaps of a *kalandaka* bird—my childish intellect—ever reach the far shore of the sky of the meaning of the Mother? Yet, because the power of the imprints of the excellent path has grown, my mind takes joy in analyzing it as much as I am able.Furthermore, among the infinite collections of Dharma spoken by our Teacher, the great guide of gods and humans, the omniscient and incomparable Śākyasiṃha, in accordance with the dispositions, inclinations, and faculties of the many varied beings to be tamed, the most supreme, excellent, and principal is this very Perfection of Wisdom, the great path that is the single way traversed by all the Victors of the three times, in its extensive, intermediate, and condensed forms. Among these, the actual meaning of this *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā*, which has become the essence, is the sequence of emptiness as explained by the great charioteer, the protector Nāgārjuna, and the sequence of the hidden meaning of clear realization as clarified by the regent Maitreya in his treatise, the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra*. Thus, the omniscient Dharma King Tsongkhapa, who is the actual Mañjuśrī, along with his spiritual sons, having combined the sutras and the treatises...Relying upon the pith instructions of the well-spoken teachings, the explanation has four parts: the meaning of the title, the translator's homage, the meaning of the main text, and the meaning of the conclusion.The meaning of the title: The first of these has three parts: the translation of the title, the explanation of the meaning of the title, and the purpose.The translation of the title: Regarding the first, although there are many ways to explain the term "India" (rgya gar)—such as that the land is vast, or that it is called "India" because people wear black hats and robes during times of mourning and white ones at other times, while the Chinese wear the opposite, thus implying the meaning of white and black—the way "gar" is written is that the prefix "da" of "dkar" (white) is dropped according to the rules of orthography, and the root letter "ka" is changed to its corresponding soft letter in the same series, resulting in "ga." As it is said, when explaining through etymology, this seems plausible. However, our own tradition is as stated in the *Vinaya-kārikā*: "Śrāvastī, Sāketa, Campā, Vārāṇasī, Vaiśālī, and the sixth is Rājagṛha; these are known as the great cities." In accordance with this, the region containing these six great cities was given the conventional name "India" (rgya gar). Within that region, there are four major language families, and in the Sanskrit or refined language, the title of this sutra appears as *Āryaprajñāpāramitāsañcayagāthā*.When translated into the Tibetan language, it appears as *’phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa sdud pa tshigs su bcad pa* (The Noble Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom). In this, *ārya* means "noble," *prajñā* means "wisdom," *pāramitā* means "perfection," *sañcaya* means "summary," and *gāthā* means "verse."Explanation of the meaning of the title. Second, regarding the meaning of the title: because it is superior to the sutras of the Lesser Vehicle and so forth in terms of the manner in which it teaches its subject matter, it is called "noble" (*ārya*). When the Perfection of Wisdom is categorized according to the types of things the term denotes, there are four: the scriptural, the path, the resultant, and the natural Perfection of Wisdom. Among these, the resultant Mother—the wisdom of omniscience—is the actual or primary Perfection of Wisdom, while the others are secondary. Because it primarily teaches the natural Perfection of Wisdom, which is the object—emptiness—and the path and resultant Perfection of Wisdom, which are the subject—the non-conceptual wisdom that realizes that suchness directly—it is called the "Perfection of Wisdom," a designation based on its subject matter. Because this text serves as a basis for gathering and holding all the precious qualities of the Great Vehicle, including the generation of bodhicitta, along with its paths and fruits, it is called a "summary" (*sañcaya*). Because it is bound by the eleven-syllable *indravajra* meter, which is a noble melody, it is called a "verse" (*gāthā*).Purpose. Third, the purpose of initially stating the Indic language is to plant latent predispositions for the language and to cause blessings to arise in one's mental continuum, and so forth. The purpose of stating the Tibetan language is to acknowledge the work done by the translators and panditas and to show gratitude for their kindness; and the purpose of juxtaposing the two languages is to facilitate an easy understanding of the distinctions between the two languages.Homage of the Translation. Second, the homage of the translation is the statement, "Homage to the noble Mañjuśrī." He is "noble" (ārya) because he has realized emptiness directly and has thus transcended the state of an ordinary being. He is "Mañjuśrī" because his mental continuum is free from the rough touch of the two obscurations and he possesses the splendor of the two accumulations, or because he possesses the splendor of the major and minor marks; thus, the phrase means that one bows to him with the three doors of respectful conduct. This sutra is an Abhidharma text that primarily teaches the higher training in wisdom, and the venerable Mañjughoṣa is the special deity of wisdom. Because one must necessarily rely upon his enlightened activity to realize the profound view of Madhyamaka, the translators included this homage in accordance with the ancient royal decrees of the Dharma Kings to identify the scriptural category, to ensure the translation is complete, and to increase merit.The Meaning of the Text. Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning of the text, as stated in the *Vyākhyāyukti*: "Those who explain the meaning of the Sūtras should describe the purpose, along with the summarized meaning, the meaning of the words, the transitions, and the responses to objections," it is taught that one must explain by way of the five branches of the method of explanation.Therefore, there are three: the purpose, the summarized meaning, and the meaning of the words.The Purpose and Meaning. Among these, one must first state the purpose and the connection, for when individuals who seek liberation engage with sūtras and treatises through the three processes of hearing, thinking, and meditating, there must be a special purpose, it must be something that can be accomplished, it must be something desired by supreme beings, and it must have a coherent subject matter. It is necessary to avoid treatises that lack a purpose, such as those concerning the observation of crows; treatises that have a purpose but cannot be accomplished, such as those concerning the taking of a crown from a *jokpo*; treatises that are not to be adopted by supreme beings, such as those concerning the taking of *mabakmar*; and treatises that lack connection, such as the words of the "Ten Pomegranates." The *Prajñāpāramitā* extensive explanation states that the text concerning the taking of *mabakmar* is a type of mantra ritual where, after performing it, one applies it to a substance and casts it into fire, resulting in sounds such as "It is permitted," or sounds such as "This is not permitted here." The words of the "Ten Pomegranates" are as follows: "Ten pomegranates, six baskets of flour, / A deer skin, a bundle of grass, / Then this young girl, / Is the property of *Sbayagrata*." Therefore, this precious sūtra possesses four special qualities, such as the purpose. Its explicitly taught subject matter is emptiness, and its implicitly taught subject matter is the eight topics and seventy points; in short, it is the complete perfection of the three trainings to be practiced by the three vehicles.The purpose is that sharp-witted disciples who delight in concise summaries can easily understand the meaning of the *Ārya-śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* through these concise words, as previously explained. The ultimate purpose, or the purpose of the purpose, is the fruit, the *prajñāpāramitā*; this is the same for all Mahāyāna sūtras and treatises. The connection is that the latter parts are linked to the former parts. Then, by stating "In order to make those four assemblies of the Bhagavan rejoice," and so forth, the first three—the purpose and so on—are explicitly taught, and the connection is taught implicitly. Even so, in the master’s *Dka’ ’grel* (Difficult Commentary), it is said: "Regarding that, the connection is taught first; the treatise that performs the accomplishment, and so on," up to, "That is also taught by the very statement of the purpose, for it is like this: this is its purpose." Since what is taught by the teacher is what performs the accomplishment, the connection should not be stated separately. The subject matter is omniscience, which encompasses the eight *abhisamaya* (realizations). From "As just taught," up to, "is the purpose of the purpose." As it is said: "What is the path to omniscience that the Teacher has explained here?" and so forth.Summary of Meaning. The second, the summary of meaning: As stated in the *Dka’ ’grel* (Difficult Commentary), "In order for the listeners to understand the meaning of the sūtra without confusion and in a differentiated manner, and for the speaker to explain it easily, the summary of meaning should be stated for the time being." If one were to explain the eight topics of the *Abhisamaya* without first showing the number of the eight categories and the number of their respective indicators, one would not know where each of the eight categories begins or ends, leading to confusion between the preceding and following sections. To eliminate this, and so that the boundaries of each topic may be understood without confusion, it is necessary to first provide a concise summary as a structural outline. When divided by way of the expressive, there are eight chapters; when divided by way of the expressed meaning, there are eight categories; and when further divided, there are seventy topics. Regarding the first, the *Ornament* states: "The *prajñāpāramitā* is the eight categories," and so on, up to "these eight," which provides the concise summary. From "generating the mind and the instructions," up to "the four are correctly stated," the seventy topics are explained in detail by their numerical count. In accordance with that, the summary of meaning stated here is as follows: Among the objects to be realized, there are the three knowledges; among the means of realization, there are the four applications; and among the fruits to be realized, there is the *dharmakāya*. Since disciples who wish to attain buddhahood must generate an aspiration for the fruit after seeing the benefits of the omniscience, the omniscience is taught first, from "The supreme joy, respect, and faith are established," up to "When one fully understands that phenomena are without intrinsic nature, this is the practice of the supreme *prajñāpāramitā*." Because one must study the path—the uncommon cause—to attain that omniscience, the knowledge of the path is taught from "Whoever does not abide in form, does not abide in sensation," up to "The fruit of omniscience and the purity of form are like the expanse of space, indivisible and uncuttable." Since the knowledge of all bases must precede the attainment of the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of all bases is explained thereafter, from "The hero who practices the *prajñāpāramitā*," up to "Like the sun free from the eclipse, shining clearly, and like fire burning grass, wood, and forests." Since the attainment of the four applications must precede the attainment of the three knowledges, the four applications are explained thereafter. To master the aspects of the three knowledges, the application of complete aspects is explained first, from "All phenomena are naturally pure and completely pure," up to "Because they do not fully reveal, the dharma of the non-retrograde is not explained; know this to be the unmanifest." Following that, because the peak *abhisamaya*—the culmination of realization that has increased through meditation after attaining the complete realization of all aspects—arises, the peak application is explained thereafter, from "The wisdom of the *arhat* stages and the *pratyekabuddha*," up to "When the *arhat* and *pratyekabuddha* are certain of the supreme enlightenment free from the vehicle, know the hero to be always in meditative equipoise." Following that, to attain stability in the aspects of the three knowledges, the gradual application—the gradual meditation on the aspects of the three knowledges—is explained by one verse, starting from "The mind is completely pure for the sake of other sentient beings." Because the culmination of the practice of the gradual *abhisamaya* leads to the attainment of the momentary application, which gains stability in the aspects of the three knowledges, that is explained by two verses, starting from "Whether one is scolded or even constantly struck." By practicing the four applications in this way, the *dharmakāya*—the fruit free from all obscurations—arises as a manifest enlightenment; thus, the fruit *dharma* is taught thereafter by one verse, starting from "Having abandoned one's own happiness, with a mind free from expectation." Following that, the method of seeking a qualified spiritual friend to generate the eight *abhisamayas* in one's own continuum, and the manner of listening to the Mother and so forth, or practicing the three, is taught from "Whatever bodhisattva wishes to remain for a long time," up to "The bodhisattva who thinks, 'I will endure all the suffering of beings,' abides in the *prajñāpāramitā* of patience." Following that, the giving of instructions as they are to a fortunate person who relies on a spiritual friend in accordance with the discipline is taught from "Those who desire peace through morality become noble," up to "The roots of virtue increase with great power, like the moon in the waxing phase, bright and without clouds." Following that, the sequence of practicing the path while possessing the instructions is taught from "The bodhisattva's generosity cuts off the hungry ghost realm," up to "Likewise, one fully upholds the continuum of the *saṅgha* and all the *dharma*." Following that, the entrustment to ensure that this *dharma* discourse remains for a long time is taught by one verse, starting from "Healing the illnesses of beings," and so forth. These are the summary of meaning.Meaning of the words: Third, regarding the detailed explanation of the meaning of the words, there is the introduction providing the context from which the sutra arose, and the explanation of the sutra that arose from it.The introduction providing the context from which the sutra arose: The first part is from "Then, the Blessed One..." up to "...spoke." The meaning is: "Then" is a connective term. Immediately after the completion of the teaching of the *Yum 'bum pa* (Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Lines) and so forth, the Blessed One, who has vanquished the four maras without exception, and who possesses the six great fortunes of qualities—as it is said, "Possessing power, fine form, glory, fame, wisdom, and perfect diligence, these six are called fortunes"—that very Blessed One, the Sugata, by the specific term "those four assemblies," consisting of the two groups of monks and nuns and the two groups of laymen and laywomen, indicates that eunuchs and others are not the assembly due to their heavy afflictions, and because the Sangha of monks and so forth are permanent or stable assemblies, they are explicitly mentioned, whereas bodhisattvas are not mentioned because they are not a stable assembly. Because those assemblies possessing the fortunes, having easily understood the great meaning of the *Yum* (Perfection of Wisdom) with little difficulty, and having generated all the qualities of the path and fruit of the Great Vehicle within their own continuums, are made truly and supremely joyful, he again teaches this profound Perfection of Wisdom, the scripture whose subject matter is the path and fruit, and at that time, having summarized the meaning, he spoke these verses that appear below, beginning with "Joy and respect..."To explain the manner of the introduction in slightly more detail: In our own tradition, it is taught that the *Yum* (Perfection of Wisdom) was taught in three stages—extensive, intermediate, and condensed—and that the *Sutra of the Summary* (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) is the eighty-fourth chapter of the eighteen-thousand-line version. Buton Rinpoche said: The extensive is the one hundred thousand; the intermediate-extensive is the twenty-five thousand; the intermediate-intermediate is the eighteen thousand; the intermediate-condensed is the ten thousand; the condensed-extensive is the eight thousand; and the condensed-condensed is the *Precious Qualities Collection*. Regarding these, the first five were taught simultaneously, as the requesters are all the same and the prophecy of the goddess of the Ganges in the *Zhing dag sbyor* (Pure Land Arrangement) is identical. There is a pervasion, for it is not appropriate for one Buddha to repeatedly prophesy the same person to enlightenment. It is stated in the commentary that the *Summary* was taught in the language of Magadha so that the four assemblies might rejoice afterward.The great Geshé of Lithang and others said: "These extensive, intermediate, and condensed sutras appear differently due to the Buddha's enlightened activity and the inclinations of the beings to be tamed, not because the sutras themselves are different; even though they were taught as a single utterance..." and so on, though the reason is not elaborated. If one asks which of these differing explanations is correct, as it is said in the *Sutra of Inconceivable Secrets* and the *Chapter of the Truth-Speaker*: "Thus, the definitive words of all sentient beings, requested by many at the same time, are understood in a single moment of mind, and he replies to each with a single melody of speech," and so on, it is not appropriate to fixate on one extreme regarding the inconceivable secrets of the Buddha's speech, which transcend the scope of the minds of ordinary beings. Therefore, the teacher explained the manner of the introduction by following the extensive and intermediate sutras, which is also said to be the intention of the master Dignāga. Thus, apart from whether the words are extensive or not, the introduction is the same for all, and it is indicated by "Thus have I heard at one time," and so on.Master Bhāviveka and others hold that the compiler of this *Sutra of the Summary* is Vajrapāṇi, while Master Haribhadra holds that it is the noble Ānanda, who assumed the manner of a śrāvaka based on the *Yongs gtad* (Final Entrustment) and so forth. This phrase "Thus" captures the entire meaning of the beginning and end of the sutra, and it is the same point as that taught in the tantras, that the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dharma are included within *evam*. "At one time" indicates that he heard this at one time and heard others at other times, showing that he himself possessed great learning; that this sutra was heard at one time and not at another, showing that the Dharma is rare; and that even though he heard it in a single moment, he did not forget it, showing him to be a person of inconceivable validity. Furthermore, because the meaning of the sutra is exactly this without addition or omission, the word "Thus" indicates the internal condition of wisdom, and the word "I" indicates the teacher, showing that he heard it directly from the Blessed One, thereby indicating that he possessed the oral instructions of the previous masters as an external condition. The word "heard" is applied to his humility, saying that it is merely hearing and not yet realization, and so on; one should know that there are many profound points.In short, Ānanda, having shown himself to be a person of validity to generate faith in future beings to be tamed, and for the sake of their listening to and holding this sutra with respect, taught it as possessing the five perfections: at the time of the perfection of time, he taught the perfection of place, and along with the perfection of the assembly, he heard this perfection of the Dharma, the sutra. Thus, it is taught as possessing the five perfections. Accordingly, the perfection of place is the Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. The purpose of mentioning both is to include both the householder and the ordained, showing that it is superior to both the place of the defiled side and the place of the purified side.Regarding Rājagṛha: It is said in the *Sutra of the Rice Seedling* that it was formerly known as the city of Rājagṛha (King's House) because, when the city of Rājagṛha (formerly known as the city of the supreme grass) was repeatedly set on fire by non-human beings and could not be inhabited, the king commanded that from then on, whoever let a fire start in their house should go and live in the cemetery of the Cool Grove, and due to karma, a fire first broke out in the king's palace, so the king went there and lived, and thus the name Rājagṛha was established, as stated by the scholar Ngawang Tendar.Regarding the naming of Vulture Peak Mountain: Scholars say it is so named because the mountain's peak has the shape of a vulture, or because it is shaped like a pile of many vultures, or because it is named for the protection of the mountain because many vultures eat corpses there, or because when the Perfection of Wisdom was taught, bodhisattvas appeared in the form of vultures on the tenth day. Since most people of that time did not see the miraculous displays at the time the Perfection of Wisdom was taught, and furthermore, the major and minor marks appeared differently due to the pure or impure karma of the beings to be tamed, and this mountain also appeared to be filled with many vultures, one should generate certainty that the spiritual friend who teaches the Dharma is in reality the Buddha himself, even if he appears as an ordinary person due to one's own impure perception, and one should become skilled in the foundation of the path, the manner of relying on a spiritual friend, and so on, and apply this to the seat of practice.The perfection of time is held by the three great oceans of the *Phug pa* (tradition) to be the fifteenth day of the month following the teaching of the Perfection of Wisdom sutra to the Nagas, when he passed into parinirvāṇa. Although there are many ways of holding this, such as those of Chim and Chag Lotsawa, our own tradition is that it was that special time, the fifteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha, in the year after the teacher Buddha passed away.The perfection of the teacher is the omniscient King of the Śākyas, the supreme one who acts to emanate and gather all the Victors.The perfection of the assembly is the great Sangha of two thousand five hundred and fifty monks, who were the ordinary assembly that remained constantly, even though there were countless monks and bodhisattvas, as only a summary was mentioned. Regarding the Sangha, it is as the sutra says: "The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha cannot be divided even by a hundred million maras; therefore, they are called the Sangha."The description of their qualities is: they are Arhats because they have vanquished the four gross maras; they are those whose taints are exhausted because the three taints of desire, ignorance, and existence are exhausted; they are those without afflictions because the three defilements of karma, affliction, and birth are absent; they are those who have mastery over their conduct because they have abandoned misconduct through the aggregate of morality; they are those who have mastery over the world and their own minds because they have abandoned desire, wrong views, and the bonds of existence through the three aggregates of concentration, wisdom, and liberation; they are those whose minds are supremely liberated because they have abandoned the obscurations of meditative absorption; they are those whose wisdom is supremely liberated because they have abandoned the obscurations of affliction."Cang shes" (thoroughbred/knowing) means fearless. Thoroughbred horses and elephants are fearless because they know whether or not there is danger on the path or place where they are going. In this context, it means they are fearless of sorrow and so on because they have abandoned suffering. They are free from the seven fears, such as being disparaged by oneself. The seven fears are: being disparaged by oneself, being disparaged by others, fear of lack of livelihood, fear of punishment, fear of lack of verses, and fear of bad migrations and death. They are fearless of the eight worldly dharmas because they have abandoned them. They are fearless of lack of understanding, wrong views, and doubt because they have abandoned doubt regarding their own realization. This is the meaning of the Arhat who is a thoroughbred, free from the four fears. In general, five types of thoroughbreds are explained: the bull thoroughbred, which has no fear of falling; the horse and elephant thoroughbreds, which have no fear of fighting; the lion thoroughbred, which has no fear because there is no harm from others; and the Arhat thoroughbred, which has no fear of riding.They are like great elephants because they possess the realization of special dharmas such as the three knowledges; they are those who have done what is to be done because they have achieved the goal of the ascetic, liberation, and have done what is appropriate, such as the qualities of asceticism; they are those who have laid down the burden because they have laid down the four burdens of the aggregates, afflictions, vows, and diligence; they are those who have attained the result by following the teaching of their own benefit, such as the qualities of abandonment and realization; they are those whose nine fetters, which constantly bind beings in existence, are completely exhausted; they are those whose minds are supremely liberated because they have directly realized the reality of the four truths through the path of seeing and meditation, so that afflictions do not arise again; they are those who have reached the other shore of all noble families, having mastery over all minds, such as the nine meditative absorptions. Since those śrāvakas are filled with the imprints of virtuous and non-virtuous actions and take rebirth in accordance with them, they are tainted; who then, other than one who possesses all these qualities, is the person? It is the Elder Ānanda, who is dear to all, who has heard much, and who has attained the joy of serving the Buddha.The perfection of the Dharma is this very precious Perfection of Wisdom sutra, which teaches the entire sequence of practice of the path of the three vehicles in the context of the causal Perfection of Wisdom without anything missing. The manner in which it was taught is through the three miraculous displays—the miracle of miraculous power, the miracle of speech, and the miracle of instruction—or through the inconceivable enlightened activity of body, speech, and mind, by which he gathered the beings to be tamed into the assembly, ripened those who were not ripe, liberated those who were ripe, and established all in the supreme fruit. Therefore, this explains the miracle of the mind's meditative absorption, the miracle of the body's miraculous power, and the miracle of the speech's manifestation of Dharma.Regarding the first, there are two parts. In the first, teaching the miracle of the king of meditative absorptions: first, the teacher creates the merit of the Perfection of Wisdom sutra, and in order to dispel the unhappiness of the followers who lack the offerings and livelihood of the assembly when they are teaching and listening to the Dharma and meditating on the stages of the path, and to encourage them to rely on having few desires and being content, he himself arranges the seat of Dharma. To show that the meaning of this sutra must be realized by meditative equipoise, he sat with his body straight and not crooked, in the vajra posture. This symbolizes the manner of correcting the motivation of the preparatory practices and the seven-fold posture of Vairocana. He made the mudra of the wheel of Dharma, fixed his gaze on the tip of his nose, and entered into the king of meditative absorptions that gathers all meditative absorptions.Rising from that, he looked upon beings with eyes of love and compassion and taught the Dharma of the Victors, which appears as various vehicles in accordance with the minds of the beings to be tamed. To show this, he emitted sixty-six hundred thousand billion rays of light from parts of his body, and by emitting natural light, he illuminated all the realms of the world and established sentient beings in unsurpassed enlightenment. Then, as a precursor to teaching the *Yum* (Perfection of Wisdom), he extended his tongue and covered the three-thousand-fold world, and from that, he emitted countless rays of light, and by teaching the Dharma preceded by the presence of many Tathāgatas who resided there, he established sentient beings in unsurpassed enlightenment as before. These are the first miracles of meditative absorption.The second is the demonstration of the miracle of the lion’s play. This is because, following that, one understands that the Mother should not be taught to those who speak the Dharma but are in an impure state, nor to those who listen to the Dharma but lack the wisdom that knows the two truths. Therefore, having entered into the meditative stabilization called the "lion’s play," which is free from the fear and trepidation of the assembly, and having preceded it with the eighteen great miraculous signs such as the shaking of the earth, one clears away all the unfavorable conditions of the world realm and purifies the place. As a result, the sentient beings dwelling there are reborn in happy states, remember their past lives, and, being overjoyed, each bows down and pays homage to the Buddha. Sentient beings whose faculties were incomplete become complete, and having established themselves in the ten virtues, their minds become workable through the joy of meditative concentration and the immeasurables. They explicitly declare that generosity, discipline, peace, perfect restraint, pure conduct, and non-harming of living beings are excellent, and thus they become possessed of the wisdom that is a suitable vessel for hearing the Mother. This is the second miracle of meditative stabilization.The second, the explanation of the miracle of the physical body, consists of two parts. The first is the demonstration of the miracle of emanation. Following that, in order to generate devotion in the beings to be tamed by showing that such a Teacher, who has attained the wisdom of omniscience, is capable of teaching this sutra, the body is adorned with rays of light as before. The body color is brilliant like refined gold, its splendor is radiant, and its glory outshines the entire world, standing out prominently; it becomes like Mount Meru outshining the lesser mountains. This is the first miracle of supernatural power.The second, the explanation of the miracle of blessing, consists of two parts. To dispel the discouragement of thinking that only such a Teacher could understand the meaning of the sutra and that others could not, and to generate enthusiasm by showing that human beings are also capable of accomplishing it, the Teacher manifested an ordinary body, appearing similar in form to the bodies of the people of this world. At that time, the beings to be tamed were overjoyed; having seen and become familiar with the Mother of the Tathāgatas shown previously, they made offerings to the Blessed One with flowers and the like. The Teacher enjoyed what they offered, and they, in turn, were delighted and rejoiced, thereby increasing their virtuous roots. Furthermore, because the assembly was at ease and their bodies were thoroughly refined, in order to increase their accumulation of wisdom, the Teacher, through his blessing, caused those flowers and other offerings to become a magnificent palace above his head, equal in size to the trichiliocosm and adorned with various types of ornaments. To dispel the thought that the Teacher was not impartial toward other beings to be tamed, he appeared to sit before each of them individually to teach the Dharma; this is the second miracle of supernatural power, consisting of the two deeds of dispelling pride and dispelling discouragement. It should be understood that these demonstrate many things, such as the spreading of the support, the unwavering nature of the offerings, and the urging to turn the wheel of Dharma.The third section, concerning the miracle of the manifestation of the Dharma, is divided into two parts. The first is the demonstration of the miracle of revealing the world systems. Regarding this, although the Teacher himself was born in an impure realm, in order to show that he is equal to other victorious ones, and in order to show the method for those to be trained who were born in other realms to complete their accumulations, he smiled. By his smiling, the beings of this realm saw the buddhas and their retinues in the world systems of the ten directions, and the fortunate beings to be trained in other realms saw the Teacher and his retinue in this Sahā world. This is the first miracle of the manifestation of world systems.The second section, concerning the miracle of the gathering of the assembly, is as follows: Then, because the *bodhisattvas*—such as the *bodhisattva* Ālokodgata, the chief of the retinue of the *tathāgata* Ratnaketu in the jewel-filled world system of the east, and the *bodhisattva* Vimalaprabha, the chief of the retinue of the *tathāgata* Vimalaprabha in the sorrowless world system of the south, and others from the world systems of the ten directions—were urged, they understood that it is not appropriate to listen to the Dharma from another without asking one’s own teacher. Therefore, those *bodhisattvas* bowed to their respective victorious ones and asked for the reason. Having heard those victorious ones speak the praises of the Teacher, they obtained permission to go to this realm as requested. In order to pay homage to this Teacher, those victorious ones offered gifts of lotuses made of various jewels, words of inquiry regarding his health, and instructions to be vigilant in that impure realm. Having received these, they paid homage to the victorious ones along the way, arrived in this realm, and, preceded by bowing to the Teacher, blessed the offerings of homage. Having settled in their respective places, they presented the previously mentioned words of inquiry and the lotuses; this is the second miracle of manifestation. Then, in order to pay homage to the holy Dharma, the Teacher scattered the lotuses in their respective directions. Emanations resided upon them, and he understood that the disciples who possessed the fortune to be shown the *Yum* (Mother/Perfection of Wisdom) had gathered. He then taught this precious *Prajñāpāramitā* sutra, which is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end. Since I have not seen the *nidāna* (foundational narrative) explained in detail in the texts of our own tradition, I have compiled this from various treatises and explained it with some elaboration, with the thought of being of some small benefit to others who share the same fortune as myself.The explanation of the actual sutra. Regarding the second, the explanation of the actual sutra, there are three parts: the explanation of the three knowledges to be known, the explanation of the four practices of the path, and the explanation of the resultant dharmakāya.The three knowledges to be known. Regarding the first, there are three: the Knowledge of All Aspects, the Knowledge of Paths, and the Knowledge of Bases.The Knowledge of All Aspects. Regarding the first, the wisdom that has reached the culmination of directly realizing the ten phenomena, such as the generation of bodhicitta, is the definition or essence of the Knowledge of All Aspects. Regarding those phenomena that characterize it, as shown in the *Ornament* from the passage beginning with "the generation of bodhicitta and the instructions" up to "the state of omniscience," there are ten: the intention, which is the generation of bodhicitta; the special feature of its subsequent growth, the instructions; the special feature of the practice, the branches of definite emergence; the support of the practice, the natural lineage; the object of the practice; the purpose of the practice; the nature of the practice itself; the practice of armor; the practice of engagement; the practice of accumulation; and the practice of definite emergence. Among these, the reason the generation of bodhicitta is taught first is as follows: just as a painter draws a plumb line to ensure that the image of a deity does not suffer from defects such as crookedness, one must, at the very beginning, clarify at least a contrived generation of bodhicitta as the motivation, so that whatever virtuous activity one performs does not go astray but becomes a cause solely for buddhahood. As Gungthang Jampai Yang stated, this is an oral instruction heard from the Yongs-dzin Rinpoche. Thus, the generation of bodhicitta.Regarding the first, the teaching on the generation of bodhicitta, there are two parts: the actual subject and the ancillary points.The actual subject: The first is taught by one verse beginning with "Joy and respect, and so forth." Although Buddhaśrī explains that the first two lines urge the suitable vessel to listen, and the remaining two lines teach the generation of bodhicitta, the master’s own position is as stated previously.The meaning of the words is as follows: "Joy and respect" refers to the supreme faith of conviction—the faith of joy in the Mahāyāna path and its fruit, the faith of intense longing to attain unsurpassed enlightenment, and the faith of certainty regarding the causal relationship that unsurpassed enlightenment is attained through the practice of the perfection of wisdom. One should listen having established this, for faith is like a mother who gives birth to and precedes all wholesome qualities. Regarding the generation of the Mahāyāna bodhicitta and so forth within one’s own continuum: having eliminated the obscurations such as the grasping at true existence that act as obstacles, and the afflictions such as the three poisons that cause suffering to the person possessing that continuum, one is then free from the stains that are to be overcome by their respective antidotes. By the great compassion, one is a noble person who has truly entered into the practice of attaining unsurpassed enlightenment—the definitive goodness of the ultimate and the temporary high status—for the sake of all sentient beings without exception. Therefore, those great beings whose continuum has been softened or pacified and made certain by the path that has emptiness as its essence and compassion as its heart, should listen to the path of the Great Vehicle—the path of the perfection of wisdom, which is included in the generation of bodhicitta and is superior to the path of the śrāvakas—which is the object of practice for heroic bodhisattvas during both meditative equipoise and subsequent attainment.Regarding this, as stated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*: "The generation of bodhicitta is the desire for perfect, complete enlightenment for the sake of others," it arises in conjunction with the seventh [type of faith], which is focused on the enlightenment that is the perfection of the welfare of others, which has become one's own companion. That special, distinct consciousness of the primary Mahāyāna mind, which resides in the lineage of the path and has become the gateway to the Mahāyāna path, is the definition of the conventional Mahāyāna generation of bodhicitta. Regarding its classification by essence, there are two: aspiration and engagement. Classified by the manner of generation, there are three, such as the king-like generation of bodhicitta. Classified by the stages of the path, there are four, such as the generation of bodhicitta of the path of aspiration. Classified by the similarity to examples and companions, there are twenty-two, from the earth-like generation of bodhicitta up to the cloud-like generation of bodhicitta.The manner in which these are taught by this sūtra is as follows: the first line teaches the manner of relying on a spiritual friend and the preliminary practices for generating the path, such as the common paths of the small and intermediate persons. The second line teaches the aspiration to seek enlightenment, and by the phrase "engaged in the welfare of beings," it shows that this desire for enlightenment is also for the sake of others; by the word "heroes," it indicates the basis, the bodhisattva; and by the word "practice," it indicates the manner of training in the path. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* says: "Subhūti, just as you should encourage bodhisattva mahāsattvas to emerge into the perfection of wisdom, beginning from the perfection of wisdom, so too should you encourage them." This teaches the generation of bodhicitta. Through these sūtra words, the person who is the basis, the purpose for which it is done, the object, and the manner of training are all taught, thus providing a complete sequence of the Mahāyāna path. Therefore, the masters have said that all the meanings of the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras are included within this, that all Mahāyāna paths are included within the generation of bodhicitta, and that it is like the root and summary of the Mahāyāna path. The *Dka' 'grel* also says: "Therefore, the generation of bodhicitta, by its nature of being like an illusion, includes the omniscience and the eight realizations; thus it is certain according to the scriptures." The *Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra* also says: "Son of noble family, the mind of enlightenment is the root of all Buddha-dharmas," and it is said to be a summary teaching because it includes all the practices and prayers of a bodhisattva.Regarding how it is included within the generation of bodhicitta: after generating the mind for supreme enlightenment, it is not enough to merely focus on the two objects of enlightenment and the welfare of others; one must also have the method and wisdom to attain them. That is, by pleasing a Mahāyāna spiritual friend through both thought and action, one listens to all the profound and vast instructions without exception. Having mastered the objects of focus of the generation of bodhicitta as the entirety of the Mahāyāna path, and having made that very generation of bodhicitta the foundation and backbone of the Mahāyāna path, one practices the union of method and wisdom, making the six perfections such as generosity and the four means of gathering disciples into its branches or parts. By practicing in this way, the mind of enlightenment, along with its branches, increases and expands higher and higher, and by traversing the ten grounds and five paths in sequence, one becomes a Buddha. Therefore, because the generation of bodhicitta is taught as the summary of the Mahāyāna path, one should use this meaning as a seed, rely on learned spiritual friends, study the scriptures in detail, and attain an unerring understanding. Furthermore, not leaving it merely as a matter of understanding, as the Great Lord [Tsongkhapa] said: "The generation of bodhicitta is the backbone of the Mahāyāna path, / The foundation and basis for all vast practices, / Like an alchemical elixir for all the two accumulations, / A treasure of merit that gathers infinite wholesome qualities. / Knowing this, the heroic children of the Conquerors / Hold the precious supreme mind as the heart of their practice. / I, a yogi, have also practiced in this way; / You who desire liberation should also train accordingly." As he said, by combining the sūtras and the *Lamrim*, one should hold the precious mind of enlightenment as the heart of one's practice and accomplish the two purposes of self and others spontaneously.Incidental: The second point, establishing through an analogy that the teaching of the perfection of wisdom by the Śrāvakas is due to the power of the Buddha, is explained by the three verses beginning with "In this Jambudvīpa." The meaning is as follows: Just as, for example, to the south of Mount Meru there is a Jambu tree, and when its fruit falls into the lake, it is given the name "Jambu," and because it is a continent surrounded by water at its borders, it is called "Jambudvīpa." Its shape resembles a chariot, with two sides measuring two thousand yojanas each, and one side measuring three and a half yojanas. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Jambudvīpa has three sides of two thousand [yojanas] and is shaped like a chariot; one side is three and a half yojanas." In this central southern continent, all the various rivers such as the Gaṅgā, Pakṣu, Sindhu, and Sītā flow, and all the trees, medicinal plants, and forests that possess flowers such as lotuses and water lilies, and fruits such as mangoes, are produced and flourish. This is due to Lake Anavatapta, which is filled with water possessing eight qualities that quells heat. The Nagas, such as the chief or lord of the Nagas dwelling in the great lake Anavatapta, and the Naga Nanda, depend upon that great master. All of these things arise from the power and glory of that great lord of the Nagas, who is supreme among those Nagas, free from the fears of sand-heat and the like, and who has attained independence.In the same way, all the Dharma, such as the twelve branches of the scriptures, that the Victor’s śrāvakas, such as Subhūti, teach—by indicating "this is the meaning of this" in order to generate the wisdom arising from hearing through the three valid cognitions and correct reasoning; by explaining the words and meanings in detail in order to generate the wisdom arising from contemplation; and by expressing them with speech endowed with the four types of reasoning, such as the methods for removing obstacles and enhancing practice, and the reasoning of performing functions, in order to generate the wisdom arising from meditation—and the fact that they bring about the attainment of the non-abiding nirvāṇa, which is the ultimate, supreme, and exalted bliss of the Buddha, the fruit of that teaching of the Dharma; and furthermore, the fact that they attain the four fruits—the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat śrāvaka—as the fruit of that teaching of the Dharma in the interim; all of these are the power, that is, the blessings, of the Tathāgata, the Great Being, who has realized the suchness of the nature of phenomena and teaches it just as he has seen it.If one asks, "For what reason is all of that the power of the Buddha?" the answer is that the supreme person, the Buddha Bhagavān, having conquered the four māras without remainder, taught the Dharma system of the selflessness of persons and phenomena. His disciples, such as Subhūti, trained in that system through the sequence of the three—hearing, contemplation, and meditation—and having realized it directly, they taught it to other trainees just as they themselves had trained. All of that is done through the power of the Buddha, and not through the power of the śrāvakas’ own strength. Furthermore, one should know that through the power of the Buddha’s blessings, even trees, those moved by the wind, and the sky produce the sound of Dharma, thereby establishing trainees in ripening and liberation; having understood these inconceivable enlightened activities and qualities, one should go for refuge from the depths of one’s heart. Regarding how this text proceeds as a corollary to the generation of bodhicitta, Khri Gung-thang-pa stated that it is established from the perspective of the fruit: because one desires to become a Buddha—who is born from the bodhicitta that acts as a summary of the perfection of wisdom, or who teaches the perfection of wisdom independently—one should train in it.Instruction. Second, regarding the instruction: it is the Mahayana speech that teaches the method for attaining what is sought for the sake of generating the Mahayana mind; this is the definition of a Mahayana instruction. Regarding this, in terms of its essence, there are two: the instruction given so that qualities already attained do not decline, and the subsequent instruction given so that qualities not yet attained may be attained. When divided in terms of what is expressed, as stated in the Ornament: "From 'the practices and the truths, etc.' to 'should be known,'" there are ten: instructions on the essence of the practice itself, the four truths as the object of focus, the Three Jewels as the support for practice, the three types of diligence as the companions of practice, the five eyes that do not rely on others for practice, the six clairvoyances as the cause for the perfection of practice, the path of seeing that sees the truths anew, and the path of meditation that familiarizes one with what has been seen. Among these, the instruction that is the primary one—which teaches the essence of the practice itself without departing from the sequence of the two truths—is taught by the single verse, "To whom, with wisdom, etc." The meaning is: for any bodhisattva, it is said that the supreme perfection of wisdom—which realizes the selflessness of phenomena and persons in the six perfections, such as generosity, which are to be practiced as the object of instruction—when one searches for and analyzes the designated meaning of the conventionally imputed [perfection of wisdom], it is not observed as established by its own essence or established by nature, but remains merely as an imputation. Furthermore, when the practitioner, the bodhisattva, searches through reasoning for the basis of designation—the aggregates—and whether it is established as one or different from what is established by nature, the essence of the person is not found or observed at all, but is like an illusion, merely posited by name and convention. The essence of the bodhicitta that is to be practiced is also not observed as being established as true in the slightest.Upon hearing the discourse that teaches that the agent, the action, and the activity are devoid of true existence, a bodhisattva—who is not confused about practicing the perfection of wisdom merely as a conventional designation, even though it does not exist in the ultimate sense, and who is not afraid, meaning not even slightly fearful, of the teaching that things are empty by nature or empty of true existence—is one who possesses the fortune to engage in the profound path of the perfection of wisdom taught by the Sugata. This means that when practicing the Mahāyāna path, one must not depart from the practice of the union of the two truths: the sequence of the path based on conventional truth, where the practitioner, the object to be adopted, and the result are practiced as being like an illusion in terms of conventional designation; and the sequence of the path based on ultimate truth, where one practices having realized those things as empty of true existence. The instruction on practice directly teaches the basis or the general aspect, and because the other is its specific quality or particularity, it is implied by the meaning. As it is stated in the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā*: "By this virtue, may all beings / Accumulate the collections of merit and wisdom, / And may they attain the two supreme *kāyas* / Which arise from merit and wisdom." Just as this states, one should know that the essential point of practice is to engage in it without departing from the union of the two truths as the basis, the union of method and wisdom as the path, and the union of the two *kāyas* as the result.Path of Preparation: The third section explains the path of preparation, which is the beginning of the meditative cultivation of the meaning of the instructions. Its definition is: the Mahayana mundane path that abides in the lineage of realization, which arises after having completed the portion of the Mahayana path of liberation that is its own cause, and which accords with the realization of the truths. Such a Mahayana path of preparation is superior to the Hīnayāna path of preparation by way of five or six distinct qualities. As the *Ornament* states, "The object of observation, the aspect, and so forth," it is superior by way of the object of observation, the aspect, the mode of engaging in the cause, the mode of apprehension, the manner of possessing the primary abandonment of the conceptualization of grasping at truth, and the division into small, medium, and great. Regarding this, in terms of its essence, there are the four [levels] such as heat, and in terms of its stages, there are twelve, with three—small, medium, and great—for each. While the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, the *Viṃśatisāhasrikā*, and others contain individual sutras for the objects of observation, aspects, and causes of practice for all paths of preparation, for this [text], there is no sutra for each of the four—heat, peak, patience, and supreme dharma—individually.The distinction of the three—the essence, the object of observation and aspect, and the cause; the distinction of the result, the concomitant, the abandonment, and the realization; and the distinction of the spiritual mentor who fully upholds [the practice].The distinction of the three—the essence, the object of observation and aspect, and the cause. Regarding the first, there are four: heat, peak, forbearance, and supreme mundane dharma.The object of observation of heat: The object of observation of heat is indicated by the passage from "Form is not, feeling is not" up to "consciousness." The meaning is this: Here, the five sense faculties, the five objects, and so forth, which are included within the aggregate of form, are composed of many particles and are accumulated, and thus they possess many parts. If one analyzes them with the reasoning that investigates the ultimate—asking whether they are established as one or many by way of their own nature—there is not even the slightest thing established by its own essence. Furthermore, since the particles that are their parts also possess directional parts, if one analyzes them as before, there is not even the slightest thing established as true. Therefore, although this form appears, it does not exist as true. Likewise, if one analyzes these feelings of pleasure, pain, and equanimity, which are included within one's own or others' continua, with the reasoning that dissects them into one and many, they are not established as true. Similarly, the aggregate of perception and the compositional factors, such as the mental factor of intention that moves the mind toward an object, also do not exist as true. Regarding such a mode, there is not even the slightest thing that is consciousness or established as true. By this, it is shown that the five aggregates, which are the primary objects of the truth of suffering, are the object of observation of the wisdom of heat. The aspect is indicated by the passage, "The abode is not even an atom." This is because it states that there is not even an atom of that which is apprehended as truly abiding. By this, it is shown that the wisdom of heat, which does not conceptually construct true existence, is the aspect.The distinction of the cause is indicated by the two lines, "He does not dwell in all phenomena," and so forth. The meaning is this: when these phenomena, such as the five aggregates, are not examined, they are established merely as conventional designations that are pleasant to experience; however, when they are examined and analyzed, one gains a special, definitive understanding that they are like dreams and illusions, devoid of even an atom of inherent existence. At that time, a bodhisattva who dwells in the stages of the path of preparation of the Great Vehicle, such as the heat stage, does not dwell in all phenomena from form up to the omniscience of the Buddha by way of clinging to them as truly existent, nor does he dwell in any of the extremes of permanence or annihilation. Rather, he practices—that is, he engages in—the perfection of wisdom. In this way, by relying on the perfection of wisdom that realizes emptiness endowed with the supreme of all aspects, without grasping at any conventional phenomena such as form through a meditative equipoise of primordial wisdom that is one-pointedly placed in suchness, and as this wisdom increases and expands further and further, one will attain the unsurpassed, great awakening of the mind-stream of the Sugatas.The object of focus of the peak: The object of focus of the peak is indicated by the single verse beginning with "How." The meaning is this: For example, a wandering ascetic—known as a craftsman or as one who wears a garland—realized through the power of his own wisdom that he could not attain liberation, which is freedom from all the sufferings of cyclic existence, by relying merely on the views of his own tradition that posit the existence of a person (pudgala) or on the meditative absorption of the formless realms that he had attained. Thus, he came before the Teacher, the Buddha, and asked what the path to attaining liberation was. When the Teacher taught the subtle selflessness of the person and phenomena, he developed supreme conviction and trust in it. By relying on the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), which is the path of realizing that there is not even the slightest object of focus of grasping at true existence, he attained nirvana, where the appropriation of the aggregates—which are propelled by karma and defilements—is destroyed, or rather, the continuity of wandering in cyclic existence is severed. Similarly, any bodhisattva who knows that all phenomena, such as form, are devoid of true existence in that way, is sustained by special methods such as great compassion (mahākaruṇā). Consequently, he does not touch the extreme of peace—nirvana without remainder—and instead dwells in the wisdom that realizes the equality of existence and peace as being empty of true existence. This is taught as the object of focus of form and so forth that is free from signs.As for the aspect, this is taught by a single verse beginning with "Also this perfection of wisdom..." The meaning is: This perfection of wisdom, which is the sole path leading to liberation—realizing that all phenomena are simultaneously empty by nature—is what is being taught. When one examines and investigates, asking, "Is it the aggregates such as form, or the substances, or the qualities, or the actions, or the universals, or the particulars, or the combinations? Whose is it? From which of the four extremes does it arise?" one finds that it is none of these, because in ultimate reality there is no arising. By that very logic, one contemplates and investigates all these phenomena, from form up to the knowledge of all modes, as being empty of their own essence. In this way, by relying upon valid reasoning—such as the arguments of being free from one or many, or the diamond slivers—when one sees them as empty by nature, the bodhisattva who is undaunted and fearless regarding the meaning of the abiding nature is close to perfect enlightenment. Thus, it is taught that the distinction of the cause and the seeing of phenomena as lacking inherent nature when analyzed is the aspect.The object of patience: The object of patience is taught by a single verse beginning with "If one does not know..." The meaning is: If, without knowing the meaning that all phenomena such as form are empty of intrinsic nature from the very beginning, one superimposes upon form the notion that it is a form established by its own essence, and similarly, if one acts with the notion of truly clinging to feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness, then one is not only acting upon signs, but even when one is single-pointedly absorbed in emptiness, if one conceptualizes, "This form aggregate is empty by nature," one is still acting upon the mental formations that construct, and the appearance of the five aggregates is not blocked. Thus, even if one meditates in that way, such a bodhisattva is acting upon signs; they have not attained the faith of conviction in the state of nature-less arising, and they are not abiding in the genuine perfection of wisdom. By this, it is taught that one is observing form and so forth, which are characterized by being devoid of essence in ultimate reality. Some hold that this sutra, considering the meaning, implies that the mere emptiness of negation—where the object of negation, true existence, has been negated—is not the ultimate abiding nature, and they hold that it is improper to grasp that "form and so forth are empty of true existence." Such views are not tenable, as they are contradicted by valid reasoning and scripture. In the Great Commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, it is stated: "When it is taught that 'in this way, things do not exist by way of their own essence,' it does not mean that one should not grasp that 'these are empty of true existence'; rather, it means that one should not grasp that 'this emptiness of things of true existence is true.'" Therefore, to hold that this text teaches that even if one grasps that "phenomena are empty," it is not to be accepted, is a great error of speaking without investigation. Both masters explained that the meaning of "viewing emptiness as a position" refers to the fixation on emptiness as a functional entity; this is the grasping of emptiness as truly existent or the grasping of emptiness as existing by way of its own essence—how could it possibly refer to the mere apprehension that things lack intrinsic nature? They further stated that if one misinterprets the meaning of the text in this way, one is disparaging it by saying that ultimate truth is impossible, and even if it were possible, by holding that cultivating certainty about it leads to grasping at signs, one becomes a great obstacle to cultivating the view that correctly determines the genuine meaning. The Heart Sutra also, in response to the question of how to practice the profound perfection of wisdom, states: "One should correctly and thoroughly look upon those five aggregates as being empty by nature." This teaches that one must look upon them as empty by nature. Furthermore, this very sutra states: "When one has analyzed conditioned and unconditioned, white and black phenomena with wisdom, and does not observe even an atom, then, if the world is wise, one goes to the perfection of wisdom." This teaches that if one sees, through the analysis of phenomena by wisdom, that not even an atom is observed, one proceeds to the perfection of wisdom. Although there are many other scriptures and reasonings, I have not elaborated upon them for fear of excessive length.The aspect is taught by the single verse beginning with, "Whatever is not form." The meaning is: one does not apprehend form as form established by its own essence; likewise, one does not apprehend feeling as established by nature, nor does one apprehend perception, the bodhisattva, and so forth as established from their own side. Furthermore, one does not engage or abide in consciousness in a way that apprehends it as established by its own mode of existence or essence. In short, for one who is in meditative equipoise resting in emptiness, the appearance of the five aggregates is blocked, and one practices without abiding in any object through belief in its truth. That practitioner of meditative equipoise does not perceive, "I am practicing emptiness," because they possess a stable wisdom that is free from all grasping at the truth of the three spheres. Having thus taught the aspect, the manner of performing the cause is as follows: one who possesses the intellect that realizes the three—the agent, the action, and the object—as unborn in truth, touches the path of seeing of the Great Vehicle, which is the supreme pacification of distractions and so forth, such as the meditative absorption named "heroic stride," and so forth, thereby completely attaining the classes of realization of the three vehicles. By this, it is taught that realizing what is ultimately without essence as being the essence of form and so forth is the aspect. "Forbearance" means being free from the manifestation of fear regarding the profound phenomena of non-arising.The Object of the Supreme Dharma: The object of the supreme dharma is taught in one verse, beginning with "Which bodhisattva..." The meaning is this: when a bodhisattva is meditating on the perfection of wisdom, which has become the essence of the path of preparation as previously explained, they abide in the meditative concentration of the supreme dharma, the path in which the manifest grasping at the self of phenomena and the self of persons in their own continuum has been pacified. Such a one has been prophesied by the Tathāgatas of the past as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. At that time, for that bodhisattva, there is no arising of the arrogant thought, "I am equipoised in emptiness," or "I have arisen from it," or "I have been prophesied." Why is that? Because they have fully understood the nature of all phenomena as being empty of true existence and equal. By saying this, it is shown that they perceive forms and so forth as being non-different in essence from the special cause through which, when its nature is realized, the Buddha grants a prophecy.The Aspect: This is taught in one verse, beginning with "Practicing in this way..." The meaning is this: if one practices in this way, without any arrogant assumption of truth regarding any phenomenon whatsoever, one is practicing the wisdom of the Sugatas. This is because that bodhisattva fully understands that the very fact that no phenomenon can be practiced in an ultimate sense is the supreme practice of the heirs of the Victorious One. The perfection of wisdom, which is the phenomenon to be practiced, such as the path of preparation; the bodhisattva, who is the practitioner; and the practice itself, which is the application—none of these are apprehended as true. Such practice, which does not apprehend the three spheres, is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. This shows the state without arrogant assumption and also indicates the special nature of the cause. Although there are twelve divisions of the path of preparation—three each for the heat and so forth, being small, medium, and great—and although the differences in their non-apprehending aspects could be correlated with the extensive, intermediate, and other sutras, one should understand that even though they cannot be directly correlated here due to the brevity of the sutra text, they are taught by implication.The distinction of the fruition, the associated, the abandonment, and the realization. Second, regarding the explanation of the distinction of the conceptualizations to be abandoned: there are two, the conceptualization of the apprehended and the conceptualization of the apprehender.Regarding the conceptualization of the apprehended as an obscuration of knowledge, if we divide it primarily, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehended as defiled and the conceptualization of the apprehended as purified. If we divide it by way of branches: regarding the conceptualization of the apprehended as defiled, there are nine types, such as the consciousness of attachment that clings to the ignorance of the afflicted as being truly existent as an object of enjoyment. Regarding the conceptualization of the apprehended as purified, there are nine types, such as the consciousness of attachment that clings to the aggregates of the purified as being truly existent as an object of enjoyment. Concerning these two types of conceptualization of the apprehended, the single verse beginning with "Whatever is not existent" indicates the object of the conceptualization of the apprehended as defiled, by way of the opposite of what is taught by the literal meaning of the object of the conceptualization of the apprehended as purified, which is the ignorance that is confused about the state of the two truths. Furthermore, any apprehended object of the defiled or purified, when analyzed by reasoning such as the refutation of production from the four extremes, is not truly existent because it cannot withstand such analysis; it is said to be without inherent existence because it is established by scripture and reasoning. Ordinary beings, having examined these phenomena correctly, posit them as existing only conventionally and not existing ultimately; yet these two—existing conventionally and not existing ultimately—are also phenomena that do not exist truly, for they are merely posited by the power of understanding both, and cannot withstand analysis by reasoning. Therefore, if a Bodhisattva knows that, just as a magical pebble appears as a chariot or an ox, yet the two—the appearance and the emptiness of it—are not contradictory, so too the two—that phenomena exist conventionally and do not exist ultimately—are not contradictory, and furthermore, that they proceed as one assisting the other, then they will certainly emerge from the extremes of existence and peace, and will attain non-abiding nirvana. Thus it is said.The second type of cognitive obscuration, the conceptualization of grasping, is divided fundamentally into two: the conceptualization of grasping at substantial existence and the conceptualization of grasping at nominal existence. When divided by way of their branches, there are nine types of conceptualization of grasping at substantial existence, such as grasping at the enjoyment of objects by focusing on the grasping of a self that is independent. Likewise, there are nine types of conceptualization of grasping at nominal existence, such as grasping at the enjoyment of objects by focusing on the grasping of a person as nominally existent. These two types of conceptualization are taught in a single verse, beginning with the words, "In this context, the five aggregates..." In that regard, the first of the nine objects of focus—the grasping at an "I" that is nominally imputed upon the five aggregates—is taught by the explicit words, and from the opposite perspective, the self that does not depend upon the aggregates is taught as the object of focus for the grasping at substantial existence.In this context of training on the path, one understands that all phenomena, such as the five aggregates, are like illusions—appearing yet lacking true existence. Furthermore, one does not make a distinction between the true and the untrue by positing that the illusion is false while the aggregates are truly existent; rather, one understands the five aggregates themselves to be like illusions, dreams, and mirages. By being free from the consciousness of various conceptualizations and by practicing in a state where all elaborations are pacified, one engages in the supreme perfection of wisdom. In this context, being free from the conceptualization of subject and object does not mean that the seeds have been abandoned, but rather that one is free from their manifestation.The third point, demonstrating the distinction of the spiritual friend who is a mentor, is taught in one verse beginning with "Possessing a virtuous friend." Regarding this, there are two types of mentors: external and internal. The external mentor, being skilled in means, teaches that "there are such faults of Māra and such actions," and acts to turn one away from them. Then, in accordance with the capacity of the trainee's mind, they gradually lead them along the paths of the small and intermediate persons—such as [contemplating] impermanence and suffering—and when the continuum is well-ripened, they act as a mentor by way of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom, such as emptiness. The internal mentor, possessing the special union of method and wisdom, acts to restrain one from the two [faults of] engaging in the lesser vehicle and clinging to true existence.The meaning of the words is as follows: Bodhisattvas possess virtuous spiritual friends who lead them onto the path of virtue by teaching them, in a complete manner, the profound reality of emptiness and the methods and wisdom such as the generation of bodhicitta, dedication, and aspiration. Furthermore, they possess both external and internal mentors—the latter being the insight (vipaśyanā) and so forth that constitutes the wisdom realizing emptiness, which is seized by special methods. Through this, having heard the perfection of wisdom, which is the mother that gives birth to the victorious ones, they do not become afraid, they never change, they realize the meaning of reality, and they do not decline from the Great Vehicle. Having thus demonstrated the distinction of the mentor by way of the direct approach, it is also taught by way of the reverse approach: any beginner who lacks faith in the Great Vehicle, who possesses a sinful friend who turns them away from it, and who is separated from the internal mentor that realizes the meaning of the perfection of wisdom through one's own power, is one who relies on others. This is like an unbaked clay pot that disintegrates when touched by water; just as pouring water into a pot that has not been fired in a kiln causes it to dissolve and the pot to be destroyed, this person, too, because they are afraid of emptiness, abandons the perfection of wisdom, and just as the pot is destroyed, all their previously existing practice and conduct are destroyed.Mahāyāna Practice. Fourth, the naturally abiding disposition (prakṛtistha-gotra) that serves as the support for Mahāyāna practice. The Ornament states: "Realization is the six dharmas, and so on, called the disposition." Regarding this, there are three sections: definition, classification, and scope. As for the first, the definition of the naturally abiding disposition is: that which is the nature of the mind (cittatā) accompanied by adventitious stains, which serves as one's own support, and which is capable of being transformed into the Svābhāvikakāya. It is also the nature of the mind in the continuum of a bodhisattva, and it is a common locus that is also the actual basis of support for Mahāyāna practice. Regarding the classification of the disposition by way of the disposition expressed by name, there are two: the naturally abiding disposition and the developmental disposition (samudānīta-gotra). Regarding the classification of the naturally abiding disposition that serves as the support for Mahāyāna practice, there are thirteen: the six dharmas of realization, namely the four [levels] beginning with heat (ūṣmagata) and the two [paths of] seeing and meditation; the practice of the antidote; the practice of abandonment; the practice of focusing on those things to be abandoned; the practice accompanied by wisdom and compassion; the practice that is uncommon to the śrāvaka disciples and others; the practice of performing the benefit of others in sequence; and the naturally abiding disposition that serves as the support for the practice of engaging in wisdom without exertion. As for the scope, it exists from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum (dharmadhātu-viśuddhi).Although the extensive sutras teach the thirteen individually, here, because the words are condensed, they indicate the naturally abiding lineage in a general way, as shown by the two lines beginning with "Why is this...?" Furthermore, if one asks why this person is designated as a "bodhisattva," the answer is that if the mind were established as truly existent, it would not provide the space for qualities to arise, and thus the name "bodhisattva" would not be obtained. However, because the naturally luminous nature of the mind—the basis from which all Buddha-qualities arise—is capable of having faults removed and capable of having qualities arise, through the wisdom of hearing, thinking, and meditating that realizes the suchness of the mind, one cuts through, without remainder, all attachment or grasping at phenomena such as form as being truly existent.
