By completely abandoning and exhausting the conceptual thoughts, along with their seeds, that are attached to all knowable phenomena as being truly existent, and by eventually attaining great enlightenment, one obtains the name "bodhisattva." For example, just as space provides the space for other things that have form, and the stages of the sun gradually rising in space obtain names such as "morning" and "forenoon," so too is this the case. The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "Impure, impure-pure, and thoroughly pure, in sequence, are called sentient being, bodhisattva, and Tathāgata." Thus, the name "sentient being" is applied to the stage of being impure due to stains, "bodhisattva" to the stage of being partially pure, and "Tathāgata" to the stage of being entirely pure. Here too, one should understand that the thirteen bodhisattvas designated for the various stages of practice are all designated based on the stages where the stains of that naturally abiding lineage—the suchness of the mind which acts as the basis or the space for the arising of qualities—are gradually purified and where qualities progressively increase.The Objects of Observation for the Practice of the Great Vehicle. Fifth, regarding the objects of observation for the practice of the Great Vehicle, the Ornament states: "The objects of observation are all phenomena," up to, "are not common to the Sage."Regarding this, there are two parts: the definition and the classification. For the first: the basis for cutting through superimpositions regarding the practice of the Great Vehicle is the definition of the object of observation for the practice of the Great Vehicle.Regarding the second, when classifying this, there are three: virtuous, non-virtuous, and neutral. There are the aggregates of worldly beings, the meditative concentrations of the continuum of the noble ones who have transcended the world, the contaminated aggregates of grasping, the uncontaminated [phenomena] such as mindfulness, the truth of the path which is conditioned, the truth of cessation which is unconditioned, the meditative concentrations which are qualities common to the three vehicles, and the eleven [qualities] which are uncommon, namely the ten powers. Although all phenomena are objects of observation for the practice of the Great Vehicle, one must primarily focus on the ultimate object of observation, the path of perfect purity. This is because if one meditates by focusing on the mind as empty of true existence, results such as seeing the cessation within oneself—like clouds vanishing into the sky or bubbles dissolving into water—the exhaustion of stains into the expanse of reality, and the establishment of the truth of cessation as the ultimate truth will come about, and because the essential point is the same. If one asks how there is no fault of redundancy with the treatises that teach the lineage when emptiness is directly taught here as the primary [subject], Gungthang Jamyang stated: "Because it is explained that the lineage is the primary nature and the object of observation is the primary manifestation, in the context of the lineage, emptiness of true existence is stated as the basis and all other things are established as its attributes, expressed in the manner of a property-possessor; whereas in the context of the object of observation, all phenomena are stated as the basis and the lack of true existence is expressed as if it were an attribute, so there is no fault."To indicate the object of practice after having indicated the lineage, he speaks the two lines beginning with "of the Victors." The meaning is: by realizing and familiarizing oneself with all phenomena as empty of true existence, one abandons the grasping at true existence along with its seeds, and thereby attains contact with the great enlightenment of the Victors, which is free from the attachment of clinging to reality; therefore, this person is given the name "bodhisattva." Since the two bodies are indicated here as the result, it is established that at the time of the cause, one focuses on both the "as it is" and the "as many as there are," and thus it is established that the object of practice is all phenomena.The purpose of practicing the Great Vehicle. Sixth, regarding the purpose of practicing the Great Vehicle, it is stated in the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* (rgyun las): "The mind that is supreme among all sentient beings," up to, "these are to be known here."Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the classification, and the scope. The first is: the ultimate result for the sake of which one engages in practice is the definition of the purpose of practicing the Great Vehicle. Regarding the classification, there are three: the great bodhisattva, the great abandonment, and the great realization. The scope exists only in the Buddha. The meaning of the three types of such great purposes is indicated by the single verse beginning with "Why is that?" If one asks, "Why is that person given the name 'great bodhisattva'?" it is because they have become the protector and ally of the great assembly of sentient beings and their many gatherings, and thus have become supreme; because they have become great, they are a "great mind." Furthermore, because sentient beings have different realms and inclinations, they rely on the forty-eight views based on the past, the fourteen views based on the future—making sixty-two wrong views—as well as the three hundred wrong views and so forth; these infinite wrong views are difficult to destroy and numerous because they have been familiarized with since beginningless time, and thus they are "great." Because one teaches the doctrine of emptiness and so forth to sever their continuity, one is "eliminating," and since one must first abandon them oneself, this is "great abandonment." Having directly indicated these two, and because when one is free from obscurations, one realizes all phenomena just as one sees forms, the obscurations that hinder realization are indicated as abandoned; thus, the "great realization" of the omniscient primordial wisdom that realizes them is also understood by implication. Therefore, because one engages in the practice of the path for the sake of attaining the result of the three bodies, one is explicitly called a "great bodhisattva."Armor Practice. The seventh is armor practice. The *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* states: "From 'Those, each giving, and so forth' up to 'explained according to the six.'" This is the bodhisattva’s yoga, which possesses the six greatnesses and accomplishes the two benefits in perfection, based on the generation of the Mahāyāna mind. It is the definition of Mahāyāna practice. When divided, for example, it is like donning armor for battle, entering the battlefield, having the allies and weapons to defeat the enemy, and defeating the enemy; there are four: armor practice, engagement practice, accumulation practice, and the practice of definite emergence. Regarding the first, armor practice, there are three aspects: definition, division, and scope. The first is the bodhisattva’s yoga, which is seized by a vast intention to practice by condensing all six perfections within each individual perfection. This is the definition of armor practice; it is synonymous with the bodhisattva’s wisdom. Second, regarding its division, there are six, from the armor practice of generosity to the armor practice of wisdom. When divided in detail, there are thirty-six, six for each, such as generosity. Third, regarding its scope, it exists from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum. This armor practice is indicated by the two lines, "Great giving, and so forth." The meaning is that, not only what has just been explained, but because one has donned great armor, one is called a great bodhisattva. What is that armor? As stated in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*: "With the intention to give all that one possesses, along with the results, to all beings..." Thus, giving away one’s body, enjoyments, and all roots of virtue of the three times is the armor practice of generosity, which possesses great giving. The armor practice of ethical discipline is that of a bodhisattva or one of lesser intellect who abandons corrupt conduct, such as the discipline of restraining from non-virtue, the discipline of gathering virtue, and the discipline of benefiting sentient beings. The "great power" refers to the latter four perfections. Even when it is difficult to bear, one is not overcome by those who do harm in return for help or who repay kindness with ingratitude; this is the armor practice of patience. One has no weariness or fatigue in the difficult conduct of the heirs of the Victorious One, such as giving away limbs; this is the armor practice of perseverance. One has one-pointed meditative concentration that is not mixed with the mental engagement of the lesser vehicle; this is the armor practice of meditative concentration. One realizes that the three—the agent, the action, and the object—are devoid of truth; this is the armor practice of wisdom. These possess great power to overcome their respective opposing forces. Because one is engaged in practicing the path and its fruit, from the generation of the mind for the supreme Mahāyāna of the Victorious Ones up to omniscience, one has donned great armor. Although Buddhajñāna applies this final line to engagement practice, the Master applies it to armor practice.The eighth, the practice of engagement: regarding the practice of engagement, the Ornament states: "Meditative concentrations, formless [absorptions], giving, and so forth, up to... should be known." Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the classification, and the boundaries. The first: the definition of the practice of engagement is the yoga of a bodhisattva seized by the wisdom of engagement, which is the practice of taking up the various causes and effects of the Great Vehicle, with the peak practice as the primary focus. The second: when classified, there are nine: the practice of engagement in the bodhisattva’s meditative concentrations and formless absorptions; that of engagement in the perfections; that of engagement in the noble paths; that of engagement in the four immeasurables; that of engagement in non-conceptualization; that of engagement in the complete purity of the three spheres; that of engagement in the purpose to be achieved; that of engagement in the superknowledges; and the practice of engagement in the omniscience of all aspects. The third: the boundaries are from the heat level of the path of preparation up to the end of the continuum. Although the specific details are taught individually in the Hundred Thousand [Verse Perfection of Wisdom] and other texts, because the words are condensed here to show only the general nature of the practice of engagement, the meaning of the two lines stating "having donned the great armor, and so forth" is: in order to practice the entire, limitless, sky-like path of the Great Vehicle, such as the six perfections, one dons the great armor of an irreversible intention of courage, and strives to eliminate the wrong views and sufferings of sentient beings dwelling in the ten directions of the world-realms, and to subdue all the deceptive arts of the māras who are sons of the gods; for that reason, one is highly termed a "bodhisattva mahāsattva." Thus, having generally indicated the practice of engagement, the specific details are implied.The Practice of Accumulation. Ninth, regarding the practice of accumulation: The *Ornament* states, "From love and generosity, the six... up to... should be known." This passage addresses its definition, its divisions, and its three boundaries. First, the definition of a bodhisattva’s yoga of the practice of accumulation is: a practice that, by being seized by the vast two accumulations, is superior to the intermediate level of the Mahayana path of preparation’s "supreme dharma" and which produces its own result, great enlightenment. Second, regarding its divisions, there are seventeen: the accumulation of great compassion, the accumulation of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, the accumulation of calm abiding, the accumulation of superior insight, the accumulation of their union, the accumulation of skillful means, the accumulation of primordial wisdom, the accumulation of merit, the accumulation of the path, the accumulation of dhāraṇī, the accumulation of the stages, and the accumulation of antidotes. Third, regarding the boundaries, it exists from the great level of the Mahayana path of preparation’s "supreme dharma" up to the end of the continuum. Furthermore, following the discussion of the practice of armor, in response to the question of how one dons the armor, the first ten accumulations are taught. Following the discussion of the practice of engagement, in response to the questions—what is this Mahayana into which one engages, to what extent has one engaged, from where does one definitively emerge, where will one abide, and what will arise—the first is from skillful means up to dhāraṇī, the second is the accumulation of the stages, the third is the accumulation of the antidotes to what is to be abandoned by seeing, the fourth is the antidote to the first conceptualization to be abandoned by meditation, and the fifth is taught as the antidote to the remaining three to be abandoned by meditation. Here, too, the two verses beginning with "For example, as a magician..." teach the first ten accumulations in response to the question of to what extent the armor has been donned. The first verse teaches the accumulation of great compassion. Then, the single verse ending with "...the supreme armor of the noble ones" teaches the nine accumulations up to the union of calm abiding and superior insight. The three verses from "Why is this..." up to "...is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom" teach the remaining seven accumulations. The meaning of these is as follows: For example, a skilled magician or one trained in magic, at a crossroads or a large public square, manifests a great assembly of people. When he displays the illusion of cutting off the many various heads of the majority of these people, those who are "killed" are merely magical manifestations and lack consciousness; therefore, because they have no fear or suffering, and no sin or the like arises for the one who kills them, in that same way, a bodhisattva also, having thoroughly understood that all these beings tormented by immeasurable suffering are, like an illusion, devoid of any truly established existence, acts for the benefit of beings through great compassion—knowing the conventional way in which it is appropriate to establish all beings without exception in happiness and protect them from suffering—without having even the slightest fear or trepidation. The reason why sentient beings are like magical manifestations is also as follows: what is called a "sentient being" is merely designated in dependence upon these five aggregates, which are the basis of imputation. In reality, form, feeling, perception, mental factors, and consciousness are not bound by the ignorance of grasping at truth, nor are they liberated by any wisdom that realizes the lack of truth, and so forth. The reason for this is that there is no valid cognition that proves these five aggregates exist in an ultimate sense. Having understood it in that way, the lack of any shrinking heart regarding the manner of engaging in the practice of the complete enlightenment—which, although not existing ultimately, exists conventionally—is the supreme armor of the noble individuals, the bodhisattvas.Why is this path named the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva? Because the word "vehicle" also carries the meaning of a "conveyance," it is called a vehicle in the sense of a conveyance because the Great Vehicle—which is comprised of the accumulation of love, generosity, and so forth—is that upon which any person mounts in order to ferry, that is, to cause all sentient beings to be led beyond sorrow. This is because this path causes both oneself and all others to proceed to the level of a buddha. The essence of this Great Vehicle is like space, because it opens a refuge of liberation for immeasurable sentient beings, and it is a great mansion, because it possesses an infinite array of qualities such as retention, eloquence, meditative stabilization, clairvoyance, and miraculous powers. Because those persons who have entered such a path of the Great Vehicle attain, in the interim, joy of mind and physical ease and happiness, and ultimately attain the distinct bliss of non-abiding nirvāṇa, it is called the supreme vehicle or the Great Vehicle. In ultimate reality, there is no person who, having mounted the Great Vehicle, can be observed to be proceeding toward the fruition of the ten stages and so forth.If one asks, "How is it that, relying upon this vehicle, it is taught that one proceeds from cyclic existence to the fruition of nirvāṇa?" it is not that one proceeds from a truly established cyclic existence to a truly established nirvāṇa. Rather, because when one searches for both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa through reasoning, one does not observe any proceeding to nirvāṇa, one must posit the attainment of nirvāṇa merely in terms of the exhaustion of cyclic existence. For example, just as the term "extinguished" is applied to the mere aspect of a fire ceasing when its fuel is exhausted—there being no fire that goes anywhere else—in the same way, because of the cause of the exhaustion of birth in cyclic existence due to karma and afflictions, it is well-stated that such a person has attained nirvāṇa, that is, liberation.The bodhisattva who practices the path does not apprehend a prior limit—the stage of an ordinary being in the past—nor a later limit—the stage of a Buddha in the future—nor the present stage of a noble one, because they have not arisen from their own side, nor will they arise later. Therefore, because the three times are devoid of being one or many that are truly established, they are pure by nature, and cannot be differentiated by any time.That which is called a "bodhisattva" is unconditioned because it is not found when analyzed by reasoning; because it is empty by nature, for that very reason there is no conceptual elaboration of attachment to the truth of form and so forth. Knowing that there is not even the slightest focus of grasping at truth in this way is what is called practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom.The Practice of Definite Emergence. The tenth, the practice of definite emergence, is stated in the Ornament as: "The objective, equality, and so forth... are called the practice of definite emergence." Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries. The first: the yoga of the pure bhūmis that unfailingly leads to the omniscient state is the definition of the practice of definite emergence. The second, its divisions: there are eight, namely, the practice of definite emergence for the sake of the three great objectives, that of equality, that of the benefit of sentient beings, that of spontaneous presence, that of transcending the extremes, that of definite emergence into the omniscient state, and the practice of definite emergence that has the path as its object. The third, the boundaries: they exist in the three pure bhūmis. Gungthang Jamyang stated that the extensive sutras explain these eight through the perspective of the basis of the quality and the quality of emptiness, and that this is a definite emergence through non-apprehension itself, in order to understand that one must practice through the perspective of non-apprehension at the beginning, middle, and end. Although Buddhashrī connects the practice of definite emergence starting from the words "whoever rides," according to our own tradition's master, the meaning taught by the five verses beginning with "the wise bodhisattva" is that when a bodhisattva who is skilled in the manner of positing conventionalities and who practices the conduct of the children of the Victorious One—such as the practice of definite emergence for the sake of the reality of suchness—analyzes with reasoning such as the refutation of production from the four extremes, they contemplate the meaning of being unborn by nature, and having realized the meaning of the unborn, they act and abide in this way.The meaning of the phrase "at the time of" (dus kyi tshe), as stated, is to refute the view held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others that time is permanent. For example, in the world, when one says, "At the time of such-and-such a previous event," one understands that the present has changed from that previous state. Thus, the phrase "at the time of" signifies that time is changing, and thereby it is able to refute the permanence of time, as stated in the *Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom*.How, then, does this exist? Even if one generates great compassion—the love that desires all beings to be free from suffering—if one is attached to the reality of a "self" and "sentient beings," then this lack of the perception of sentient beings is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the essence of the definitive departure for the sake of all purposes.If one asks what fault arises from perceiving sentient beings: if one generates the perception that oneself and sentient beings truly exist, and likewise generates the perception that suffering also truly exists, then one practices the perfections, such as generosity, with difficulty. Thinking, "I shall work for the benefit of sentient beings and eliminate their suffering," the bodhisattva who, through attachment to the reality of a "self" and "sentient beings," thoroughly conceives of them as truly existent, is bound by the mental continuum of grasping at truth. Therefore, from that fault of grasping at "self" and "other," all faults, such as attachment and aversion, arise. As the Lord of Logic said:If there is a self, there is the perception of an other.From the division of self and other, attachment and aversion arise.From being thoroughly entangled with these,All faults come to be.Therefore, practicing in this way is not the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.If one asks, "How, then, should one practice?" it is reasonable to work for the benefit of others and liberate them from suffering because sentient beings and suffering do not exist truly. Regarding that lack of true existence, among the two—phenomena and persons—and among the two—self and others—if one first looks at how this appears to one's own mind, it is easy to identify the object of negation. By virtue of that, it is also easy to ascertain emptiness, the negation of existence that negates that object of negation. Therefore, a bodhisattva should first know that they themselves lack intrinsic nature. Then, just as one is not established by intrinsic nature, one should know that all sentient beings are also not established by intrinsic nature. Just as all sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one should know that all phenomena, such as the generation of bodhicitta, lack intrinsic nature. Having realized that, one understands the union of the two truths, where the essence is inseparable, by not conceptualizing true existence in either the ultimate, which is unborn, or the conventional, which has birth. By knowing the state of the two truths as they are and abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, one is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom, the supreme path of definitive emergence.If one asks what is to be attained by that non-conceptual primordial wisdom, it is the Buddha’s mind—the non-conceptual primordial wisdom that abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, having abandoned the extremes of arising and truly passing away or ceasing, in an ultimate sense, regarding all phenomena, such as the ten phenomena including the generation of bodhicitta, or all phenomena from form up to the omniscience, which are all the names of phenomena in the nine worlds that can be expressed. This mind has abandoned all decay and harm without exception, and because there is no decline from it, it is deathless; there is nothing else superior to that supreme primordial wisdom of omniscience. Because it brings about the attainment of that very phenomenon which is supreme and unsurpassed, this path of conceptualizing all phenomena as being ultimately unobservable is the supreme perfection of wisdom, the path of definitive emergence that is to be practiced. By the phrase "the supreme deathless primordial wisdom" and so forth, the two aspects of the path of definitive emergence—the abandonment and the realization of one's own benefit—are indicated.Any bodhisattva who, having gained certainty through valid cognition regarding the stages of the path of definitive emergence and so forth, practices and experiences them as previously taught without doubt or hesitation, is said to be endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom seized by skillful means; such a person should be known as one who abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, both in cyclic existence and in peace.To have fully realized that the phenomena of the basis, path, and result are devoid of intrinsic nature, equal in being empty of true existence, and of a single taste, is to practice the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of accomplishing definitive emergence. This is what is meant. Because this text summarizes all the meanings of the hundred-thousand-line scripture, it would have been appropriate to arrange the chapters in accordance with that, but because those of lesser intellect would not understand it, it was not so arranged; likewise, it was not done in accordance with the twenty-thousand-line scripture either. It is stated in the difficult-points commentary that the chapters were arranged in accordance with the eight-thousand-line scripture so that it might be easily understood and known to have a single meaning. Having thus finished explaining the ten phenomena that characterize omniscience, the indication of the chapter titles and the conclusion of the section in connection with the Abhisamayālaṅkāra is as follows: from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, a Profound Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities, Clarifying the Reality of Dependent Arising*, this is the first chapter, on entering into omniscience, and the commentary on the first section.Knowledge of the path: Since one must train in the knowledge of the path—the uncommon cause of omniscience—in order to attain that omniscience, the second section explains the knowledge of the path. As stated in the *Ornament*: "From 'making dim' and so forth, up to 'the knowledge of the path itself is explained in that way,'" the wisdom of an arya bodhisattva, which is possessed of the realization of emptiness directly within the continuum of a person who possesses their own continuum, is the definition of the knowledge of the path. There are eleven phenomena that characterize the knowledge of the path: the knowledge of the path of the path-knowledge limbs, the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the śrāvakas, the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the pratyekabuddhas, the path of seeing of the Mahāyāna, the function of the path of meditation, the path of meditation of aspiration, the three of praise, honor, and exaltation as its benefits, the path of meditation of dedication, the path of meditation of rejoicing, the path of meditation of accomplishment, and the path of meditation of utter purity.To reveal the first limb of the knowledge of the path, from "in order to make the gods favorable" up to "its activity is known," it is said. Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the classification, and the boundaries.The definition: As for the first, that special quality which is conjoined with great compassion, and which is included within any one of the three—the cause, the essence, or the result of the knowledge of the path—is the definition of the limb of the knowledge of the path.The classification: As for the second, when classifying it, there are five: the support, which is free from manifest pride; the material cause, which is the generation of the mind of enlightenment; the pervasion by the cause, which is the lineage; the nature, which is not abandoning cyclic existence; and the function, which is the gathering of others into one's circle and so forth.The boundaries: As for the third, the boundaries, it exists from the time of not having entered the path up to the stage of a Buddha. That limb of the knowledge of the path is taught by one verse, beginning with "Whoever, in form..." According to the *Sampuṭa-ṭīkā* of the Buddha’s feet, it appears correct to apply this to the "congruent with definite discrimination" which is the cause of the knowledge of the path; however, here, the *Sampuṭa-ṭīkā* of the Master is primarily taken as the basis. The meaning of its words is: a bodhisattva does not abide in the form aggregate in the manner of being fixated on it as truly existent, and likewise does not abide in feeling; and one who does not abide because of being fixated on perception as truly existent, and likewise does not abide in volitional factors, and does not abide in consciousness, or in any object whatsoever by way of being fixated on it as truly existent—to realize those directly as empty of truth and free from proliferation, and to remain in meditative equipoise upon that, is to abide in their suchness, which is the reality of those things. Such a state is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the knowledge of the path.Regarding the manner in which this teaches the limb of the knowledge of the path, although the *Difficult Commentary* provides no more clarity than simply stating "abiding, there are five types," when looking at the flow of the discourse, it shows that by abiding in the suchness of the five aggregates, practicing the perfection of wisdom, and attaining qualities, one should not be satisfied or arrogant, but must train in the higher paths; thus, it teaches that one is free from the obstacles of the basis. Because the term "abiding" (gnas te) indicates through the power of its words that one must not be satisfied merely with abiding in the aspect of wisdom, but must also add the aspect of method upon that, it teaches that the knowledge of the path arises only for one who practices a complete union of method and wisdom, and not for others; thus, it teaches the certainty of each respective stage. Furthermore, while "abiding" can also refer to meditating by taking suchness as the object of apprehension, the *Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom* states that it is done by taking the naturally abiding lineage as the basis, which is pervaded by the causal lineage, and that it teaches both the nature and the functions.The Knowledge of the Path of the Śrāvakas. Second, regarding the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the Śrāvakas, there are two: its actual essence and its cause, the aids to penetration.The actual essence. Regarding the first, the *Ornament* states: "Regarding the manner of the knowledge of the path itself... one should know this path of the Śrāvakas," and so forth. Concerning this, there are three parts: its definition, its divisions, and its levels.The definition. Regarding the first: the knowledge of an Ārya of the Mahāyāna that abides in the category of clear realization to be known for the sake of guiding those to be tamed who are of the Śrāvaka lineage, by way of being seized by the three—the generation of bodhicitta, dedication, and the wisdom realizing emptiness—is the definition of the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the Śrāvakas.Divisions. Second, regarding its divisions, there are sixteen by way of aspects, and three by way of the path, which are the path of seeing, the path of meditation, and the path of no-more-learning that have become that.Levels. The third is from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the level of a Buddha. This is taught in a single verse, "Permanent and impermanent," and so forth. Although the *Extensive Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom* suggests that "permanent, impermanent, pleasant, painful," and so forth, teach the aspects of the first two truths, and "attaining the fruit, the level of an Arhat," and so forth, teach the aspects of the path of cessation, when examining the *Commentary on the Summary* by the Master, I wonder if the passage from "permanent and impermanent" up to "selfless" teaches the aspects of the truth of suffering, and "thusness" and "thus empty" teach the aspects of the latter three truths; those possessed of analytical intelligence should examine this in detail.The meaning of the words is as follows: regarding phenomena such as form, one does not abide by way of clinging to them as truly existent, such as: the permanence that is non-decaying; the impermanence that is the opposite of that; the pleasure that has the aspect of soothing sensation; the suffering that is associated with contamination; the pleasantness that is agreeable to the mind; the unpleasantness that is disagreeable; the existence of a self of the person that has become its own essence; the selflessness; and thusness—that is, existing in the ultimate sense—and emptiness, meaning that although they appear to be true, they are empty because they are established in that way or as such. Furthermore, one does not abide through clinging to the attainment of the three fruits—Stream-enterer, Once-returner, and Non-returner—nor to the level of a Śrāvaka Arhat, nor to the level of a Pratyekabuddha, and likewise, one does not abide through clinging to the level of a Buddha. In short, one does not abide by way of truly clinging to any phenomenon included within the three—the basis, the path, and the fruit—as being this or that.This means that the path of the Śrāvaka, which realizes the sixteen aspects such as impermanence directly, is a path to be known by Bodhisattvas, but they do not practice it by way of seeking the enlightenment of the Lesser Vehicle. Rather, it is shown that they perform the three—generation, knowledge, and perfection—for the sake of guiding those of the Śrāvaka lineage, by way of uniting method and wisdom, such as the generation of bodhicitta, dedication, and the wisdom realizing emptiness.The causes of that, the factors of definite discrimination. Second, in order to demonstrate the causes of that, the factors of definite discrimination, one verse is spoken, beginning with "Just as the Guide..." The meaning is as follows: Regarding the analogy of not abiding in any phenomenon whatsoever, just as the mind of the Guide, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is the unconditioned realm—meaning it does not abide in the expanse of nirvana, which is peaceful merely by the measure of the cessation of birth in existence—likewise, it does not abide in the side of the conditioned, the three realms of cyclic existence, through grasping at truth. A bodhisattva practices without abiding in any extreme of existence or peace. In that way, having realized that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, even though they abide on the path of the factors of definite discrimination and so forth, they abide without grasping at them as true. This is to abide in the very reality of the free-from-elaboration, without abiding in any phenomenon whatsoever in a definitive sense. It is said that this manner of abiding is the abiding in the perfection of wisdom, which is the essence of the meaning, as taught by the Victor, the King of Dharma. Thus it is said.The knowledge of the path of the Solitary Realizer. Third, regarding the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the Solitary Realizer, the Ornament states: "Because of realizing the self-arisen nature, up to, one should know the perfect collection." Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the levels.The definition. The first is: the wisdom of a Mahayana noble that abides in the category of realizations to be known for the sake of guiding disciples of the Solitary Realizer lineage by way of being seized by three excellences, which is the definition of the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the Solitary Realizer.The divisions. Second, when divided, there are three: the paths of seeing, meditation, and no-more-learning.The levels. Third, regarding the levels, it exists from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the level of buddhahood. Here, in teaching the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the Solitary Realizer, there are two: the direct and the incidental.The direct. First, it is taught by a single verse, "Those who wish to become..." and so forth. This is to clarify the doubt that, since the two—the Hearer and the Solitary Realizer—are similar in that they both seek liberation for their own sake alone, it is not appropriate to teach the path of the Solitary Realizer separately from the Hearer. For the time being, if one teaches that the Solitary Realizer is superior to the Hearer, one can infer the system of their vehicles; thus, the difference between the two is as follows: Hearers, at the time of their final existence, possess two distinct qualities: they attain their own awakening after listening to instructions from others, and after attaining the result, they teach the Dharma to others by means of sound. Solitary Realizers, at the time of their final existence, are called "self-arisen" because they actualize awakening by their own power without relying on the Buddha or others to teach them the Dharma, and they possess the two distinct qualities of being superior by teaching the Dharma to others through the magical display of a body without sound. Having thus stated that they are superior, one must then teach the essence of the path of the Solitary Realizer. Teaching that essence is as follows: as explained previously, since it is impossible to attain any of the three awakenings without realizing that the basis, the path, and all aspects are empty of true existence, one must train in the perfection of wisdom, which is the meaning of the heart. This means that those beings who think, "I shall become a Hearer, a disciple of the Sugata," or those who think, "I shall become a Solitary Realizer," whose primary task is to abandon the conceptualization that grasps at external objects, and likewise those who wish to become a King of Dharma, a Buddha, a Bhagavan—in short, if one wishes to attain any of the three awakenings, one cannot attain any of those results without relying on this path of patience, which is not afraid of the profound reality of emptiness and realizes that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature. It is like not being able to see the landing place for going to the far or near shore of the ocean without relying on a boat. This shows that the knowledge of the path is the object of the path of the three vehicles, but it primarily teaches the abandonment of the conceptualization grasped by the Solitary Realizer. Some hold that Hearers and Solitary Realizers do not realize the subtle selflessness of phenomena, but this directly contradicts this sutra. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* states: "O sons of gods, therefore, whoever wishes to attain the result of a Stream-Enterer and wishes to abide in the result of a Stream-Enterer will not succeed without relying on this patience. Apply this likewise to those who wish to attain the result of a Once-Returner, and those who wish to abide in the result of a Once-Returner, up to those who wish to abide in the Self-Awakening." And the *Vajracchedikā* also says: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Stream-Enterer think, 'I have attained the result of a Stream-Enterer'?" Subhūti replied, "No, Bhagavan. Why? Because, Bhagavan, he has not entered into anything; therefore, he is called a Stream-Enterer." And the *Ārya-Rāṣṭrapāla-paripṛcchā-sūtra* says: "Those who do not know the way of emptiness, peace, and non-arising wander in the world; those who possess compassion lead them through a hundred methods and means." This and many other definitive-meaning sutras state that realizing emptiness is necessary for liberation from cyclic existence, and it is outside the system of Ārya Nāgārjuna, Candrakīrti, and others. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Liberation comes from the exhaustion of karma and defilements. Karma and defilements come from conceptualization. These come from mental fabrication. Fabrication is stopped by emptiness." And the glorious Candrakīrti proves through three reasonings and many scriptural citations that Hearers and Solitary Realizers also have the realization that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature. In his own commentary on the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, it is clearly established: "In this system, Hearers and Solitary Realizers also have the knowledge that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature." If it were not so, because they lack the complete knowledge that things are without intrinsic nature, just as they are free from worldly desire, they would be surpassed by the Bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening through his own analytical reasoning; and like non-Buddhists, they would not abandon all the subtle propensities that operate in the three realms. Because they focus on the intrinsic nature of form and so forth, they fall into error and do not realize the selflessness of the person, because they focus on the aggregates, which are the basis for the imputation of a self. As stated in the *Ratnāvalī*: "As long as there is grasping at the aggregates, there is grasping at an 'I'. If there is grasping at an 'I', there is karma, and from that, there is birth. The three paths, without beginning, end, or middle, are like a firebrand in the circle of cyclic existence; because they are mutually causal, this is cyclic existence. Because one does not see them as having two natures or as existing in the three times, the grasping at an 'I' is exhausted. From that, karma and birth also [cease]." This is what was said, and as proof, he cited the *Samādhirāja-sūtra* and others. The difference between the Great and Small Vehicles is not established by way of view, but by way of the Bodhisattva's aspiration, vast conduct, and the difference in dedication. As stated in the *Ratnāvalī*: "In the Hearer vehicle, the Bodhisattva's aspiration, conduct, and dedication are not taught; how could one become a Bodhisattva? The meaning of abiding in the Bodhisattva conduct was not taught in the sutras. It was taught in the Great Vehicle; therefore, the wise should hold to it." However, the way in which there is a difference regarding whether or not emptiness is realized and whether or not emptiness is perfectly meditated upon, through countless variations of reasoning, should be understood by studying the Madhyamaka treatises in detail.Incidental: The second point, which explains that everything from the teaching and listening to the Dharma, up to the attainment of the fruit after practicing, is devoid of true existence and like an illusion, is taught by the three verses beginning with "Teaching the Dharma." The meaning is this: the teacher teaches the Dharma, the student listens correctly, and whatever the Dharma to be taught may be, one reflects correctly upon the meaning of what has been heard. By practicing the path, one attains the four fruits of the śrāvaka, such as the stream-enterer; likewise, one attains the paths of seeing, meditation, and no-more-learning of the pratyekabuddha; likewise, one realizes the enlightenment of the Buddha, the Bhagavat, who is the refuge, protector, and guardian of the three worlds. By the power of practicing the Mahāyāna path—which is endowed with perfect wisdom, skilled in accomplishing one's own and others' benefit, and clear in intellect regarding the methods of the path, thereby uniting method and wisdom—one attains the ultimate fruit, which is non-abiding nirvāṇa. The Tathāgata, the perfectly completed Buddha, has taught that all of these, when examined and analyzed by the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, are devoid of even the slightest true existence and are empty of truth, like an illusion. The Extensive Mother states: "O sons of the gods, you should view listening to the Dharma from me as being like an illusion and a magical creation," and so forth, up to: "If there were any dharma superior to nirvāṇa, I would also view that as being like an illusion." The Eight Thousand Verse [Prajñāpāramitā] also says: "Then those sons of the gods thought, 'What is the nature of listening to the Dharma from the noble Subhūti that we should seek?' Then, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Subhūti knew the conceptualizations of those sons of the gods' minds with his own mind and said to them, 'O sons of the gods, you should view listening to the Dharma from me as being like an illusion and a magical creation,' and so forth, up to: 'O sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion; O sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream,' and so forth, up to: 'The perfectly completed Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream,' and so forth, up to: 'Even nirvāṇa is like an illusion and like a dream; what need is there to speak of other dharmas?'" Who, then, is the person capable of learning this meaning as explained with reverence? Those four types of persons do not fear this profound meaning of the ultimate nature just explained. Who are these four? They are the bodhisattva who is learned in the ultimate truth, the pratyekabuddha who is merely at the stage of gathering practice, the non-returning practitioner of the path of preparation, and the noble arhat who has cleared and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obstructions and has abandoned doubts regarding the profound meaning of the ultimate nature. The fourth is one who, even if a beginner, is fully embraced by a spiritual friend who is capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom without error, due to having performed superior deeds for the Buddhas of the past. Regarding the phrase "bodhisattva learned in the truth" here, one must understand it as referring to a pratyekabuddha in the actual sense, as the basis is explicitly taught as a pratyekabuddha. The explanation in the Eight Thousand Verse [Prajñāpāramitā] and other texts that a pratyekabuddha is called a "bodhisattva" or "son of the Victor" is because they are called "bodhisattva" for attaining enlightenment for their own benefit, and "great being" (mahāsattva) for teaching the Dharma without words, as stated in the extensive explanations of the perfection of wisdom. I wonder if it is acceptable to interpret the explicitly taught "ordinary" as the pratyekabuddha and the "primary" as the bodhisattva, though this requires further investigation.If one asks, "Having thus indicated the basis, is it the case that a bodhisattva trains in the manner of knowing the path of the pratyekabuddhas?"—a bodhisattva is skilled in accomplishing the purposes of those of the three lineages and in practicing the paths of the three vehicles. Having realized all phenomena as empty of true existence and free from conceptual proliferation, they ultimately establish the manner of the single vehicle. Such a person, who engages in the perfection of wisdom—which is the realization of non-conceptualization, seized by special methods such as great compassion—does not train in the stage that brings about the attainment of a śrāvaka arhat for their own sake. Nor do they train in the stage that brings about the attainment of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha who realizes the conditions. Rather, for the sake of attaining the omniscience that lacks nothing in terms of the purposes of the three lineages, they train in accordance with the Dharma from which all buddhas have departed and will depart.Training in the path by way of focusing on omniscience and not apprehending true existence, and not training through focusing on the inferior vehicle or through attachment to true existence—by realizing that both of these are not established as truly existent, and thus not training in any path of focusing on the inferior vehicle or attachment to true existence—this is the authentic path of training in the knowledge of the path, which is the bodhisattva’s path of knowledge. Thus it is said.That knowledge of the path which is the knowledge of the path of the solitary realizer also does not arise without cause or condition, so its cause, the factors of definite emergence, is taught by the single verse beginning with "The increase of form..." The meaning is this: that in which a bodhisattva does not train and which he abandons is not the training for the sake of grasping—by way of attachment to true existence—the increase or the complete loss, that is, the decrease, in an ultimate sense, of all phenomena of the side of defilement, such as form, or of all phenomena of the side of purification, such as the foundations of mindfulness. Because all these phenomena are by nature pure, they are not apprehended in an ultimate sense as increasing, decreasing, arising, or ceasing. Therefore, one does not train through an application that involves grasping or generating in one's own continuum—out of manifest attachment—any of the diverse aspects of the phenomena from form up to omniscience; rather, one trains by way of not apprehending, such as the factors of definite emergence. For the sake of others, one conventionally grasps and attains even omniscience by way of knowing it to be without nature, and by relying on the practice of the path in which method and wisdom are conjoined, one definitely emerges into—that is, attains—that ultimate state of Buddhahood. This is the way in which bodhisattvas who delight in the qualities of the Great Vehicle train in the path.Regarding the phrase "form does not increase or completely diminish," it is said in the *Ornament* that this corresponds to two points: the statement that there is "no increase or decrease," and the statement that "because it is not grasped," one has patience because one does not apprehend it.The Path of Seeing of the Bodhisattva. The fourth, the path of seeing of the bodhisattva, is stated in the *Ornament* as: "Patience toward the truths and the truths, up to the moment of the knowledge of the path." Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries.The definition. First, the definition of the Mahayana path of seeing is: a Mahayana clear realization of the truths, which is seized by the wisdom that directly realizes emptiness within the continuum of a person who possesses that continuum.The divisions. Second, if divided, there are two: the wisdom of meditative equipoise and the wisdom of subsequent attainment. When distinguished by way of their objects and aspects, there are sixteen moments of patience and knowledge.The boundaries. Third, it exists only on the path of seeing. Regarding the explanation of such a Mahayana path of seeing by way of its benefits, there are two: the direct explanation and the incidental meaning.The direct explanation. First, this is indicated by two verses, beginning with "Form is not the perfection of wisdom." The meaning is: what is the nature of the perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of the path of seeing? Form is not one with the perfection of wisdom, which is the subject that realizes its own mode of existence, because they are distinct. There is no perfection of wisdom—the subject of form—that is distinct in essence or exists as distinct in an ultimate sense, because it is not perceived as such. Likewise, the aggregate of consciousness, and the aggregates of perception, feeling, volition, and compositional factors are not one with wisdom, nor do they exist in a manner where the perfection of wisdom—the subject—is distinct in essence, because they are not established as one, distinct, or as object and subject in an ultimate sense. This dharmadhātu, which has become the object of the wisdom of meditative equipoise of the Mahayana path of seeing, is, in the view of that non-conceptual wisdom of meditative equipoise, the suchness of a non-affirming negation that is free from all conventional marks and dualistic conceptual elaborations. It is similar to the designation of the "element of space" (ākāśadhātu) in relation to the mere exclusion of tactile contact, because there is not even an atom of dualistic phenomena such as oneness or distinctness.As it is said, "The perfection of wisdom should be sought in the chapter on Subhūti of the Mother Sutra," and in that regard, "Kausika, the perfection of wisdom should not be sought in form, nor should it be sought apart from form, because those phenomena have a single characteristic, which is the characteristic of having no characteristic," and so forth, as has been taught. This verse specifically singles out and teaches the aspect of the truth of suffering from among the four truths. As for the general teaching on the aspects of the four truths, among the sixteen aspects such as impermanence that are the objects of the Mahayana path of seeing, the nature or essence of the truths of suffering is the dharmadhātu, which is empty of being established as a self of phenomena or a self of persons; it is without beginning or end, and because it is not limited by directions or boundaries, it is infinite. Regarding the nature of the truth of the origin, which is the cause that produces the aggregates and so forth of sentient beings, it is also infinite because of the equality of the dharmadhātu, which is empty of true existence. Just as the "element of space" is posited in relation to the mere exclusion of tactile contact, the nature of the dharmadhātu of the truth of cessation, where obscurations have been exhausted, is likewise infinite.The wisdom that knows the two truths, the worldly conventional truth and the ultimate truth, which is the truth of the path, is also infinite because it is empty of a self, for all phenomena are of one taste in being empty of true existence.Incidental Meaning: The second, the incidental meaning, is this: If one asks why it is asserted that all phenomena are empty of true existence, it is because all phenomena are merely designated by names. Therefore, it is taught that those who are proceeding to the farther shore of perfect view must utterly destroy the perception of clinging to true existence and meditate. The Guide, the Fully Perfect Buddha, has proclaimed and taught that because of perceiving all phenomena as having a self, one remains here in this place of cyclic existence. By destroying the perception of grasping at a self through the wisdom of individual analysis, and by realizing the non-existence of true existence directly, one acts as the direct antidote to all that is to be abandoned by seeing through the path of seeing, and by completely abandoning it through the path of liberation, one proceeds to the farther shore of perfect abandonment.Therefore, those bodhisattvas on the path of seeing who have attained such a view, which is free from all perceptions of grasping at true existence, abide in the Buddha’s word that teaches, for instance, that they will not turn back in this life, will remember their future births, and, having traversed the stages and paths, will attain buddhahood under such and such a name. If one asks, "Since there is the practice of the path and so forth, does that not mean there is inherent existence?"—if the Sugata, the teacher who has become a valid authority, were to proclaim even for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges that sentient beings exist, it would still be the case that, because they have been unborn by nature from the very beginning and are pure, with no defilements having entered their nature, sentient beings could not possibly exist in an ultimate sense or arise by way of their own nature. Therefore, the direct realization of the meaning of being unborn by nature is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom, which constitutes the essence of the path of seeing.The practice of the path of seeing is taught by way of an example, stating that one will attain the prophecy of the Tathāgata. The Victorious Śākyasiṃha, who has conquered the enemy of the four māras, spoke thus: "At the time when I, the teacher Śākyamuni, was speaking in accordance with this supreme perfection of wisdom, which constitutes the essence of the path of seeing, the supreme being of old, Dīpaṃkara, prophesied to me, 'Young Brahmin, in a future time, you will become a buddha.'" Therefore, those to be trained in later generations should also understand that this is taught in meaning as: "Abiding in this perfection of wisdom, you will be prophesied by the buddhas and will attain complete and perfect buddhahood." Thus, one should apply oneself to the practice of the Great Vehicle path with the persistence of a flowing river. This is the commentary on the second chapter, the chapter on Śakra, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent arising.The Path of Meditation. Fifth, in order to teach the function of the path of meditation, it is stated in the *Ornament*: "From 'thoroughly pacifying' and 'all' up to 'enlightenment and being an object of worship'." Regarding this, there are three parts: its definition, its divisions, and its levels.Definition. Regarding the first: the benefit attained through the power of cultivating the Mahayana path of meditation, which serves as the method for attaining one's own [goal], is the definition of the function of the Mahayana path of meditation.Divisions. Regarding the second, if one divides these, there are six: the function of pacifying pride and the like by bringing the mind under control; the function of regarding all sentient beings as spiritual friends and thus being respectful and bowing to them; the function of overcoming the afflictions such as the three poisons; the function of not being oppressed by the harms of humans and non-humans; the function of accomplishing perfect, complete enlightenment; and the function of the place where the bodhisattva who is the support resides becoming a site of prostration and worship for all beings.Levels. Regarding the third: it exists from the first level up to the level of a Buddha. Furthermore, because the aspiration for the goal arises upon seeing the fruit, the function of the path of meditation is taught immediately following the path of seeing, without mentioning the path of meditation itself; this is indicated by a single verse beginning with "Perfection of wisdom..." The meaning is: this perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the path of meditation, is that in which the protectors, the fully awakened Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and all the bodhisattva heirs of the Conqueror, at all times, whether in meditative equipoise or subsequent attainment, engage and abide. Any son or daughter of noble family who, with faith and respect, holds this text in their mind and fully understands all its meanings through the wisdom that is the nature of hearing, reflecting, and meditating, will not be harmed by external poisons, weapons, fire, or water. Not only that, but they will also not be harmed by afflictions such as the poison of reifying true existence, the weapon-like hatred, the fire-like desire, or the water-like ignorance. Even if Māra—such as the powerful Dga'-rab-dbang-phyug who creates obstacles to the path—or the army of Māra, or those who are the black associates of Māra’s faction, seek an opportunity, they will not find one, because of the power of the nature of reality and because the Buddhas and bodhisattvas protect, guard, and conceal them as if they were their own beloved children. Here, the phrase "with respect" indicates the function of bowing to all, and in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, the function of the path of meditation is taught by such statements as "Bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be thoroughly disciplined and free of pride."The path of meditation of firm conviction. Regarding the explanation of the sixth, the path of meditation of firm conviction, there are three parts: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries.The definition. Regarding the first, a Mahayana subsequent clear realization is the definition of a Mahayana path of meditation.The divisions. Regarding the second, when dividing that, there are two: the path of meditation with conceptualization that is contaminated, and the path of meditation without conceptualization that is uncontaminated.The contaminated path of meditation. Regarding the first, there are three: the path of meditation of firm conviction, the path of meditation of dedication, and the path of meditation of rejoicing.The path of meditation of firm conviction. To explain the first of these, the path of meditation of firm conviction, the Ornament states: "Firm conviction of one's own benefit, and so forth," up to "is held to be of twenty-seven types."Definition. The definition of the path of meditation of firm conviction is a Mahayana subsequent clear realization that has conviction in being the source of the three meanings of the Mother.Divisions. When divided, there are three: the path of meditation of firm conviction for one's own benefit, the path of meditation of firm conviction for the benefit of others, and the path of meditation of firm conviction for the benefit of both. Each of these has three—small, medium, and great—making nine, and since each of those is further divided into three, such as the small of the small, there are twenty-seven.Boundaries. The boundaries exist from the first to the tenth bhūmis. The explanation of the three—the path of meditation of firm conviction for one's own benefit, for the benefit of both, and for the benefit of others—is that while there is no difference in terms of the intention to benefit others, they are divided into three from the perspective of the mode of practice in application.The path of meditation of firm conviction for one's own benefit. To explain the first of these, the path of meditation of firm conviction for one's own benefit, it is taught through three verses beginning with "Some, the Sugata..." The meaning is that these paths of meditation are taught by way of their benefits. As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "The Buddha does not pass into parinirvāṇa, and the Dharma does not disappear," and "If the body has no bones or blood, how could there be relics?" In the ultimate sense, the Buddha does not pass into parinirvāṇa, nor does the holy Dharma disappear; until the cycle of existence is emptied, the enlightened activity of his body, speech, and mind occurs without effort and spontaneously, without interruption. Although the wisdom-body lacks relics and the like, one should understand the manner in which he manifests inconceivable, miraculous emanations that pervade space, such as displaying the manner of passing into parinirvāṇa and placing relics in the world in accordance with the receptivity of those to be tamed, being skilled in the means of taming them and possessing an inconceivable power of aspiration. Therefore, if someone were to construct a stūpa of the bodily remains containing the essence of relics of a Sugata who has passed into parinirvāṇa, and if that stūpa were made of the seven precious substances—gold, silver, vaiḍūrya, crystal, copper, red pearls, and the essence of stone—and they were to make offerings to it; and if, not just one, but as many such Sugata stūpas as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were constructed, and with them they filled all the countless and limitless Buddha-fields, and—taking this as an example by way of a complete examination—if all the beings residing in those countless, infinite fields were to do nothing other than trade, agriculture, and the like, and instead, with superior offerings of divine flowers, highly fragrant incense, and marvelous unguents, were to make offerings day and night, at all three times, without attachment, and were to make offerings in that manner for an eon or more than an eon, they would indeed possess immeasurable merit. However, if a being, for the sake of their own perfect benefit, were to generate conviction and write down this text of the Perfection of Wisdom—which completely teaches the means and wisdom, the Mother of the Sugatas, from which arise the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and other supreme qualities of the Guide, the King of Victors—and were to keep it in hand, make offerings to it with flowers and unguents, and pay even a little homage for a short time, then the merit of the former, having constructed such stūpas of the Sugata's bodily remains and making offerings to them, would not even equal a fraction of the merit of the latter, who has written down this sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom and made offerings to it, not even by the count of hundreds of thousands of millions.The reason for this is also because the Sugata and the stupas of his relics arise in dependence upon this Mother, it is said.[Meditation on the meaning of the two, the path of meditation.] To demonstrate the second, the meditation on the meaning of the two, it is taught in four verses beginning with "The Victor's wisdom." The meaning is this: This Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, is a great mantra or an unsurpassed mantra because it pacifies the afflictions in the mental continuum of oneself and all others. Regarding this, in general, a mantra refers to that which is capable of pacifying harm from humans and non-humans merely by being uttered by sages who have attained the truth of speech, and although there are ordinary ones, this perfection of wisdom, as previously explained, is a great and unsurpassed mantra. It is called the "mantra equal to the unequalled" because, by relying upon it, one becomes equal to the unequalled—the Buddha—or because one attains Buddhahood. This is because it pacifies all phenomena belonging to the suffering of the body, such as illness, and mental grief, such as being separated from what is loved, for the immeasurable and manifold realms of sentient beings, and because it causes the attainment of Buddhahood. Those Buddhas who have passed away in the past, and those who currently live and dwell as protectors of the world in the ten directions, have also trained in this mantra equal to the unequalled and have become unsurpassed kings of physicians who dispel the sins, obscurations, suffering, and illnesses of all sentient beings.If the manner in which a Tathāgata is generated is thus, then what is the manner in which a bodhisattva performs their task? All those bodhisattvas who, through engagement with sentient beings, directly accomplish benefit and happiness, and who, with a heart of compassion, practice the conduct of the heirs of the Victorious One—such as generosity—will all, having trained in this great mantra, the perfection of wisdom, and having become skilled, touch upon the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment in the future, that is, they will attain buddhahood. One should understand that all happiness—both the happiness of individuals included within the conditioned cycle of existence and the stainless happiness of the noble lineage that has attained liberation through the abandonment of defilements, which is unconditioned—arises from this perfection of wisdom.What is the analogy for how this becomes the basis for all mundane and supramundane qualities? Just as seeds, such as barley, when planted and remaining intact in the earth, emerge as sprouts and the like once they have encountered the gathering of their respective causes and conditions—such as water, manure, heat, and moisture—and subsequently grow into various forms of fruit, in the same way, all the immeasurable qualities of the five perfections, such as generosity, and the fruit of unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment, arise from this perfection of wisdom.When one is fully seized by the wisdom that realizes the three—the agent, the action, and the object—as devoid of true existence, then generosity and the rest become perfections, and the ultimate fruit, the dharmakāya, is accomplished. For example, just as a universal monarch always travels along a certain path, and other kings also travel along that very path and pay homage, and just as the precious wheel and the rest—the seven precious royal attributes and the fourfold gathering of the army—all travel along without ever separating from him due to the power of his merit, in the same way, wherever in the continuum of a person and in whatever stage of the paths and levels this Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, exists or proceeds, from that very point all the paths comprised of the accumulations of merit and wisdom—such as love, compassion, and the mind of enlightenment—and all the qualities of the Buddha-fruit also proceed and are attained. Therefore, a supreme being who seeks unsurpassed enlightenment should have faith in and aspiration for this Mother, the perfection of wisdom. This is the commentary on the third chapter, which concerns the holding of the immeasurable benefits of the perfection of wisdom and the paying of homage to the stūpa, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.The Path of Meditation on the Intention for the Benefit of Others. The third section, which teaches the path of meditation on the intention for the benefit of others, explains the meaning of the nine verses beginning with "The Victorious One [said to] Śakra." The Blessed One, having conquered the four māras, placed before Śakra, the lord of gods who possesses the splendor of a hundred ordinary gods, all the Buddha-fields as numerous as the grains of sand in the Ganges, filled to the brim and overflowing with the relics of the Victorious Ones. When asked to choose between these and a volume of the Perfection of Wisdom, the reply given to the inquiry was: "If there were Buddha-fields as numerous as the grains of sand in the river Ganges, and all those fields were filled to the brim and overflowing with the relics of the Victorious Ones, I, the lord of gods, would choose this very Perfection of Wisdom written in a volume."Why would one choose the volume of the Perfection of Wisdom? It is not that I, Śakra, lack respect or faith in the relics; I have the utmost respect for them. However, the reason for choosing the Perfection of Wisdom is that such a perfection of wisdom thoroughly encompasses and permeates all paths, and by relying upon it, those very relics of the Victorious One become worthy of being honored and worshipped by all the beings of the world. Just as ministers and others who rely upon a king are themselves honored and receive service from others, the relics of the Buddha, which possess immeasurable qualities, are established as such by relying upon the perfection of wisdom.If one were to think, "Although it came about through the power of the perfection of wisdom, since the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa and is now devoid of such activity, the relics are not worthy of being worshipped," then to establish that they are worthy by way of an analogy: A wish-fulfilling jewel, which is endowed with all qualities such as granting what is desired and is of immeasurable value, is worthy of being honored in whatever container—such as a casket, a box, or a reliquary—it is placed or kept. Even if that jewel is removed from that container, one still feels great joy toward the casket that previously held it, thinking, "This is different from others because it is a container that held a precious jewel," and the fact that the container attained such qualities is due to the power of that precious jewel.In the same way, through the qualities of the supreme precious perfection of wisdom, even though the Victor has passed into parinirvāṇa, the relics—which are like its container—have attained immeasurable qualities, such as being worshipped by others and eliminating the obscurations and misdeeds of sentient beings. Therefore, for that reason, any bodhisattva who rejoices in, aspires to, and wishes to fully grasp the immeasurable qualities of the Victor for the sake of others should write down this perfection of wisdom, and should hold, bind, and take it up; for this is the sole gateway to being liberated from all the bonds and obscurations of grasping at characteristics.If one asks, "Since there are other perfections such as generosity, why is the perfection of wisdom alone made the primary focus and established as the three aspirations?" then, in order to show the reason for that, it is said: Because one must practice generosity by way of grasping it through the wisdom that realizes the non-apprehension of the three spheres—the object to be given, the giver, and the recipient—the phenomenon that precedes the perfection of generosity is wisdom; and likewise, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration must also be preceded by wisdom.Why is it that all virtuous phenomena, such as generosity, when bound by the grasping of characteristics and tainted by the stains of inferior mental engagement, fall into cyclic existence or the extreme of peace and are thus wasted? Because one does not wish for them to be wasted in that way, one dedicates them to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and through the perfection of wisdom—which is the wisdom that realizes non-apprehension—one fully grasps generosity and the rest as the path of the utterly pure perfection of wisdom. Thus, this perfection of wisdom demonstrates the singular method of the path, wherein all virtuous phenomena, such as generosity, are unified as the cause of buddhahood. For example, in the Jambudvīpa, there are thousands of millions of distinct trees, such as sandalwood and agarwood, which possess a great variety of forms, such as diverse colors, shapes, scents, branches, fruits, leaves, and flowers. Yet, regarding their shadows, they are merely designated by the name of being the "shadow of a tree"; the shadows themselves do not possess the diverse colors, scents, and so forth, that the trees have, nor do the shadows exist in and of themselves as the distinct varieties of the individual trees. In the same way, these five perfections of the Victor, such as generosity, also only attain the name of "perfection" and become supramundane perfections when they are grasped by the wisdom that realizes the non-apprehension of the three spheres; and this occurs through the power of this perfection of wisdom.If one dedicates all roots of virtue, such as generosity, for the sake of attaining omniscience, then these six perfections—which are the causes of the fruit of all those roots of virtue, known as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening—will become undifferentiated and of a single taste; once the two bodies, the dharmakāya and rūpakāya, are spontaneously accomplished, enlightened activity will become equal to the expanse of space. This is the commentary on the fourth chapter, which expresses the qualities, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the true nature of dependent origination.Knowing that the abandonment of the faults of artificiality through these three types of conviction is what constitutes familiarization, and in order to abandon that artificiality, the text demonstrates the characteristics of an artificial perfection of wisdom by way of what follows: "If a bodhisattva, while not yet truly understanding the profound meaning of the Mother—the meaning of emptiness—as it is, and while clinging to these five aggregates—namely, form, perception, feeling, volition, and consciousness—as being true, teaches them as being impermanent, suffering, and lacking a personal self, and so on, and speaks of and meditates upon this as the perfection of wisdom, that is a mere semblance of the perfection of wisdom, or an artificial perfection of wisdom." This is because it merely indicates a path that takes the elaborations of conventional grasping as its object of focus. Those learned ones who have realized the meaning of the actual state of things without error will always teach and uphold the meaning of the scriptural teachings of the perfection of wisdom sutras and the like without error; they will never cause the essence of the teachings to degenerate or perish.Having thus shown that the semblance of the perfection of wisdom is to be abandoned, the text explains how to train in the authentic perfection of wisdom by way of the reverse approach: "When one does not apprehend form as being truly existent, and likewise does not apprehend feeling, does not apprehend perception as being truly existent, does not apprehend consciousness, and also does not apprehend volition as being truly existent, but thoroughly understands that all phenomena of cyclic existence and transcendence—characterized by the nature and specific attributes of form and so on, such as impermanence—are empty in the manner of being unborn by nature, and teaches others in that way, this is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom, the authentic perfection of wisdom."The Benefits of the Path of Meditation of Resolute Belief. The seventh, the benefits of the path of meditation of resolute belief, is as stated in the *Ornament*: "Regarding the perfection of wisdom... [up to] ...it is desired that they be venerated and praised." The definition of the benefits of the path of meditation of resolute belief is the qualities attained through the power of meditating on the path of meditation of resolute belief, which serves as the method for attaining one's own goal. When divided, there are twenty-seven. The scope extends from the second moment of meditating on the path of meditation of resolute belief up to the stage of a Buddha. To show that the Buddhas offer praise, veneration, and commendation to a Bodhisattva who has such resolute belief, in order to encourage them as they enter the higher paths, the meaning of the seven verses beginning with "Some, [like the sands] of the Ganges..." is as follows: Compared to a person who establishes or settles as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in the fields of the Buddhas into the state of a Hearer or Solitary Realizer Arhat, the person who writes down this perfection of wisdom and gives that volume to a supreme sentient being, a Bodhisattva, possesses merit that is far more superior.Why is that? Because the former is for the benefit of a portion of sentient beings, whereas the latter becomes the benefit of all sentient beings. Those supreme beings of speech, the Bodhisattvas, having trained in this path, teach here that all phenomena are by nature empty.
