Having heard, realized, and meditated upon that meaning of emptiness, those of the Hearer lineage with dull faculties quickly touch and attain the liberation that is complete release from cyclic existence; those of the Solitary Realizer lineage with medium faculties, having seen that meaning, attain the awakening of a Solitary Realizer; and those of the Great Vehicle lineage with sharp faculties, having realized that all phenomena of cyclic existence and nirvana are equal in being empty of true existence, come to touch the awakening of a Buddha.To illustrate the example of that which does not arise if the cause is absent: just as in the world it is entirely non-existent and impossible for a trunk or a tree to arise without the proximate cause of a sprout, how could branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arise from that which lacks a trunk? They do not arise.In the same way, if the sprout-like bodhicitta—both relative and ultimate, which is the primary meaning taught in the Mother Sutras—is absent, it is entirely non-existent and impossible in the world for a tree-like Victorious One to arise; and if that is absent, how could Indra, Brahmā, Hearers, and the like arise—being comparable to branches, leaves, and so forth, which are the fruits of having practiced the virtues and the path taught by the Buddha’s Dharma—since there would be no cause?Just as when the solar disk rises and at that time spreads an infinite web of light in the ten directions, the sentient beings of the world exert themselves in performing many kinds of karmic activities, in the same way, when I, as a learned one, have generated within my own continuum the relative and ultimate bodhicitta for the sake of attaining the result—the omniscience of the perfection of wisdom—then, in dependence upon that, the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha arises. By that very wisdom acting as the dominant condition, the rays of the profound and vast Dharma are spread to those to be tamed, whereby sentient beings become endowed with the qualities of the Sugatas, both the temporary higher status and the ultimate attainment.To demonstrate through the method of negation that without bodhicitta those results do not exist: for example, if the great Naga Lord in Lake Anavatapta were not to exist, how could the rivers such as the Ganges, which arise through his power, flow here in Jambudvīpa? If there were no rivers, there would be no moisture, and thus flowers such as the padma and utpala, as well as fruits, would not arise. In the great ocean as well, the many diverse forms of jewels that arise from the combination of the touch of water would also cease to exist.In the same way, if in this world realm there were no scriptural teachings and bodhicitta—which is like the Naga Lord and possesses the essence of emptiness and compassion—how could there arise in this world the stream of wisdom that brings about the benefits and happiness originating from the power of the Sugatas and that serves to eliminate the obscurations of negative karma? It would not arise. If there were no such stream of wisdom, there would be no increase in the qualities of the grounds and paths, such as the perfection of generosity; if those were absent, the three fruits of awakening would not exist, and the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha, such as the ten powers, which are like an ocean of abandoned and realized qualities, would also not exist. Therefore, one should know that generating within one’s own continuum the two types of precious bodhicitta—which is the sole root and source of all the qualities of the path and fruit of the Great Vehicle—and exerting oneself in the methods to ensure it does not degenerate but rather increases and expands further and further, is the root of all excellence.For instance, if in this world realm all the various light-emitting creatures—such as stars, lamps, and fireflies that dispel darkness and make forms visible—were to emit their lights all at once to illuminate the directions, the emergence of a single ray from the sun’s orb would be far more excellent and supreme; indeed, the other lights of the various illuminators, such as stars, would not even be able to compare to a mere fraction of the sun’s light. In the same way, śrāvakas and others cannot compare to the qualities of a bodhisattva. Therefore, one should know that the praise and commendation bestowed upon bodhisattvas by the Buddhas is well-founded. This is the commentary on the fifth chapter, the chapter on the enumeration of merit, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.The path of meditation on rejoicing, like the *Śatasāhasrikā* and so forth, is also the path of meditation on dedication in the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra*. Although it is taught in the eighth [chapter], there is no contradiction in meaning, so here the order is reversed and the path of meditation on rejoicing is taught as the eighth. To teach this, a verse appears in the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* beginning with "By means of skill and non-observation..." and ending with "...is stated here." The realization that includes the understanding of the sound and meaning of cultivating joy in the roots of virtue of oneself or others, combined with the Mahāyāna, is the definition of the path of meditation on rejoicing. In terms of division, there are two: the path of meditation on rejoicing in the roots of virtue of oneself, and the path of meditation on rejoicing in the roots of virtue of others. Its scope extends from the first ground to the end of the continuum. Since the increase of the roots of virtue to be dedicated to unsurpassed awakening depends on rejoicing, the path of meditation on rejoicing is taught first. The meaning of the single verse beginning with "The assemblies of śrāvakas..." is as follows: Even if the assemblies of śrāvakas generate a great hundredfold collection of merit, which is fully endowed with roots of virtue arising from giving, morality, and meditation practiced for their own benefit, they cannot compare to even a fraction of a single moment of a bodhisattva’s mind of rejoicing, which is seized by the wisdom that realizes the roots of virtue of all ordinary and noble beings as unobservable, and by the special skillful means of dedicating them to unsurpassed awakening. This is because śrāvakas do not possess such special skillful means and wisdom.The Path of Meditation of Dedication. To explain the ninth, the path of meditation of dedication, the *Ornament* states: "The special thorough dedication, / ... / Is the nature of the arising of great merit." The path of realization that follows the Great Vehicle, which includes the realization that holds the meaning of the words as being compatible with transforming the roots of virtue of oneself or others into a limb of perfect enlightenment, is the definition of the path of meditation of dedication. Regarding its divisions, there are twelve: the path of meditation of special thorough dedication, the path of meditation of dedication characterized by non-apprehension, the path of meditation of dedication characterized by being non-erroneous, the path of meditation of dedication of seclusion, the path of meditation of dedication that recollects the nature of the Buddha’s collection of merit, the path of meditation of dedication of skill in means, the path of meditation of dedication of signlessness, the path of meditation of dedication permitted by the Buddhas, the path of meditation of dedication not included in the three realms, the path of meditation of minor dedication from which great merit arises, the path of meditation of intermediate dedication of great merit, and the path of meditation of great dedication of great merit. The levels range from the first to the tenth. Since the roots of virtue that were previously increased inexhaustibly through rejoicing also depend upon dedication to be transformed into unsurpassable enlightenment, the path of meditation of dedication is taught after the path of rejoicing. To explain this, the meaning of the eight verses beginning with "In the past, in times gone by" is as follows: Regarding the many billions of past Buddhas who appeared in the past, those infinite past Buddhas who resided in thousands of billions of boundless realms, and those protectors of the world who have passed beyond the extremes of existence and peace, who are currently living and dwelling and, in order to exhaust the suffering of beings, are teaching the precious Dharma—from the time they first generated the mind for supreme enlightenment and firmly established it in their own continuum, up until they attained complete and perfect buddhahood and led countless beings to be trained out of cyclic existence, the merit of those victors' initial generation of the mind up until the time their holy Dharma disappeared or was exhausted, the roots of virtue of great magnitude such as the six perfections and the four means of gathering, the results such as the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha that were attained, and furthermore, all the roots of virtue, both contaminated and uncontaminated, of all the Buddha's sons, the bodhisattvas, as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—in short, all individuals, whether learners or non-learners—are to be gathered together by one's own intellect. That bodhisattva should rejoice in them from the depths of their heart with great joy, without jealousy or the like, and having been seized by the wisdom that realizes the mind, the generation of the mind, and the three spheres as non-apprehensible, one should dedicate all those roots of virtue of oneself and others for the sake of attaining unsurpassable great enlightenment as a cause for accomplishing the benefit of beings who are equal to the limits of space.Having thus generally explained the dedication of the Great Vehicle, in order to teach that one must perform the dedication in a special way by means of not apprehending the three spheres, [it is said:] regarding such a dedication, if there arises a perception of truly clinging to or holding as truly existent the thought that "this is the mind that dedicates," and if there arises a perception of true existence regarding enlightenment, which is the object toward which one dedicates, and a perception of true existence regarding sentient beings, who are the objects for whose sake one dedicates, then, because one is bound by the perception or the grasping at signs that fixates on the three spheres—the agent, the action, and the object—as truly existent, one remains in a view that has a focus of grasping at true existence; and because that mind has an apprehension attached to the three spheres through the clinging to true existence, it is not understood as a dedication that is of the nature of being non-erroneous.If one asks, "How then should one dedicate?" if a bodhisattva understands that all these phenomena, such as the virtue to be dedicated and the mind that dedicates, are by nature ceased and that their true existence is exhausted or non-existent; and that the unsurpassable enlightenment, which is the object toward which one dedicates, is also not established as truly existent or is exhausted; and because all phenomena—the object of dedication, the dedicator, and the object toward which one dedicates—are unborn and exhausted by their own nature, and there is not even the slightest thing established from its own side; if one comes to know the way in which, in ultimate reality, the phenomenon or mind that dedicates never dedicates the virtue to be dedicated to any phenomenon that is the object of dedication, or that there is nothing to be dedicated, then being possessed of such a thorough knowledge that the three spheres of dedication are devoid of true existence is what is called a perfect dedication.In this regard, others say: If one defines pure and impure dedication based on the absence or presence of the perception of signs, why is it that in some sūtras, focusing is taught as the primary element? This is taught in order to introduce certain beginners, and it is taught to show that those who are pure, yet bound by intense attachment, are not entirely and perfectly pure. If one dedicates while perceiving and clinging to the three spheres of dedication—the act, the agent, and the object—as signs, that is not a perfect dedication.If, however, one dedicates by perceiving those three phenomena as devoid of the signs of true existence and by thoroughly understanding them as non-existent and like an illusion, that is a perfect dedication to enlightenment. For example, just as eating fine food mixed with poison may appear pleasant for a time but ultimately leads to destruction, the Victor has taught that, in the same way, even though white dharmas are virtuous, focusing on them with a perception that clings to them as truly existent is like eating fine food mixed with poison.Having thus explained the method of dedication in detail, it is taught in order to summarize: since the method of pure and impure dedication has been explained previously, one should learn to dedicate correctly by understanding the faults and virtues in this way. How is this done? The Victors, the perfectly complete Buddhas, have realized and understood without error the rejoicing, the virtues to be dedicated, and the methods of dedication, and so forth. Through their wisdom, they understand what the nature or form of dedication is in conventional terms, what the infallible results that arise from it are and what they are like, and what the characteristics of those phenomena are in terms of ultimate non-conceptualization. Having understood the reality of these as it is, they perform rejoicing and dedication. By thinking, "I too shall perform such rejoicing and dedication in accordance with them," one performs a dedication that, even if one is not personally skilled in the method of dedication, is a perfectly pure dedication because it is performed in accordance with the method of dedication of the Victors. This is as stated in the *Bhadracaryāpraṇidhāna*: "Just as the heroic Mañjuśrī realized..." and so forth. To show the result of such dedication: if one dedicates to great enlightenment by being seized by the wisdom that realizes all one's own and others' merit as non-conceptual, it is a perfectly pure dedication, like fine food without poison. Its result is not abandoning the Buddha, or rather, attaining it, and it is the correct expression of the Great Vehicle teachings spoken by the Victors.That is the meaning of the statement: "The hero, the bodhisattva, who dedicates in such a way that there is no apprehension of true existence, outshines all those bodhisattvas in the world who possess the apprehension of grasping at signs." This concludes the commentary on the sixth chapter, on dedication, from the *Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.Regarding the path of meditation of accomplishment: to demonstrate the path of meditation of accomplishment, the *Ornament* states, "Its supreme essence," through to "the great purpose of establishing." The definition of the path of meditation of accomplishment is: any realization of the Mahayana untainted path that leaves a trace of the ultimate realization that is to be attained by oneself. Regarding its divisions, there are five: the essence of that path of meditation of accomplishment; the supremacy of that path of meditation of accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom; that path of meditation not conceptualizing all phenomena as truly established; that path of meditation establishing all phenomena without apprehension of true existence; and the great purpose of attaining the result of that path of meditation, which is buddhahood. Its scope exists from the first ground up to the tenth. To demonstrate such a path of meditation of accomplishment, the four verses beginning with "Like the blind without a guide" teach what is called the supremacy among the five paths of meditation of accomplishment. For example, even if tens of millions of blind people who lack a guide or leader to lead them on the path gather together, if they neither see nor know the path leading to the city, how could they possibly enter that path and reach the city? That is an impossibility.In the same way, if one lacks this perfection of wisdom—which is like an eye that realizes the nature of reality—then the five perfections, such as generosity, are like the blind; they are not embraced by the wisdom that constitutes the essence of the accomplishment that acts as a guide to lead one to the higher grounds, such as Pramuditā, and because they lack that companion, they are unable to reach the city of perfect enlightenment. At the time when the paths of generosity and so forth are well-embraced by the wisdom that realizes the three spheres are devoid of true existence, then those practices of generosity and the rest find their eyes, receive the name "perfection," and easily proceed to or attain the city of omniscience.As for the analogy for these, it is like a painting of a king or similar figure: even if all other parts are completely finished, if it lacks just one eye—if that is missing—then as long as the eye has not been painted, the painting is not complete, and one does not receive the wages or reward. Therefore, once one has gained certainty in the way that this very wisdom, which realizes emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, is the supreme essence of the path of the Great Vehicle, those of the lineage of the supreme vehicle should make that excellent path manifest in their own continuums through study, reflection, and meditation. At the time when one examines and investigates the conditioned phenomena of the three realms, the unconditioned phenomena of emptiness, the virtues embraced by the white aspiration for enlightenment, and the virtues of the Hearer continuum down to the lesser phenomena, using the wisdom that investigates the nature of reality, and thereby dismantles the objects of apprehension of grasping at characteristics, realizing that not even an atom of them is observed or exists as established from its own side—at that time, one is counted as having what is called the perfection of wisdom. This is similar to how space is merely the negation of obstruction and, because it lacks any form that constitutes its own essence, it does not depend on anything at all.At that time, because it is taught that even the mental attachment to the reality of the dharma-dhātu is erroneous, it is said: If, even though one is seized by skillful means, one is bound by the grasping of characteristics and wanders, thinking, "I shall practice this perfection of wisdom, the mother of the victorious ones," while being attached to the object of emptiness as real; and if one has a mind that is attached to the reality of "liberating many millions of beings who are touched by suffering or tormented by suffering," then that bodhisattva, who fully conceptualizes self and others as truly existing as sentient beings, is called one who has an object of apprehension. Such a practice is not the supreme or authentic practice of the perfection of wisdom. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* states, "The perfection of wisdom is to be made manifest," and so forth. Although the perfectly pure path of meditation must be taught after this, as the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states, "Attending to the Buddha, giving, and so forth," one must know the two causes for the arising and non-arising of the perfectly pure path of meditation. Therefore, to teach the cause for its arising first, the meaning of the single verse concerning the bodhisattva and so forth is as follows: Any bodhisattva who, in previous lifetimes, has pleased the Tathāgatas and, while practicing the conduct of a child of the victorious ones, has listened to this profound sūtra of the perfection of wisdom with respect, held it, and practiced it through reflection and so forth—such beings, having been born in this world now, due to the power of their previous imprints and good causes, become expert in the meaning of the perfection of wisdom and free from hesitation or doubt regarding its profound meaning. Upon hearing this sūtra, that person generates the perception of the Teacher, thinking, "I have seen the Teacher," and by that cause, they will quickly realize the perfectly pure path of meditation, the great peaceful enlightenment.To demonstrate the causes for not arising, two verses are spoken, beginning with "In former lives..." The meaning is: If a bodhisattva, while previously practicing the conduct of the heirs of the Victors, has accumulated merit by honoring billions of Buddhas and offering vast provisions, but has not engaged in listening, reflecting, and so forth upon the Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, and lacks faith in it, and has not made the aspiration to realize its meaning, then even if they obtain a human body in the present, upon hearing this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, they are unable to immediately realize its profound meaning. Because of that small-mindedness, they abandon this sutra of the perfection of wisdom and do not uphold it. By abandoning it, they also abandon the Buddha, the Jewel, and, lacking the refuge of the holy Dharma and the companionship of the noble Sangha, they go to the Avīci hell and experience suffering for eons; thus, it is said that the disadvantages are immeasurable. This is what is meant.Summarizing the meaning of arising and not arising, and providing instruction with examples on how one should train with faith and respect in the Perfection of Wisdom sutra, the author, out of compassion for future disciples, gives this advice: "Because the benefits and disadvantages of having or lacking faith in the Perfection of Wisdom are such, if you desire to touch or attain the supreme wisdom of the Buddhas, you should have faith in this Mother of the Victors and engage in it through listening, reflecting, and meditating." The reason why this is necessary is that, at this time when we have encountered the Buddha’s teachings, which are like an island of precious jewels, and possess the protection of a virtuous friend, we must make our lives meaningful. For example, it would not be right to go to an island of jewels, only to have one's previous trade goods exhausted and, having found no jewels at all, return empty-handed; for there is no greater loss or more wretched method than that. Therefore, those who are fortunate should, upon this basis of leisure, apply themselves with the perseverance of a flowing river to accomplish the two purposes. This concludes the commentary on the seventh chapter, the chapter on the hells, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.The Path of Meditation of Complete Purity. The eleventh, the path of meditation of complete purity, is stated in the *Ornament* as: "The purified result, form and so forth... up to... the path of such is the purified." It is defined as a Mahayana path of realization that is untainted and that establishes the traces of the ultimate abandonment that has become its own object of attainment. Regarding its divisions, there are nine, from the path of meditation of complete purity of the small-of-the-small up to that of the great-of-the-great, which are the antidotes to the nine sets of abandonments of meditation. This and the path of meditation of accomplishment are identical in meaning, differing only in their conceptual aspects. Its boundaries exist from the first bhūmi up to the tenth bhūmi. Of such paths of meditation of complete purity, there are two:General Exposition. The first, the general exposition, consists of one line of verse, "The purity of form, and so forth..." The meaning is this: because stains have not entered into the nature of reality, all phenomena included within the aggregates, elements, and sense-sources, such as form, are primordially pure and luminous by nature. However, because they are grasped in a distorted way by the ignorance of grasping at true existence, afflictions such as attachment arise; thus, these are called adventitious stains. As long as one is obscured by grasping at true existence and does not clearly see the nature of reality, form and so forth are described as impure. When the obscuring stains are purified and the nature of reality is clearly seen, the nature of reality of form and so forth is not tainted by stains, and thus they are primordially pure. That purity, and the fact that one’s own way of seeing has become congruent with it, is the reason why the object—the aggregate of form and so forth—is pure of stains, and the subject—the perfection of wisdom or the fruit of the state of a spiritual practitioner, from the path of seeing and the path of liberation up to buddhahood—are both one in meaning. Therefore, because a "purity of the fruit" cannot be established as something separate from that "purity of form and so forth," one should understand that these two cannot be mentally separated and are of one essence. In dependence upon that manner of the purity of the fruit, it is at that time described as the "purity of the object, form." For example, when a cataract or the like appears as falling hairs upon a form, one says the form is not clear, but when the cause of the delusion, the cataract and so forth, is removed, one says the form is clear.Explaining the distinctions of purity. Second, regarding the explanation of the distinctions of purity, three lines are spoken, beginning with "The purity of the result and of form." In this regard, the Ornament states:"Because of the loss of the three—defilements, knowables, and the path—The purity of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas,And the bodhisattvas is partial;The buddha’s is entirely pure."As stated, the śrāvaka arhat has abandoned only the defilement-obscurations, and the pratyekabuddha arhat, who is like a rhinoceros, has abandoned the defilement-obscurations and a portion of the cognitive-obscurations, namely the conceptualization of grasping; thus, their purity is partial and not absolute purity. However, because the buddha, the noble one, has abandoned the two obscurations without remainder through the path of cessation in his mental continuum, this is absolute purity or ultimate purity. Just as previously explained, the purity of form and the purity of the result are of one essence; likewise, when the stains to be abandoned—which are the share of the uninterrupted path that brings about the attainment of the result, the path of liberation—are purified, the objects thereof, such as form, must also be posited as purified by those very stains of one's own continuum. This is because the perfection of wisdom, which is the subject devoid of the single stain to be negated, or the purity of the result, and the purity of the objects such as form, are inseparable in essence and cannot be conceptually divided as distinct. Similarly, when the nine cycles of the Mahāyāna path of meditation, from the second to the tenth bhūmi, have served as the direct antidote to their respective stains to be abandoned—from the great conceptualization of grasping and fixation down to the subtle—and have abandoned the two obscurations without remainder, the result, which is included by the path of cessation in the buddha’s mental continuum, becomes the entirely pure omniscience. Thus, these three—the ultimate purity of omniscience, the purity of the path of cessation attained as the respective result by the path of learning, and the purity of the phenomena of the basis, such as form, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—merely appear as distinct in conventional reality. In ultimate reality, this is like the space element having no distinctions of different essences; because the naturally pure dharmadhātu is inseparable and cannot be conceptually divided into different essences, for all dharmadhātu is of a single nature. Having thus finished explaining the eleven phenomena that characterize the knowledge of the path, the conclusion of the section is: this is the commentary on the second chapter from the work titled "The Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Reality of Dependent Arising, a Profound Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities."Knowledge of the Bases. Having thus explained the knowledge of the paths, in order to teach the knowledge of the bases which purifies the knowledge of the paths, the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states: "By means of knowledge, [one does not remain] in existence," and so forth, ending with, "Thus, it is asserted as the knowledge of all." The definition of the knowledge of the bases is: a cognition that is conjoined with the wisdom directly realizing selflessness within the continuum of a person possessing their own continuum, and which resides in the lineage of realization of the Lesser Vehicle. There are nine [types of] phenomena that characterize the knowledge of the bases: the knowledge of the paths that does not remain in existence due to knowledge, the knowledge of the paths that does not remain in peace due to compassion, the knowledge of the bases distant from the resultant Mother, the knowledge of the bases near to the resultant Mother, the knowledge of the bases of the discordant side, the application of the knowledge of the bases, the equality of the mode of apprehension of the application, and the path of seeing. Because there are nine, a single verse appears, beginning with "By means of knowledge, [one does not remain] in existence," and so forth, which teaches the first two. The definition of the knowledge of the paths that does not remain in existence due to knowledge is: a cognition of a Great Vehicle Noble Being that resides in the lineage of realization which prevents the extreme of existence in relation to the conventional basis. That and the knowledge of the paths of the Śrāvakas are synonymous. Regarding its divisions, there are three: the Great Vehicle path of seeing, the path of meditation, and the path of no more learning. Its boundaries extend from the Great Vehicle path of seeing up to the level of a Buddha. The definition of the knowledge of the paths that does not remain in peace due to compassion is: a cognition of a Noble Being's continuum that resides in the lineage of realization which prevents the extreme of peace in relation to the conventional basis. That and a cognition of a Great Vehicle Noble Being that resides in the lineage of realization of a special method are synonymous. Regarding its divisions, there are three: the Great Vehicle path of seeing, the path of meditation, and the path of no more learning that have become that. Its boundaries are the same as the former.The path of wisdom that does not abide in cyclic existence and the path of compassion that does not abide in peace—in order to explain these two, namely the path of wisdom that does not abide in cyclic existence and the path of compassion that abides in peace, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "How does the hero act?" is as follows: The heroes, the bodhisattvas, who cannot be swayed by the grasping at true existence or the grasping at self-importance, even while acting within the realms of cyclic existence, see the faults of cyclic existence. By abiding in the perfection of wisdom, which is seized by special means and wisdom, they have truly transcended being born into cyclic existence through karma and defilements that are attached to any of the realms of the three worlds of cyclic existence. Yet, even having transcended, they do not abide in the extreme of either cyclic existence or peace, nor do they abide in the one-sided peace of nirvāṇa that is completely liberated from existence like the śrāvakas. Although they have eliminated the karma and defilements that cause one to be born into existence helplessly, they fully demonstrate being born into cyclic existence through the power of compassion and aspiration. As stated in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*: "The noble ones have eradicated the suffering of sickness, aging, and death from the root." Just as this states, although they are free from aging, sickness, and death, they demonstrate the process of passing away for the sake of others, because they are wise ones who possess special means, such as great compassion and the mind of enlightenment, and special wisdom that realizes both existence and peace as empty of true existence. By stating this, it directly teaches the two paths that do not abide in the two extremes of existence and peace, and implicitly teaches the two types of knowledge of the basis: the knowledge of the basis that is far from the resultant Mother [of the Buddhas] due to not being skilled in the means to stop the two extremes of existence and peace, and the knowledge of the basis that is near to the resultant Mother due to being skilled in those means. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* also states: "Bhagavān, the perfection of wisdom does not abide on the near shore, it does not abide on the far shore, and it does not abide in the long space between the two."The base-knowledge distant from the resultant Mother. Third, in order to teach the base-knowledge distant from the resultant Mother, it is stated in the Ornament: "Because it is perceived as having signs, and is not a method, it is distant." What is this base-knowledge? That which is devoid of great compassion and bound by the apprehension of true existence is the definition of the base-knowledge distant from the resultant Mother. That and the base-knowledge of the discordant side are synonymous. Regarding its boundaries, it exists from the path of seeing of the Lesser Vehicle up to the path of learning of the Lesser Vehicle.The base-knowledge near to the resultant Mother. Fourth, regarding the base-knowledge near to the resultant Mother, it is stated in the Ornament: "Because it is skilled in methods, it is explained as being truly near." That which is a cognition in the continuum of a Great Vehicle Superior residing in the lineage of realization of the Great Vehicle, and which is conjoined with great compassion and the wisdom that directly realizes emptiness, is the definition of the base-knowledge near to the resultant Mother. That and the base-knowledge of the remedy are synonymous. Regarding its boundaries, it exists from the path of seeing of the Great Vehicle up to the stage of a Buddha. The manner in which these two are taught by this sutra is as just explained.The base-knowledge of the discordant side. Fifth, regarding the base-knowledge of the discordant side, it is stated in the Ornament: "From 'the aggregates such as form' up to 'the discordant side'." What is this base-knowledge? That which is devoid of the two—the special wisdom and the special method—is the definition of the base-knowledge of the discordant side. That and the base-knowledge bound by the apprehension of true existence in the continuum of a Superior of the Lesser Vehicle are synonymous. Regarding its boundaries, it exists from the path of seeing of the Lesser Vehicle up to the path of no-more-learning of the Lesser Vehicle. The meaning of the three lines taught by this sutra to demonstrate this, beginning with "these beings," is as follows: Because these beings, obscured by ignorance, are attached to the true existence of the mire of the five aggregates of name and form, which are difficult to transcend, they wander in the wheel of cyclic existence—from the peak of existence down to the Unrelenting Hell—like a wind-wheel of the spheres that constantly rotates, driven by the stars. Because the twelve links of dependent origination, from ignorance to aging and death, arise in a continuous chain like a wheel of fire. Knowing that these confused beings who have fallen into this place of cyclic existence are like animals caught in an inescapable net, tormented by manifold sufferings and difficult to liberate, Bodhisattvas who are skilled in wisdom and method should work for the benefit of others without attachment to the place of cyclic existence.The remedial class of the knowledge of bases. The sixth, the knowledge of bases of the remedial class, which is seized by the antidote to the grasping at signs, is stated in the Ornament as: "There is no ego-grasping regarding giving and so forth," up to, "That is considered inconceivable." The definition of the knowledge of bases of the remedial class is: a cognition in the continuum of a Mahāyāna noble, which abides in the class of realizations of the Lesser Vehicle, and which is seized by the two special qualities of method and wisdom. That and the knowledge of bases in the continuum of a Mahāyāna noble are synonymous. Its scope exists from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the level of a Buddha. Regarding the demonstration of that, it is said: "Possessing wisdom, one moves about like a bird in the sky." The meaning is: just as a deer caught in a hunter's net is ignorant, one should understand the manner in which one suffers in this place of cyclic existence and is difficult to liberate. Then, Bodhisattvas who possess the great compassion of non-referential love and the wisdom that realizes the natural state, and who are not bound by the delusion of grasping at "giving and so forth" as truly existent, do not abide in this place of cyclic existence due to attachment, just as a bird, though moving in the sky, does not abide in the sky; rather, they move about for the sake of others. This is what is meant.The application of the knowledge of bases. The seventh, the application of the knowledge of bases, is stated in the Ornament as: "Form and so forth, that as impermanent and so forth," up to, "the seven types of appearances are the means of knowing." The yoga of a Bodhisattva that meditates as an antidote to either the inverted clinging to the essence and characteristics of the conventional mode of existence, or the inverted clinging to the essence and characteristics of the ultimate mode of existence, is the definition of the training of a Bodhisattva as taught in the context of the knowledge of bases. When divided, there are ten: the application that negates clinging to true existence regarding the subjects, such as form and so forth; the application that negates clinging to true existence regarding the attributes, such as impermanence and so forth; the application regarding whether or not form and so forth are complete as a support for qualities; the application of non-attachment through clinging to the true existence of form and so forth—these are the four regarding the object. Furthermore, there is the application of the perfection of wisdom not increasing or decreasing in the ultimate sense; the application of the non-existence of a true agent; the application of the three types of difficult deeds; the application of the existence of results in conventional terms despite their non-existence in the ultimate sense; the application of enlightenment not being dependent on others; and the application that negates clinging to true existence regarding the seven types of appearances by way of illustrative examples. Its scope exists from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum.The Equality of the Modes of Apprehension of that Application. The eighth, in order to teach the equality of the modes of apprehension of that application, states: "Without conceit regarding form and so forth, / That is the equality of the four aspects." That yoga of a bodhisattva, which is seized by the wisdom that prevents the belief in truth regarding the divisions of the bases, their signs and definitions, and the objects and subjects, is the definition of the equality of the application of the bodhisattva taught in the context of the knowledge of the bases. When divided, there are four: the equality of the application of having no conceit of truth regarding the nature of form and so forth; the equality of the application of having no conceit of truth regarding their signs and definitions; the equality of the application of having no conceit of truth regarding their divisions; and the equality of the application of having no conceit of truth regarding their objects and subjects. The boundaries are the same as those for the application. To summarize and explain these two, one verse is stated, beginning with "Conduct is completely pure." The meaning is: A bodhisattva who realizes that all phenomena, such as the aggregates, are empty of truth and equal, and whose conduct is completely pure, does not engage through a belief in the truth of the nature of form or its characteristics, such as impermanence. Likewise, one does not engage through a belief in truth regarding consciousness, perception, the three feelings of pleasure, pain, and equanimity, or the mental factor of intention. Thus, that conduct of a child of the Victorious One, which does not engage through a belief in truth regarding any object, is what completely abandons all attachment born of belief in truth; and it is the practice of the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas, who are completely liberated from all attachment born of the apprehension of truth. This is what was stated. This is the commentary on the eighth chapter, the chapter on complete purity, from the "Jeweled Lamp that Clarifies the Reality of Dependent Arising," the profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā*.The Path of Seeing. The ninth [chapter] teaches the path of seeing, from "the truths such as suffering" up to "the moment of knowing all." In this context, the Mahayana clear realization of the truths that directly realizes the free-from-elaboration [nature] as taught directly here is the definition of the path of seeing as taught directly here. Regarding its divisions, there are sixteen moments of knowledge and forbearance of the Mahayana as taught directly here. Its boundary exists only within the Mahayana path of seeing. In explaining this very path of seeing, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "Thus practicing" is as follows: A bodhisattva who, having realized and familiarized themselves with all phenomena as empty of true existence and free from elaboration as previously explained, and who is skilled in the meaning of the nature of reality and possesses clear intelligence, gradually trains in and practices the path. By attaining the Mahayana path of seeing, they cut through all attachment to true existence, becoming free from all that is to be abandoned by the path of seeing without remainder, and without attachment to manifest grasping, they proceed from the path of meditation and so forth to the higher [stages].Just as the sun, when freed from the planet known as Rāhu, shines with brilliant rays, and just as fire, when kindled, burns all grass, wood, and forests, so too does the non-conceptual timeless awareness, which is the union of method and wisdom, act like the sun’s light and fire to clear away and destroy the darkness and forests of the two obscurations. This is what is said. According to the Master, one must make a chapter break here, for he applies this single verse, "All phenomena," to the summary of the practice of complete realization. According to the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vṛtti* of Jñānapāda, the section from "The Victorious One is the supreme deity" onwards is applied to the practice of complete realization, and by making a chapter break at its beginning, the text of the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* appears to be arranged mostly in that way. However, our own tradition follows the Master’s commentary, as Gungthang Jampai Yang also did in his annotations and so forth, where he makes a chapter conclusion after explaining the nine phenomena that characterize the four knowledges. This is the commentary on the third chapter from the work entitled *The Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Profound Reality of Dependent Arising: A Commentary on the Precious Qualities Collection*.The Four Applications of Practice. Having thus finished explaining the three knowledges, which are the objects of knowledge, the second part is the explanation of the system of the four applications of practice. Regarding these, there are two: the result of mastery over the application, and the cause and effect of stability.The result of mastery over the application. The first consists of two: the application of complete aspects, which is the cause of mastery, and the peak application, which is the result.The application of complete aspects, the cause of mastery. To explain the first, the Ornament states: "From 'aspects, applications, and so forth' up to 'this includes skill in means.'" A bodhisattva’s yoga, conjoined with the wisdom that meditates by gathering the aspects of the three knowledges, is the definition of the application of complete aspects. This and the bodhisattva’s knowledge are one in meaning. When divided, there are one hundred and seventy-three in terms of aspects, and twenty in terms of applications. Its scope extends from the path of accumulation of the Great Vehicle up to the end of the continuum. There are eleven phenomena that characterize the application of complete aspects: aspects, applications, qualities, faults of application, definitions, the path of liberation, the community of irreversible learners, the application of the equality of cyclic existence and peace, the application of the purification of the field, and the application of skill in means; because there are these eleven.Aspects. To explain the first, the Ornament states: "From 'the varieties of the knowledge of the basis' up to 'they are explained as thirty-nine.'" Regarding the aspects taught here, there are two: definition and division. The first is: that knowledge which is capable of overcoming its own discordant factors is the definition of the aspects of knowledge of the antidote taught in this context. Regarding the second, when divided, there are twenty-seven aspects of the knowledge of the basis, thirty-six aspects of the knowledge of the path, and one hundred and ten aspects of the knowledge of all aspects, totaling one hundred and seventy-three. Concerning the determination of the nature of these aspects to be meditated upon, the meaning of the verse beginning with "all phenomena" is as follows: all phenomena, from form up to the knowledge of all aspects, are pure because they are not truly established or established by way of their own nature, and they are completely pure because they have not been obscured by defilements in their abiding nature. When a bodhisattva looks upon and abides in the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the application of complete aspects that realizes that suchness of the abiding nature, then the bodhisattva who is practicing the perfection of wisdom also does not apprehend as truly established all the phenomena of the basis, path, and aspects that are to be looked upon as not truly established. Abiding one-pointedly in the realm of the non-conceptual, which is empty of true existence, is to practice the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the bodhisattva’s path of manifest realization. This explains the one hundred and seventy-three aspects by way of their being the means of attainment. It should be known that the explanation by Buddhasrī in the *Sdug 'grel* (Summary Commentary) that this verse applies to the path of seeing of the third chapter does not accord with the commentary of the Master. This is the commentary on the ninth chapter, the chapter of praise, from the *Precious Qualities Collection* commentary, the *Lamp of Jewels that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Profound Reality of Dependent Arising*.Application. Second, in explaining the application of meditating on those aspects, because it is necessary to first identify the person who is the basis for practicing the application, the text first teaches the vessel for the application by stating the four verses beginning with "To the Victorious One..." The meaning is: The King of Gods, Śakra, asked the Victorious One, the Buddha, the Blessed One, a question. He asked how bodhisattvas, who have performed meritorious deeds for previous Victorious Ones and have cultivated roots of virtue, and who possess the protection of a spiritual friend, should exert themselves in the conduct of the perfection of wisdom and how they should meditate through application. In response, the Buddha taught: To realize that there is not even an atom of truly established existence in phenomena such as the five aggregates and the eighteen constituents, and to not exert oneself through attachment to true existence, but rather to abide in the application of non-apprehension regarding phenomena such as the aggregates and not exert oneself through grasping—this is the unerring diligence of bodhisattvas. Any person who, having heard from the Mother Sutras that all these phenomena, from form up to the omniscience of the Buddha, are explained as being like illusions and magical emanations—even though they are not established by their own nature, all the functions of cause, effect, and dependent origination are validly established in mere conventionality—and who, upon hearing this, is not only not afraid of its meaning but is free of doubt, and who, with faith and joy, diligently practices and applies themselves to learning the perfection of wisdom, that sentient being should be known as having entered the Mahayana path long ago. It should be known that they have previously performed meritorious deeds, such as serving and making offerings to many tens of millions of Buddhas and offering monasteries, because without a special cause having preceded it, one would not attain the faith of conviction in the profound meaning of emptiness and proceed to put it into practice. To teach, by way of a metaphor, the relief of those who have realized the deeds that transcend obstacles, such as listening to the Mahayana, the text states: Just as a person who has entered a vast, many-league-long path through a desolate wilderness, which is frightening due to robbers and the like, sees at some point a pleasant and abundant forest at the border of a wilderness and a village where cowherds of a city reside, and thinks, "These are signs that a village or city is near," thereby finding relief from the fear of robbers and wild beasts, and from then on is free from the fear of robbers and the like; in the same way, when one desires to attain the supreme enlightenment for the sake of others and searches for the path of means to attain it, whoever obtains the good fortune of listening to this Mother of the Victorious Ones, the perfection of wisdom, and engaging in it through hearing, contemplation, and meditation, attains relief from the suffering of cyclic existence and has no fear of falling into the extremes of existence or peace. They do not fall into the level of the śrāvaka arhats, nor do they fall into the level of the pratyekabuddhas, for they are irreversible from the Mahayana path. Thus it is said.Having thus indicated the basis, the nature of the application that relies upon it is stated in the *Ornament* as: "Because of not abiding in form and so forth," up to "that is pure and with limits." Regarding the application, there are three: definition, division, and stage. The first is the bodhisattva yoga seized by the wisdom of the union of calm abiding and special insight, which focuses on the emptiness directly taught in this context. This is the definition of the primary application directly taught in this context. Regarding the second, when divided, there are five based on their nature: the application of not abiding while being attached to form and so forth as true; the application of prohibiting the abiding in them through attachment to truth; the profound application of realizing the suchness of the four, such as form; the application of difficult-to-fathom depth that realizes the nature of the path; and the immeasurable application that realizes the nature of the aspects of form and so forth as immeasurable. There are seven based on the person who is the basis: the application of having attained a prophecy; the application of being firm in non-retrogression; the application of definite emergence; the application of being uninterrupted; the application of being near to enlightenment; the application of quickly attaining buddhahood; and the application of the benefit of others. There are four based on the method of completing the meditation on the Mother: the application of realizing that in ultimate reality there is no increase or decrease; the application of not seeing phenomena and non-phenomena and so forth in ultimate reality; the application of not seeing the inconceivable form and so forth; and the application of not conceptualizing form and so forth as signs or characteristics, along with the application of non-conceptualization. There are two based on the result: the application of giving the jewel of the result, and the application of purification. There is also the application of stage, making nineteen. The application of the great difficulty of long-term realization is not the primary application itself, but since it is an application nonetheless, there are twenty applications when counted. The third, the stage, is as follows: the application of the great difficulty of realization is from the Mahayana path of accumulation, and the primary applications are from the heat level of the Mahayana path of preparation up to the end of the continuum. The other previous applications cannot be directly applied to the sutra, but the nature of the uninterrupted application is taught by preceding it with an analogy, as stated in the two verses beginning with "Just as a person [going to see] the ocean..." The meaning of this is: For example, when a person goes to see the water of the ocean, if that person sees trees, forests, and mountains in the direction ahead, they know that the great ocean is still far away. If they do not see those signs of distance, such as mountains, and the ground becomes gradually level and low, and they do not see the far shore, then they think, "Now the great ocean has become near to me," and they have no doubt about it and know it even from afar.In this way, for those who have entered perfectly into the supreme enlightenment for the sake of others, the fortune of gradually engaging through hearing, contemplating, and meditating upon this Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, should be understood as being close to the great ocean of the dharmakāya, the wisdom of omniscience, because they have attained the special capacity to accomplish enlightenment. Therefore, even if a person who possesses the application, which is the main part of the Mahāyāna path, has been explicitly prophesied by the Guides that "you shall attain buddhahood," they know that the buddha-enlightenment will be attained or touched by them without long delay. When the conceptualizations of the path of seeing, which are like the signs of mountains and forests, do not appear in the supreme dharma, they are understood as being close to the path of seeing, which is like the ocean; by this, the quality of attaining the dharmakāya is also indicated. Following that, to demonstrate the tenth application, the application close to enlightenment, which transcends the conceptualizations of the path of preparation below the supreme dharma—which is like old foliage—and becomes the basis for new, untainted phenomena—which is like fresh foliage—one verse is spoken, beginning with "In the fine season of spring..." For example, when, in the fine season of spring, the withered leaves fall to the ground from a tree trunk, that tree, without long delay, produces or generates new leaves, fruits, and flowers from its branches. Likewise, whoever obtains this perfection of wisdom in their hands will attain the enlightenment of the Guides without long delay, and through the rūpakāya, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree, they will fulfill the hopes of beings just as they desire. By this, the quality of accomplishing the sambhogakāya is also indicated.To demonstrate the application for quickly attaining complete enlightenment, the meaning of the one verse beginning with "For example, a woman..." is as follows: Just as a pregnant woman who has conceived a child in her womb is distressed by experiencing the suffering of childbirth, and that state is the measure of the time having arrived for her to give birth to that child, in the same way, any bodhisattva who, through listening to and contemplating this sūtra of the noble perfection of wisdom, generates a longing for the goal of desiring to attain the higher path and a joy of a very clear mind, and then practices it through application, will quickly come to touch upon great enlightenment. As the Lord of Logic (Dharmakīrti) stated: "That which is an inference that an effect arises from the gathering of causes, because it does not depend on another factor, is stated to be nature." By this, the quality of attaining the nirmāṇakāya is also indicated. Although Buddhaśrī explained this differently, it is set forth here according to the commentary of the Master (Haribhadra). The application of preventing increase and decrease is the meaning taught by the two lines beginning with "The perfection of wisdom..." When a yogi who is cultivating the application acts in accordance with listening to, contemplating, and meditating upon the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom, they do not see in the ultimate sense the increase—that is, the arising—of phenomena of the side of defilement and the side of purification, such as form, and the characteristics indicated by that, nor do they see the complete decrease—that is, the cessation and decline—of them, because all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, without increase or decrease, being empty of true existence and like an illusion.In explaining the practice of not perceiving phenomena, non-phenomena, and so forth, the meaning of the two lines beginning with "Whoever, with phenomena..." is as follows: Any bodhisattva who does not perceive, in an ultimate sense, virtuous phenomena, non-virtuous phenomena, or the suchness of phenomena—the dharmadhātu—and who, while abiding in that suchness which is free from proliferation and in which all focal points of grasping at characteristics have been pacified, does not touch upon—that is, does not abide in—a nirvāṇa that is merely one-sided peace, but rather abides in the supreme prajñā that transcends the extremes of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.Qualities of the Application. Third, regarding the qualities of the application, the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states: "The subduing of the power of Māra, and so forth, are the fourteen types of qualities." The definition of the qualities of the Mahāyāna application is the benefit attained through the power of meditating on the Mahāyāna application, which serves as the method for attaining one's own goal. Regarding their classification, there are fourteen: the quality of subduing the power of Māra through the power of meditating on the application; the quality of the Buddha’s intention and knowledge; the quality of the Buddha’s direct realization; the quality of becoming near to perfect enlightenment; the quality of great significance and so forth; the quality of utilizing the domain; the quality of the perfection of all stainless qualities; the quality of becoming a spokesperson; the quality of not being divided by adverse factors; the quality of the arising of unique roots of virtue; the quality of fulfilling one's vows; the quality of fully grasping the vast fruit; the quality of accomplishing the benefit of sentient beings; and the quality of definitely attaining the Mother. Their scope extends from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the Buddha ground. To explain these qualities in general, the meaning of the verses beginning with "Whoever practices here..." is as follows: Any bodhisattva who meditates on the two types of selflessness and who practices and engages in this Mahāyāna application in accordance with the truth does not conceptually construct—by way of grasping at them as truly existent—the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and so forth. Likewise, they do not conceptually construct as truly existent the path and so forth, such as the five faculties, the powers, the bases of miraculous power, the establishments of mindfulness, the seven limbs of enlightenment, and so forth, nor the fruit—the supreme peace of nirvāṇa and enlightenment. Furthermore, they do not conceptually construct the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense spheres. By engaging in the Mahāyāna application, which generates qualities such as the subduing of the power of Māra through the blessings of the Buddha, while abiding in suchness—which is free from proliferation and devoid of all conceptual constructs of dualistic appearance—they are engaging in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the essence of all aspects, and in non-conceptual primordial wisdom. In the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, holding the perfection of wisdom, and so forth," he stated. This is the commentary on the tenth chapter, which expresses the qualities of holding, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of Fortunate Ones*, the profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the suchness of dependent origination.Faults of Application. Fourth, in order to demonstrate the faults of application, the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* states: "The faults are to be understood as definitely being sixty, divided into four sets of ten." The definition of a fault of application is an activity of Māra that creates obstacles to the arising, abiding, or completion of application, whichever the case may be. Regarding their classification, there are forty-six, ranging from the difficulty of attainment to the generation of joy in that which is not in accordance with the nature of reality. Because there are twenty-three adverse conditions that prevent the arising of application and twenty-three missing favorable conditions, they exist from the stage of not having entered the path up to the seventh stage. Since they are explained in detail in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* and other texts, they can be correlated with the sūtras one by one, but in this *Sañcayagāthā*, only about seven or eight are applied. Regarding this, there are two parts: the faults to be eliminated and the explanation of the antidotes that eliminate them.The faults to be eliminated. Regarding the first, there are two parts: the question and the response.The Question. First, regarding the question, the two lines beginning with "To the Buddha, the Moon of Speakers" are stated. To that Buddha, the Blessed One, who is the Moon of Speakers skilled in teaching the Dharma, the Elder Subhūti posed a question, asking: "What are the obstacles that hinder the practice of the application of bodhisattvas who delight in the qualities of the Great Vehicle?"The Response. Second, regarding the response, the two lines beginning with "The Teacher replied" are stated. In response to the question posed in that manner, the Teacher replied that the obstacles that hinder the practice are many, and that from among them, a small portion will be fully explained here for the time being; having thus provided the connection,Furthermore, among the forty-six faults of practice, there are eight that are explicitly taught here. The first is instability, characterized by being conceited due to overly rapid confidence and then turning back midway. Regarding the meaning of the single verse beginning with "By the Victorious One," it is as follows: When one is engaged in reading, holding, reciting, or teaching this Perfection of Wisdom, which is the Mother of the Victorious Ones of the three times, there arise various unfixed and diverse types of confidence regarding objects such as forms and sounds, as well as various states such as agitation, dullness, sleepiness, regret, attachment, and aversion. Due to the power of these, one does not accomplish the benefit of oneself and others, such as realizing the meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom, but instead, while reading, reciting, or teaching, one quickly fades away like a flash of lightning, cuts off one's exertion, and completely falls away from the practice; this should be known as the work of Māra.To demonstrate the actual cause of abandonment—that is, holding to the reason for turning away and forsaking the Great Vehicle canon—the single verse beginning with "When this is taught" is stated. When this sutra is taught, some develop doubts and hesitation, thinking, "The Guide has not explicitly mentioned or indicated my name in this Mother sutra, nor has he mentioned my lineage, the region where I dwell, or my clan." Thinking that they have not been clearly prophesied, they wonder, "What is the point of listening to this? This is not the speech of the All-Knowing One." By holding to this reason for turning away from the Mother, and with that distorted mind, they do not listen to that profound Dharma but rather forsake it; this is the work of Māra.The decline of attachment to the reason, that is, the decline of grasping at it specifically, is the meaning of the two lines beginning with "Not knowing in that way." Just as the perfection of wisdom is the root of the Great Vehicle path, those individuals who are influenced by Māra—those who are ignorant and deluded—abandon this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom, which is like the root of the Buddha, and, obscured by ignorance, seek out the collections of the śrāvakas, which are like branches and leaves; this too is the work of Māra.The decline of holding the supreme vehicle in every respect is the meaning of the two lines beginning with "Even having found the elephant." How is this? Just as a person searching for an elephant, even after finding the actual elephant, abandons it and instead searches for the elephant's tracks, so too, after hearing the perfection of wisdom, which teaches the complete method and wisdom, they abandon the diligent practice of it and seek out other sutra meanings of provisional intent; this should be understood as being just like the example given, and this too is the work of Māra.The decline of experiencing the supreme bliss of the fruit of excellent flavors is the meaning of the one verse beginning with "For example, someone with a hundred flavors." For example, just as someone who has found food possessing a hundred flavors, without tasting its flavor, having found the finest food, searches instead for poor food such as sixty-day rice, so too, any beginner bodhisattva who, having found this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, does not practice to accomplish the enlightenment of a Buddha, but instead relies on texts that teach the path for attaining the stage of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha arhat to seek unsurpassed enlightenment, is just like the example given above; this too is the work of Māra.Savoring the taste of gain, honor, and praise and looking toward them is the meaning of the two lines beginning with "Desiring honor." This means that one comes to desire to savor the taste of one's own fame and the honor and respect shown by others, comes to desire the acquisition of food, wealth, and the like, and, with a mind accompanied by the desire to look at various forms and the arrangements of objects, one becomes involved in associating and becoming intimate with householders and the like; being distracted by many activities and thus declining from listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth is the work of Māra.Seeking skill in means from the scriptures taught by Māra that are not the path is the meaning of the two lines beginning with "Having abandoned the Dharma." Having abandoned the practice of the Mahāyāna Dharma, one comes to engage in various worldly activities that are not the Dharma, and having cast aside the excellent path that leads to the attainment of Buddhahood, one wanders off onto the wrong path taught by Māra; this is the work of Māra.The listener having great aspiration but the teacher being diminished by indolence, whereby the listener also becomes faithless and turns away from listening to the Dharma, is the meaning of the one verse beginning with "Those who, at that time." This means that at the time when those listeners, who with great earnestness have gone to listen to this supreme Dharma out of aspiration and faith in the Mother (Prajñāpāramitā), find that the one expounding the Perfection of Wisdom sutra has become distracted by gain, honor, and the like, those listeners perceive that the Dharma speaker is attached to and obsessed with base activities such as delighting in gain, honor, and fame. Consequently, they find no joy in listening to the Dharma, and, becoming faithless and feeling uneasy with the thought, "I shall not request the Dharma now," they depart; this too is the work of Māra, which becomes an obstacle to listening to the Perfection of Wisdom and so forth.To summarize their meaning: the meaning of the four verses beginning with "At that time" is that these various works of Māra, which obstruct the preparations such as the gathering of those who teach and listen to the Perfection of Wisdom sutra, will arise at that time. What are they? At the time of listening to and contemplating this Dharma, those Māras who are hostile to the Dharma and are tormented by suffering and pain will agitate the minds of many monks who uphold this sutra. Through various means of obstruction, they will prevent the holding and contemplating of the meaning of this Perfection of Wisdom. Many such obstructive phenomena, not explained here but appearing elsewhere, will occur; one should know that all such obstacles are the work of Māra. As it is said in the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra*: "O son of noble family, know that all engagement in non-virtuous phenomena and all abandonment of virtuous phenomena are the work of Māra." The reason for the abundance of obstacles is established by way of an example: just as those who have obtained priceless, invaluable treasures, such as the king of wish-fulfilling gems, find them extremely rare and difficult to obtain, and once obtained, they are constantly subject to harm from enemies, thieves, and the like, in the same way, the Mother of the Victors, the supreme, priceless Dharma of the Perfection of Wisdom, is extremely rare, and because the Dharma is profound, it is constantly subject to many harms. For those beings of small intelligence who have newly entered the Mahāyāna and have not yet found this rare and profound Dharma—this precious Perfection of Wisdom sutra—Māra will strive to create obstacles and will initiate hindrances.The Antidote that Dispels. Second, the antidote that dispels is the meaning of the five lines of verse beginning with "The buddhas of the ten directions." Even though there are many such obstructions, they will not be able to find an opportunity. Why is that? Because the buddhas of the ten directions, whose power and might cannot be rivaled even in the slightest by the efforts of such demonic obstructions, protect, guard, and conceal those practitioners, thereby engaging them in fully upholding the perfection of wisdom. From the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Hopes of the Fortunate, an Explanation of the Precious Qualities Collection that Clarifies the Reality of Dependent Arising*, this is the commentary on the eleventh chapter, the chapter on Māra.If one asks why all the buddhas attend to and protect that person, this is established by an analogy: just as when a mother falls ill, her many children all become distressed and attend to her by seeking a physician to cure her sickness, in the same way, all those Bhagavan Buddhas of the world systems of the ten directions strive to dispel the influence of Māra and attend to this supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the mother that gives birth to each of them, consisting of the generation of bodhicitta and the realization of emptiness. Thus it is said.The Characteristics of Application. A Brief Presentation. Fifth, in order to teach the characteristics of application, the *Ornament* states: "That by which it is characterized is the characteristic," and so forth, providing a brief presentation through a single stanza.Detailed Explanation. Regarding the detailed explanation, it is stated: "From the arising of the Tathāgata, up to the assertion of four characteristics." Regarding that, there are two parts: the characteristics and the divisions.Characteristics. The first is: a bodhisattva’s yoga, seized by the union of calm abiding and special insight, which serves as the method for attaining the resultant perfection of wisdom that is its own objective; this is the definition of the yoga of the path of the perfection of wisdom. This is the general definition of application. As for the object to be characterized, when considered generally, it is the yoga of the path of the perfection of wisdom itself; here, the "application" in the phrase "definition of application" is also that very path of the perfection of wisdom, and its definition is what is called the definition of application.Divisions. Second, regarding the divisions of that, there are ninety-one: forty-eight knowledge-characteristics that characterize the application of the three knowledges; sixteen distinctive characteristics that characterize the application that is superior to the application of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; eleven activity-characteristics that characterize the application possessing distinctive functions for accomplishing the benefit of others; and sixteen essence-characteristics. Regarding the first of these, there are three, and the first four knowledge-characteristics—the knowledge-characteristic of knowing the arising of the Tathāgata, and so forth—are taught in the two stanzas beginning with "Those who have passed..." The meaning of these is as follows: If this perfection of wisdom is called the "Mother of the Victors," how does it become a mother? Just as in the world one is called a "mother" because she gives birth to a child and establishes him in his tasks, so too, all the Tathāgatas, the Blessed Buddhas who have already passed away in the past, those who currently reside in the worlds of the ten directions as protectors of the world, and all those who will arise in the future, all emerge from this very perfection of wisdom; therefore, it is the mother of all the Victors of the three times. By this, the knowledge-characteristic of knowing the arising of the Tathāgata is taught. The fact that the Buddhas, having seen the suchness of all phenomena included within the world—that is, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—exactly as it is, teach it to other beings to be trained, also arises in dependence upon this very perfection of wisdom, the mother that gives birth to the Victors. This Mother also reveals to her own offspring, the noble Buddhas, the immeasurable and infinite mental activities of other sentient beings—those that are gathered within, those that are distracted outward, those that are accompanied by attachment, those that are free from attachment, and so forth. Furthermore, the suchness of the world’s five aggregates, the suchness of the śrāvaka arhats, the suchness of the pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of the bodhisattva heirs of the Victors are not established as different in essence, and thus they are one. Since they are not different in terms of the nature of the reality-realm (dharmadhātu) that is devoid of any truly established entity, this suchness is one. One should understand that this suchness, which is the reality-realm, is what the Tathāgata has known and realized exactly as it is, and then taught to others. By these sutra passages, one should understand that the knowledge-characteristics, such as knowing the world and the non-destruction of the world, and knowing the mental activities of sentient beings, are for the most part directly taught in the literal words.The second point, demonstrating the signs of the knowledge of the path such as emptiness and signlessness, explains the meaning of the three verses beginning with "The world of the wise." The meaning is this: The Buddhas, the Bhagavats, who are wise regarding the mode of being, whether they appear in the future, or are currently living and abiding in this world system, or have passed into parinirvāṇa, abide like space in the nature of a non-affirming negation, which is established by way of merely negating the object of negation—inherent existence—which is a faultless dharmatā that has been pure from the beginning, where phenomena are empty by nature, and which cannot be altered by anyone and never changes. Bodhisattvas—that is, the bodhisattvas—having correctly realized this mode of being, suchness, which is free from conceptual proliferation, and having practiced it by uniting method and wisdom, when at some point their realization reaches perfection, they have gone to or realized the suchness of all phenomena exactly as it is; and for that reason, the name "Tathāgata" (Thus-Gone One) has been bestowed upon the Buddhas.If one asks how the Buddha works for the benefit of sentient beings after having realized that all phenomena are empty by nature: this is the domain of the Guides, the Buddhas, who possess the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, and who abide by relying upon this perfection of wisdom, which is like a divine pleasure grove from which arise boundless, undefiled joys. Although they completely deliver boundless sentient beings from the many sufferings of cyclic existence, such as birth, aging, sickness, and death, and from the three lower realms, there never arises in those Buddhas the perception of sentient beings as truly existent. While remaining in meditative equipoise on the dharmatā, they work for the benefit of others effortlessly and spontaneously.The manner of subduing opponents and teaching the profound doctrine of emptiness is also like this: just as the lion, king of beasts, dwelling in the ravines of the snowy mountains, causes fear in many predators and small animals—such as tigers, leopards, bears, and wild dogs—by roaring without harming any living creature, so too do the Buddhas, the lions among men, relying upon the profound meaning of the perfection of wisdom, which is emptiness, cause fear in many non-Buddhists who have fallen into the abyss of the view of a self, and they proclaim in the world the marvelous and vast sound of the ultimate dharma. Furthermore, a bodhisattva, having perfected the three gateways to liberation, becomes a Buddha; although they deliver countless sentient beings from the sufferings of the lower realms, they do not have the perception that suffering and sentient beings are truly established, and thus they teach that there is no defilement, no purification, no substantiality, no essence, and no basis.The third section, which demonstrates the signs of omniscience such as the Tathāgata’s abiding in happiness within the vision of the Dharma, explains the meaning of the three verses beginning with "Just as one dwelling in the sky."
