In order to clarify this through an example:For example, just as the body of a magically conjured person is not invisible to anyone, and although it is empty by its own nature, it can still be designated by a name, and there are even those in the world who describe its manner of being; in the same way, a bodhisattva who practices through the gateway of the three liberations does not abide in the extremes of either cyclic existence or peace, yet they appear in the world and can be designated by a name.The summary and explanation of the infinite skillful means is as follows: If someone were to ask a bodhisattva about the nature of the conduct in which the conqueror’s children should abide, or about the manner in which the dispositions, intentions, and faculties—sharp or dull—of those to be trained exist, [and] that bodhisattva does not know the dispositions and inclinations of those to be trained, does not teach the profound dharma of emptiness and signlessness, and—because they are unable to ascertain that the bodhisattva is irreversible—does not explain the qualities, tokens, or aspects of the irreversible stage, then it should be understood that this [bodhisattva] has not been prophesied as irreversible. Conversely, one who knows these things and is skilled in teaching the dharma in accordance with the intellect of those to be trained should be known as one who has attained the tokens of irreversibility. Having thus explained the eleven qualities that characterize the application of complete realization, the conclusion of the section is: This is the commentary on the fourth chapter from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.Having finished explaining the application of complete realization, which is the cause that brings about mastery over the four applications of practice,The result, the peak application. Second, in explaining the peak application which is the result of mastery, the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states: "Its realization and development, and so forth, up to the peak realization." The yoga of a bodhisattva, which is seized by wisdom that has surpassed the path of accumulation of the Great Vehicle through the condensed meditation of the three knowledges, is the definition of the peak application. That and the application of engagement are synonymous. There are eight phenomena that characterize the peak application, because there are the four peak applications of the four paths of preparation such as heat, the peak application of the path of seeing, the peak application of the path of meditation, the uninterrupted peak application, and the mistaken practice to be eliminated. Regarding the levels, it exists from the heat stage of the path of preparation of the Great Vehicle up to the end of the continuum.The peak application of the heat stage. Among these, explaining the first, the peak application of the heat stage: The *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states, "Even in dreams, all phenomena... up to... are asserted as the twelve aspects." Regarding this, there are three: definition, division, and levels. As for the first, the definition of the peak application of the heat stage is that first part of the Great Vehicle’s path of definite discrimination that has attained any one of the twelve signs of having attained the peak application. Second, regarding its division, there are three: small, medium, and great heat. Third, regarding the levels, it exists only in the heat stage of the Great Vehicle’s path of preparation. In explaining the peak application of the heat stage, which is characterized by twelve signs such as becoming weary of cyclic existence even in dreams, viewing all phenomena as like dreams, and pacifying the harms of beings through truthful speech, there are the explanation of the first eight signs and the two incidental topics.The detailed classification of the signs. First, the meaning of the three verses beginning with "Arhats and..." is as follows: Through the power of having long practiced the Great Vehicle path, which is a union of method and wisdom, one does not desire—let alone actually see—the qualities and happiness of the three realms of cyclic existence, even in dreams. This applies to the levels of the śrāvaka arhats and the pratyekabuddha wisdom, which is the "pratyekabuddha" referred to as the "condition-born buddha," and thus the inferior vehicles. Furthermore, any bodhisattva who sees in dreams or similar states the buddhas surrounded by vast oceans of retinues, and who sees those buddhas teaching the Dharma to beings, should be understood as having attained the signs of the peak application, or as having been prophesied by the buddhas that they will not regress from the Great Vehicle’s enlightenment into an inferior path. By this, the first two lines indicate the realization of method, and the subsequent two lines indicate the second sign, which is that of seeing the buddhas and them teaching.Furthermore, that bodhisattva, having seen in a dream many sentient beings dwelling in the three lower realms, out of compassion, in that very instant, makes a prayer to cut off the continuity of the lower realms, and by the power of that, sees their sufferings pacified. Also, if, upon waking from a dream, they see a village or the like burning with fire, they are not afraid, for they have been prophesied as irreversible; thus, by the blessing of uttering the power of truth—such as saying, "By this truth and by these words of truth, may this fire be pacified"—the power to pacify the mass of fire is achieved. This should be understood as having been prophesied by the victors of the past as irreversible from complete enlightenment. This verse indicates the sign of abandoning the lower realms and the sign of pacifying fire and the like through truth. Likewise, when they see that in the human world sentient beings are harmed by the spirits of demons and tormented by many different kinds of illnesses, that bodhisattva, possessed of compassion and wishing to protect them from suffering both permanently and temporarily, causes those [afflictions] to be pacified through the blessing of uttering words of truth and so forth. However, they do not become arrogant, thinking, "I possess great power," nor does the pride of holding oneself as supreme arise; this should be understood as a sign of having been prophesied as irreversible or having attained the peak application. By this, the sign of the peak application, which pacifies demonic spirits and the like merely by uttering words of truth, is indicated. When explaining the first sign in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, it is explained in detail from the passage, "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, sees all phenomena as like a dream, and does not make them manifest, Subhūti, this is also..." up to the twentieth chapter, the chapter on skill in means. This is the commentary on the twentieth chapter, the chapter on skill in means, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.Incidental Topic: Regarding the second incidental topic, having branched off from the two signs—the pacification of a burning city through the utterance of a truth-statement and the pacification of harm from non-human spirits—the text explains how Māra acts, not as a sign of irreversibility, but otherwise, by stating the meaning of the eight verses beginning with "If that..." In this way, when a burning city or the harm of non-human spirits and the like are pacified through the power of Māra by means of an utterance of truth, if that bodhisattva thinks, "Because various blessings have been accomplished or attained through my own words of truth, I am a bodhisattva who has received a prophecy, as I possess such qualities and powers," and thus arrogance arises; or if he becomes arrogant, thinking, "Other bodhisattvas will prophesy me and speak of my fame," and thereby disparages other bodhisattvas, then one should know that such a person, dwelling in pride and arrogance, is a person of inferior intellect and immature mental continuum who is fit to be deceived by Māra, because he possesses the arrogance and the pride of hoping for fame. Based on that, one should understand how Māra acts.The explanation of the Māra that arises from the basis of names: A Māra that causes conceit and arrogance to arise also emerges from the basis of names. In this way, Māra the Wicked One will approach that bodhisattva in the guise of a Buddha, a monk, or the like, and speak as follows: "These are the names of you, your parents, and your ancestors back through seven generations of your lineage," and while speaking those names, he will also speak in accordance with what you have previously thought in your own mind, saying, "This is the name you will have when you become a Buddha." He will clearly state whatever qualities that person currently possesses, such as the ascetic virtues of begging for alms or wearing rags, the possession of novice or monastic vows, or the possession of the yoga of calm abiding and special insight, and he will further say, "In your past lives as well, your manner of ascetic virtues and the like were just as they are now." When the person hears those words spoken at that time, that bodhisattva, who has developed manifest arrogance and conceit based on that basis or cause—the mere name that describes his own qualities—should be understood as one whose conceit has been fully stirred up by Māra and who is of inferior or low intellect.The manner in which Māra enters even when one has practiced seclusion: In general, there are two types of seclusion: external seclusion from busy distractions and internal seclusion from mental distraction. Among these, for a bodhisattva, the primary seclusion is from the inferior mental engagement that causes distraction from the Great Vehicle. Therefore, even if one dwells by relying upon a secluded village, a great city, a mountain cleft, a remote hermitage, or a forest retreat that is physically secluded from busy distractions, free from the movement of people and the clutter of possessions, if one develops the conceit of thinking, "I am one who dwells in seclusion, having been highly praised by the Sugata," and consequently praises oneself while disparaging other bodhisattvas who dwell in cities, it should be understood that such a bodhisattva’s mental continuum has been completely corrupted or stirred up by Māra, and that they are of small intellect and not of good character.In order to define the seclusion of a bodhisattva, to provide an analogy for the meaninglessness of it if that seclusion does not arise, and to demonstrate how one should not search for it merely through outward appearances if it does arise: [The text] explains that [a bodhisattva] may dwell in cities like Luṣapha, in regions like Campaka, or in towns like Pāṭaliputra. While dwelling there, apart from striving to mature sentient beings who are not yet mature, to liberate those who are mature, and to accomplish unsurpassed enlightenment, that bodhisattva never generates the desire for the state of a śrāvaka arhat or a pratyekabuddha. This is what the Sugata has declared to be the true seclusion of the bodhisattva sons; for if one’s own mind is secluded from the mental engagement of the inferior vehicle, then no matter where one dwells—in a village or elsewhere—one is dwelling in the supreme seclusion.However, a bodhisattva who does not dwell in such seclusion, but instead dwells for many years in a mountain cleft five hundred leagues away, a place completely secluded from the bustle of people and filled with dangerous snakes and the like, yet who does not understand what this internal seclusion is, will develop a superior conceit, thinking, "I am one who dwells in the supreme seclusion." By dwelling in a manner similar to the inferior mental engagement, such a person is not dwelling in the seclusion of a bodhisattva, because they are corrupted by inferior mental engagement.Due to the power of such conceit, when they see other bodhisattvas who are striving for the benefit of others, who have attained the four dhyānas, the five powers, the five faculties such as faith, the three gateways to liberation, and the heroic-march samādhi, and who are traveling through villages and cities to benefit others and lead sentient beings to maturity and liberation—because they do not understand the intent and conduct of those [bodhisattvas], they disparage them, thinking, "These are not practicing in a hermitage or in seclusion." The Blessed One has declared that such a person is within the domain of Māra, for they have come to dwell in a realm where Māra finds an opportunity.If, then, dwelling alone is not what is meant by seclusion, what is seclusion? If a bodhisattva, whether dwelling in a town or in a wilderness, is free from the mind that desires to attain either of the two vehicles—the Śrāvaka or the Pratyekabuddha—and has become solely and definitively committed to the path of supreme enlightenment, this manner of being is the pure seclusion of bodhisattvas who have entered upon the welfare of beings. Not understanding this, if one judges a bodhisattva who dwells in such seclusion by thinking, "He has warmth,"—that is, by measuring his level of spiritual heat—and concludes, "This is not dwelling in seclusion," then that person who makes such a judgment will himself fall away from the qualities of the stages and paths. Therefore, the Sage, the Blessed Buddha, has said, "Except for one like me, a person should not measure another person, for they will fall away," and as stated in the sutra, "A bodhisattva should realize the understanding within his own continuum and should not seek to find fault in others." Thus, to generate the perception of them as teachers and to act with respect toward all sentient beings is the primary training for bodhisattvas. This is the commentary on the twenty-first chapter, the chapter on Māra, from the *Precious Qualities Collection* commentary, the *Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, which clarifies the profound reality of dependent origination.The second point is that since the prevention of such occurrences depends upon relying on a spiritual friend, the text instructs one on the necessity of relying on a spiritual friend and, in order to explain the signs of non-retrogression for that reason, it sets forth the meaning of two verses beginning with "Therefore." Because many obstacles arise that obstruct the practice of the Mahāyāna path, one must recognize them and turn them back, and for that reason, one should rely on external and internal spiritual guides. Regarding the one who relies, they possess an intense resolve to seek supreme, unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of others, and they are skilled in the methods to accomplish it; thus, when the method is taught, they will certainly subdue pride and the like, which hold oneself as supreme. To illustrate this, just as in the world a multitude of sick people rely on a skilled physician to cure their own illnesses, one should rely on a spiritual friend who possesses the characteristics in a proper manner, without distraction, through both intention and application—viewing oneself as the patient, the one who speaks the Dharma as the physician, the Dharma as the medicine, the diligent practice as the healing of the illness, the Tathāgata as the holy being, and the teaching of the Dharma as something that will long endure.If one asks who the spiritual friend to be relied upon is: one should rely upon the external spiritual guide, consisting of the Blessed Buddhas and the bodhisattvas who have entered into the practice of the path to supreme enlightenment, and the internal spiritual guide, consisting of the six perfections of the path, as a spiritual friend. Because those Buddhas and bodhisattvas are the ones who point out the path of the Mahāyāna, they are called the external spiritual guide, and because these six perfections of the path are what must be practiced and accomplished, they are called the internal spiritual guide. Since these two prevent one from falling into the lesser paths and the like, by relying on these two types of spiritual guides, one will quickly realize the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Buddhas through two types of causes; for it is a principle of dependent origination that one’s own result arises from the complete fulfillment of the perfect conditions. This is what is meant. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* also explains this, from the passage "Then, Blessed One..." to "First of all, one should rely upon and respect a spiritual friend," and so forth. In order to explain the sign of learning the perfection of wisdom, which is the internal spiritual guide, it sets forth one verse beginning with "The Victors of the past..." The way in which the six perfections act as the internal spiritual guide is as follows: the great path that is the single journey for all the Victors of the three times—those Victors, the perfectly complete Buddhas who have already passed away in the past, those who have not yet come and are future Buddhas, and those who currently reside in the ten directions teaching the Dharma—is none other than these six perfections; there is no other, for it is impossible to attain Buddhahood without relying on the six perfections, and one cannot achieve the path other than through them. These six perfections are what remove the darkness of the obscurations of mental afflictions for those who have entered the path or method of supreme enlightenment, and they act as an illuminator that clarifies the path of realizing selflessness. Because they remove the darkness of the obscurations of knowledge, they are a lamp; because they illuminate through the path of seeing, they are light; and because they bring the path of the supreme vehicle, such as the path of meditation, to complete fulfillment, they are the supreme teacher. This is what the Victors have explained. Thus, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* states: "These six perfections are the teacher. The six perfections are the path. The six perfections are the light. The six perfections are the lamp. The six perfections are the radiance. The six perfections are the protector. They are the refuge. They are the foundation," and so forth. In summary, for the attainment of Buddhahood, the spiritual friend who points out the six perfections and one’s own practice or conduct—these two causes—are indispensable.To explain that realization which is free from grasping—whereby, even when the signs of having attained the peak training are present, no grasping arises, and one understands how all faults and qualities arise merely as conceptual imputations—the text states the four verses beginning with "How is the perfection of wisdom..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: Just as the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* states, "The perfection of wisdom is characterized by emptiness," so too, how is the essence or characteristic of the perfection of wisdom empty by nature? It is because it is devoid of the nature of being one or many that would be truly established. Likewise, one should know that all these phenomena, such as form, are also empty by nature, just like that perfection of wisdom, in terms of their mode of existence or characteristics. If one thoroughly understands that all phenomena, from form up to omniscience, are empty of their own essence and are devoid of the marks of true establishment, then at the time of practicing the signs of having attained the peak training as previously described—or, in this way, practicing here—one is practicing the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas.If all phenomena are empty by nature, how then do sentient beings become defiled or purified? To explain the answer to this: ordinary sentient beings, by superimposing attractiveness or unattractiveness and thoroughly conceptualizing through improper mental engagement, give rise to desire for the food of sensory objects such as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile sensations. Those who possess a mind attached to cyclic existence, such as these desirable qualities, are like a fly circling the scent of filth; because they are constantly revolving from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, they become defiled. Furthermore, apart from being established merely as conventional illusions, the two—the self and the virtuous phenomena of the self—are not truly established and are empty by nature, for they are not produced in the ultimate sense. However, childish beings who are unskilled in the meaning of the mode of existence grasp at what is ultimately non-existent as being existent; this is like someone who imagines they have tied a knot in empty space. Because they are bound in their mental continuum by such distorted conceptualization, it is difficult for these beings to be liberated. The way in which they become miserable in cyclic existence due to the power of grasping at truth—even though things are not established in the ultimate sense—is as follows: for example, when a distorted mind, through the perception of suspicion, gives rise to the manifest conceptualization that "poison has been taken" or "poison has entered the body," even though in reality no such poison has entered, the power of that conceptualization causes suffering to arise and leads to fear and fainting. This is just like a person who, though innocent, begins to tremble in fear merely because an enemy or someone else has said to them, "You are going to be killed."In the same way, ordinary beings who are childish and have not attained the path of the noble ones, despite the fact that there is no ultimate establishment, grasp at a self as existing by nature and, by focusing on the eyes, nose, and so forth, claim things as "mine." From this habituation to the path, there arises a conceptualization that is not correct, which perceives a self and what belongs to a self as true. By the power of that, they accumulate karma and, in cyclic existence, are repeatedly born and destroyed—that is, they experience a continuous stream of various sufferings such as death, decline, and unhappiness. Just as it has been taught that, due to the power of total ignorance and delusion, one is thoroughly afflicted by grasping at a self and what belongs to a self even though they do not exist in reality, it is also taught that a bodhisattva who realizes the non-existence of a self—that is, who realizes the meaning of selflessness directly—and who knows and habituates to the nature of reality, will attain the state of liberation, which is complete purification. This, however, is in terms of conventional reality; in terms of ultimate reality, it is said that a bodhisattva who correctly knows that for any person whatsoever there is no becoming afflicted or becoming purified, will realize the perfection of wisdom, which understands the equality of cyclic existence and nirvana as being empty of true existence. This is explained in the *Eight Thousand Verse Perfection of Wisdom* by such passages as: "Subhūti asked, 'Bhagavan, what is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom?'"The Peak Application. The second, the peak application, is stated in the Ornament as: "From the sentient beings of the Jambudvīpa... to the nature of the sixteenfold increase." Regarding this, there are three parts. The first is: the second of the two [types of] concordant factors for definite emergence of the Great Vehicle, which attains the sixteenfold increase of merit superior to worshipping Buddhas equal in number to the sentient beings of the three-thousandfold world system, is the definition of the peak application. The second, when divided, consists of the small, intermediate, and great peak applications. Its boundary is found solely in the peak of the path of application of the Great Vehicle.Regarding the sixteenfold increase of merit in the peak application, the first is the peak application of the increase of merit superior to worshipping Buddhas equal to the sentient beings of the three-thousandfold world system, including Jambudvīpa. The meaning of the two verses beginning with "In Jambudvīpa..." is as follows: Taking the limit of the investigation as an example, if all the sentient beings of the three-thousandfold world system, represented by the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, were to obtain human bodies, and all of them were to generate the mind for unexcelled, perfectly complete, supreme awakening, and for many millions of thousands of years were to make vast offerings to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and give immeasurable gifts to sentient beings, and were to dedicate all those roots of virtue for the sake of the benefit of beings as the cause of supreme awakening, there would be immeasurable merit in that. However, if a Bodhisattva were to exert themselves in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is of the nature of the peak realization, then—let alone for a long time—even if they were to meditate on the path in accordance with that perfection of wisdom and teach it to others for just a single day, the heap of merit from the giving described above would not be able to compete with, that is, would not be capable of matching, that merit. Therefore, one must engage in this meditation on the perfection of wisdom, or the peak application, constantly and without negligence. This is what is meant.The development of the union of means and wisdom is explained in one verse, beginning with "The perfection of wisdom..." Those yogis who practice the supreme perfection of wisdom by way of the peak of the peak-application generate great compassion for all sentient beings tormented by suffering and work for the benefit of beings, yet they have no perception of sentient beings as truly existent. At the time when they possess this excellent path that unites compassion without apprehension and wisdom, those bodhisattvas who are skilled in means become the supreme objects of offering or fields of merit for all beings, and they always fully enjoy the meaningful alms and so forth that are offered by the inhabitants of the world.The manner in which one must exert oneself in that path of the union of means and wisdom, along with an analogy, is explained in three verses beginning with "The bodhisattva..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: Any bodhisattva who abides in the peak-application and so forth, wishing to liberate from the bondage of karma and defilements those sentient beings—comprised of the five classes, including gods, humans, and the three lower realms, who have been connected as fathers, mothers, and so forth since beginningless time in this place of cyclic existence—and wishing to liberate them from the suffering of cyclic existence, relies upon the vast path, the path of the Great Vehicle. Desiring to reveal that very nirvana, which does not abide on the shore of the ocean of cyclic existence, to the realm of sentient beings, they should exert themselves day and night, without distraction, in the perfection of wisdom that realizes emptiness, accompanied by compassion.Explaining the signs of keeping the perfection of wisdom in mind by way of clarifying that meaning through an analogy: For example, if a person were to find a supreme jewel—which they had not found before, meaning it is difficult to find—at another time, and were to become extremely joyful, but then, immediately after finding it, were to fall under the sway of carelessness and distraction, causing that jewel to be lost, then, because it was lost, they would constantly long for it, thinking, "When will I find that jewel again?" and would be perpetually miserable. Just like that analogy, a bodhisattva who has entered the path of supreme enlightenment, having found this perfection of wisdom—which is like a supreme jewel that is extremely difficult to find and of great significance—should practice yoga upon it and never abandon it. Just as one who, having found that previously lost jewel again, takes it up with joy, wraps it in cloth and the like with great diligence, and, fearing that it might be lost or snatched away by others, quickly goes to their own home and treasures it, whereby the sorrow of being parted from the jewel and the suffering of poverty are pacified, so too, if a bodhisattva constantly exerts themselves in meditating on the perfection of wisdom, they will quickly attain unsurpassed enlightenment. Thus it is said. This is the commentary on the twenty-second chapter, the chapter on the spiritual friend, from the *Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.To demonstrate how the path of the union of method and wisdom suppresses the discordant factors, and to teach the three types of development—such as patience regarding non-arising phenomena—combined together, the meaning of the two verses beginning with "Like the sun and clouds" is explained. For example, when the sun, which is free from clouds and possesses a network of extremely luminous rays that vanquish all dense darkness, rises, it suppresses the light of all sentient beings—such as fireflies, which possess only a tiny amount of light and can only dispel the darkness immediately surrounding their own bodies—as well as the light of the gathering of stars and the light of the moon, and so forth. Likewise, the bodhisattva who practices the supreme perfection of wisdom, which possesses all aspects, is like the sun free from the clouds of obscuration. By radiating the light of the teachings that demonstrate the selflessness of phenomena and persons, the wise one, practicing emptiness and signlessness by nature, completely vanquishes the dense darkness of views, such as the view of the transitory collection. In doing so, they suppress and are superior to all beings who are like fireflies, śrāvaka arhats who are like other creatures, pratyekabuddhas who are like stars, and many other bodhisattvas who are unskilled in method. By the phrase "practicing emptiness and signlessness," the development of patience regarding non-arising phenomena and the non-apprehension of both enlightenment and the agent of enlightenment are taught, and the development of superiority over arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and others is indicated.To explain the method of ripening other beings to be trained, and to elaborate on the increase of all the hosts of gods who have approached, two verses are spoken, beginning with "Like a prince." The meaning is this: For example, a prince who wishes to benefit his subjects by giving away wealth, who protects all people from harm, and who desires to accomplish the purpose of benefit and happiness, is skilled in means and possesses a fine character; he becomes the foremost of all the king’s sons. Because he is honored by all the subjects and because each one of them wishes to accomplish their own purpose, it becomes fitting for them to go into his presence. If that prince, even at a time when he has not yet become king, benefits many sentient beings and makes them joyful, then it goes without saying that when he is consecrated as king, has attained the means of governance, and has become a king abiding in the kingdom, he will accomplish the purpose of the subjects and make them joyful. In that same way, a wise Bodhisattva who practices the conduct of a son of the Conqueror with a heart of wisdom and compassion also gives the nectar of Dharma to the assembly of fortunate beings and, by means of leading them onto the path and so forth, makes gods and humans joyful, so that the gods of the desire realm, the six classes, and others come into his presence to listen to the Dharma and pay him homage. If this Bodhisattva, even now while in the stage of the path of learning, strives to accomplish the benefit and happiness of many sentient beings, then it goes without saying—because it is unnecessary to state—that when he becomes a Dharma King, a Buddha, and abides in the wisdom of omniscience, he will perform the benefit of all wandering beings. This is the commentary on the twenty-third chapter, the chapter on Śakra, from the "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Lamp," a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.To explain the two types of flourishing—the flourishing of suppressing all Māras, and the flourishing of dwelling with respect for other bodhisattvas, just as one does for a teacher, and remaining equal to them in training—the text states, "At that time," and so forth, for six verses. The meaning is this: at the time when one is practicing the path that unites skillful means and wisdom, which the adverse forces are unable to suppress, the sinful Māras dwelling in the trichiliocosm think as follows: "This bodhisattva is passing beyond my domain; once they attain buddhahood, they will cause many sentient beings to pass beyond as well, and thus my domain will become empty." Thinking this, their minds become filled with anguish, and they reflect, "I am unable to create obstacles." Overcome by grief and despair, and because of this, suffering physically and mentally, they become discouraged and weak. Unable to bear being tormented by such suffering, they think, "How can I cause this bodhisattva to turn back and retreat from the path of the Great Vehicle?" They then create obstacles and, in order to show the bodhisattva great terrors, they manifest various magical displays, such as setting the directions ablaze and sending down shooting stars.Who is that bodhisattva who, even when the Māras act in this way, cannot be caught off guard? At whatever time those bodhisattvas who are skilled in wisdom and means possess a most intense aspiration that does not deviate from the path of the Great Vehicle, they constantly, day and night, contemplate and reflect upon the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom. At the time when they do so, the body and mind of that bodhisattva move without fear of the precipices of existence and peace, like a bird moving through the sky, because they abide on the path that unites skillful means and wisdom. Therefore, how could the sinful Māras and their dark cohorts ever find an opportunity to catch such a bodhisattva off guard? They cannot.How an opportunity is found when faults enter into one’s own conduct is as follows: At whatever time bodhisattvas become angry with one another, engaging in conflicts such as striking one another with their bodies, or in disputes involving verbal abuse or litigation before a king, and, being inharmonious, possess minds inflamed by hatred, at that time the sinful Māra becomes extremely joyful and at ease. The reason for this is the thought that because those two bodhisattvas have committed the fault of engaging in conflict, they have become distant from the wisdom of the Victorious Ones and have created an obstruction to the path of the Great Vehicle. In this way, both of them become distant from the wisdom of the Buddha and become like the *rākṣasas* and *piśācas* who are wicked and cause harm, and both of them, through their conflict, cause their own vows to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings to degenerate. How could there be any attainment of enlightenment for one who is devoid of the patience that is the antidote to the hatred that causes compassion, loving-kindness, and the *bodhicitta* to degenerate? It is like a seed burned by fire, from which no sprout can emerge. At the time when bodhisattvas engage in conflict with one another, the Māras, together with their retinues or factions, become extremely joyful. Therefore, the sutras explain extensively that the faults of anger are greater than the faults of desire, for even if desire has been present for a long time, a single moment of anger causes loving-kindness and compassion to degenerate and destroys the roots of virtue. As the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*, quoted in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, states: "For one who acts with a mind of malice toward another, neither the hearing of moral discipline, nor meditative concentration, nor dwelling in solitude provides protection; neither does giving nor the worship of the Buddhas provide protection." And the *Mañjuśrī-vikrīḍita-sūtra* states: "Mañjuśrī, 'anger' is so called because it utterly destroys the roots of virtue accumulated over a hundred aeons; therefore, it is called 'anger'." And the *Maitreyasiṃhanāda-sūtra* also states: "One should retreat a hundred *yojanas* from a place of hateful conflict; one should not give rise to a mind of hatred. Compared to abusing, beating, and attacking with weapons all the sentient beings in a billion-fold world system, it is a far greater fault to give rise to a single thought of malice or hatred toward another bodhisattva; by this, a bodhisattva is wounded and impaired. Just as iron cannot be cut by anything other than iron, the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva are exhausted by the hatred of another bodhisattva, and cannot be exhausted by others. Therefore, one should act toward one another with respect and reverence, and one should generate the perception of a teacher even toward a bodhisattva who has just generated the mind of enlightenment." It is said that anger toward a bodhisattva who has received a prophecy is a particularly grave fault. If a bodhisattva who has not yet received a prophecy of non-retrogression from the Great Vehicle becomes angry with a bodhisattva who has received such a prophecy or the signs thereof, and engages in physical or verbal conflict without performing confession of the fault or abandoning the angry mind, then for as many moments as that angry mind—which possesses the fault of being like a barren field where the harvest of virtue cannot grow—has arisen, one must don the armor of training in the path and entering the path for an equal number of aeons. The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* also quotes the *Maitreyasiṃhanāda-sūtra*: "If a bodhisattva were to abuse, beat, or strike with a fist all the sentient beings in a billion-fold world system, by that alone the bodhisattva would not be wounded or injured. However, if a bodhisattva were to engender even a single moment of malice, harshness, or a hateful mind toward another bodhisattva, by that alone the bodhisattva is wounded and injured. Why is that? If they have not abandoned omniscience, then for as many moments as a bodhisattva has generated malice, harshness, or a hateful mind toward another bodhisattva, for that many aeons must they don the armor of patience." Thus it is said. Therefore, those individuals who wish to practice the path of the Great Vehicle should not provide an opportunity for anger, even if it costs them their lives, and should make loving-kindness, compassion, and the *bodhicitta* the foundation of their practice.Since the faults of anger have been explained above, the way to rely upon patience is as follows: Because the Buddhas have attained or reached great awakening through the perfection of patience, this opposing state of an angry mind is not good. One should generate the mindfulness that it destroys the roots of virtue accumulated over many eons and causes love and compassion to diminish. One should confess each instance of that negativity with intense regret, and resolve not to commit such faults again in the future. Thinking, "I must not allow this unwholesome mind to find an opportunity to arise in my continuum," one should not take delight in conflict and the like; that is how one arrives at this path of the Great Vehicle, the Buddha-Dharma. Thus it is said.This concludes the commentary on the twenty-fourth chapter, on manifest pride, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.In order to demonstrate the two types of development—those that are primarily internal, such as the two types of development that arise because one has become a lineage-holder of the Buddhas and because one attains the fruition of Buddhahood itself—the meaning of the two verses beginning with "When training, whoever..." is as follows: When a bodhisattva is training on the path of the Great Vehicle, they do not ultimately accept any phenomena to be trained in, such as the three trainings or the six perfections. They do not perceive as true the self who is the trainee, nor the phenomena in which they are to be trained. Furthermore, they do not conceptually construct as true either the antidote—the bodhisattva’s training—or its opposing state—the non-training of anger and the like. Rather, they understand both of these as being equal in being empty of true existence. Whoever trains in this way is training without error in this perfection of wisdom, which is the phenomenon that brings about the attainment of the rank of Buddhahood.A bodhisattva who trains without departing from the sequence of the two truths in this way—knowing this training—will never, at any time, decline from the training in wisdom and meditative concentration, nor will they become lax in ethical discipline; this is how they become a lineage-holder of the Buddhas. Furthermore, such a bodhisattva trains in this supreme path in order to attain or realize the Buddha’s qualities, such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; thus, the reason for attaining Buddhahood itself is demonstrated. That bodhisattva is one who excels in the training of meditative concentration and the training of ethical discipline, and is skilled in the training of wisdom. The reason for this is that they train through the method of knowing that there is not even the slightest perception of the three spheres as true, and that they are devoid of true existence. Thus it is said.To explain the development of the non-arising of opposing factors such as avarice, two verses are taught, beginning with "The wise one who illuminates." The meaning is as follows: when a bodhisattva who is skilled in the meaning of the two truths trains in this way in the perfection of wisdom—which illuminates the profound phenomena of emptiness—they do not generate even a single moment of non-virtuous thought, such as the grasping at truth or avarice, which are afflictive conceptualizations contrary to the path of omniscience. This is because there is no refuge for the darkness of evil conceptualizations within their own mental continuum, which is pervaded by the light of wisdom that realizes profound emptiness; it is just as, when the sun moves through the sky, not even the slightest darkness can remain in the space before it, as it is completely suppressed by the sun's rays. Thus it is said.To explain, with an analogy, the development of the way of practicing by gathering all the perfections within the perfection of wisdom, two verses are taught, beginning with "The perfection of wisdom." The meaning is as follows: for those who have trained without error in this way in the perfection of wisdom, all the perfections, such as generosity, are gathered within this perfection of wisdom that realizes the non-apprehension of the three spheres. For example, just as it is taught in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* (Net of Brahmā Sūtra) that all sixty-two evil views—which rely on the extremes of the past and future, such as the view of the permanence of the self and the world—are gathered within it, in that same way, it is taught that all these perfections, such as generosity, are gathered within the practice of the perfection of wisdom that realizes emptiness endowed with the supreme of all aspects, which is seized by the lack of any incomplete aspect of skillful means.For example, just as when the life faculty ceases, all other faculties, such as the eye faculty, however many there may be, also cease, in that same way, it is taught that for bodhisattvas who are supreme in their skill in the way of practicing the Mahāyāna path while engaging in the perfection of wisdom, all other trainings in the perfections are gathered within this practice of the perfection of wisdom, and it is taught that if this perfection of wisdom is absent, all the others are absent as well.To explain the two types of increase—the increase of attaining all perfections and the increase of drawing near to enlightenment—one verse is spoken, beginning with "The bodhisattva who is skilled..." The meaning is: a bodhisattva who is skilled in means and wisdom studies the qualities of the grounds and paths of the śrāvakas, and likewise all the qualities of the pratyekabuddhas, in order to care for the beings to be tamed by those paths, and although they care for those beings to be tamed, those bodhisattvas do not abide in those paths of the lesser vehicle, nor do they generate the desire to attain their fruits. Thinking, "This path is merely to be known or to be studied for the sake of caring for other beings to be tamed, but it is not to be realized," they therefore study all the paths of the three vehicles. These increases are explained in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* by such passages as, "Subhūti, if all the sentient beings in the Jambudvīpa were to obtain a human body without any sequence, and having obtained a human body, were to generate the mind for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment," and so forth. This is the commentary on the twenty-fifth chapter, the chapter on training, from the *Lamp of Jewels that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, which Clarifies the Profound Reality of Dependent Origination, a Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection*.The peak application of forbearance. Third, regarding the peak application of forbearance, the *Ornament* states: "From 'the three knowledges' ... to 'is termed stability'." Regarding this, there are three points: definition, classification, and stage. The first: the third of the three aspects of the path of preparation that are in accordance with the three knowledges, which is the perfection of wisdom that has attained stability in not being divided regarding the welfare of others, is the definition of the peak application of forbearance. The second: as for its classification, there are the small, medium, and great peak applications of forbearance. The stage is only in the forbearance stage. To explain that very stability or peak application of forbearance that has attained a firm realization of method and wisdom, one verse is spoken, beginning with "irreversible awakening." Although *Buddhaśrī* applies this to the "all-abiding mind," it is as the Master applies it to "stability." That is, having attained a firm realization of method and wisdom, a person who is a bodhisattva—who has entered into the practice of the perfections and so forth, with a firm and intense aspiration to generate the mind of awakening, desiring to establish those who are proceeding toward supreme awakening so that they do not turn back from the Great Vehicle—if another person sincerely rejoices in that generation of the mind, then, although the kings of mountains, the Mount Merus, existing in this trichiliocosm can be measured by being weighed on a scale, the merit of rejoicing in the roots of virtue of that bodhisattva cannot be measured in such a way, because it is infinite. Gungthang Jamyang said that by means of rejoicing, the firm realization of method and wisdom is indicated, and thus it is a hidden meaning.The Peak Application of Supreme Dharma. The fourth, the peak application of supreme dharma, is stated in the Ornament as: "The four continents and the emptiness, etc., up to... the meditative concentration is fully proclaimed." Regarding this, there are three points. First, the definition of the peak application of supreme dharma is: that fourth factor of the Mahayana aids to penetration, which has attained a mind that rests entirely upon that which transcends the limits of meditative concentration, from the perspective of the ripening of the capacity to generate the Mahayana path of seeing, which serves as its own result. Second, regarding its divisions, there are three: small, medium, and great supreme dharma. Third, regarding its boundary, it exists only within the Mahayana path of preparation of supreme dharma.In explaining the peak application of resting the mind entirely, the meaning of the one verse beginning with "seeking virtue" is as follows: Why is it that rejoicing in the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva in this way is a cause for great merit? It is because by rejoicing in that virtue of a bodhisattva alone, one also indirectly rejoices in the masses of merit of all those in the world who seek their own virtue and all those sentient beings who desire to benefit others. Why is that? Because all the virtue accumulated by a bodhisattva is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; therefore, those irreversible bodhisattvas, having attained all the qualities of the omniscient Victor through the power of that excellent path, in order to exhaust without remainder the suffering of sentient beings wandering in cyclic existence, bestow the gift of Dharma throughout all worlds and establish all sentient beings without exception on the path to enlightenment. Thus it is said.The Peak Application of the Path of Seeing. In explaining the fifth, the peak application of the path of seeing, the Ornament states: "From 'in entering and in turning back' to 'that which is included is here the path of seeing.'" There are three points regarding this. First, the definition of the peak application of the path of seeing is: a Mahayana realization of truth that abides as the direct antidote to the seeds of the conceptualizations to be abandoned through seeing. Second, regarding its divisions, there are two: meditative equipoise and subsequent attainment; and when divided by way of what is to be abandoned, there are four peak applications of the path of seeing, which are the antidotes to the four conceptualizations to be abandoned through seeing. Third, regarding its boundaries, it exists only in the Mahayana path of seeing. In explaining the peak application of the path of seeing, there is the explanation of the conceptualizations to be abandoned and the explanation of the path of seeing as the antidote.Explaining the conceptualizations to be abandoned. This has two parts: the actual meaning and the related implications.The actual meaning. The first of these also has two: the conceptualization of the apprehended as cognitive obscurations and the conceptualization of the apprehender.Regarding the conceptualization of the apprehended as cognitive obscurations, the first of these also consists of two: the conceptualization of the apprehended as engaging and the conceptualization of the apprehended as withdrawing.To explain the conceptualization of the apprehended as engaging, the first of these, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "A bodhisattva..." is taught. A bodhisattva who abides in the non-conceptualizing primordial wisdom of reality, and who thoroughly understands that all phenomena of defilement and purification are by nature empty, and in the ultimate sense are signless and without the proliferations or aspirations of true existence, does not seek enlightenment through the door of grasping at true existence or holding to the two extremes, by means of the two types of wisdom that realize that defilement, purification, the apprehended, the grasper, the abandoned, and the antidote are all without true existence. That yogi, who abides on the path of seeing, which is free from all proliferations of dualistic appearance, is one who strives for the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the essence of the path of seeing and the path of meditation. Thus it is said.The conceptualization of the apprehended as withdrawing. To explain the second, the conceptualization of the apprehended as withdrawing, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "That space element..." is taught. For example, since space is merely the absence of obstruction, there is no such thing as the essence of that space element itself being incompatible with coexisting in that space, nor does it act as an obstacle to the arising of other material things; for the space element and what is called space are both equivalent to non-existence, and therefore no material object can ever attain its essence. Just like that analogy, a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, which realizes that the nature of the path of seeing—such as what is to be adopted and what is to be abandoned, or what is to be relinquished and the antidote—is equal in being empty of true existence, also abides in the space-like primordial wisdom that is non-conceptual; they possess the greatness of practicing in such a way that all conceptualizations that grasp at the inferior path as something to be withdrawn as true are completely pacified. Thus it is said.To explain the second, the conceptualization that grasps at a basis where a person exists substantially, the meaning of the two verses beginning with "In the midst of a crowd..." is taught. For example, in the midst of a large crowd of people gathered to watch a spectacle, a conjured person—that is, a person emanated by means of magical mantras and substances—does not think to themselves, "By means of my perfect form and various activities, I shall delight this large crowd of people." Yet, even though they do not think this, they perform the very activities that make the spectators happy and delighted, and they clearly display various miraculous feats such as walking and sitting. Even if the crowd of people sees this, that illusory emanation possesses no established human body, possesses no mind, and its name also does not exist as established in the ultimate sense.Likewise, bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom, without conceptually grasping the nature of the path of seeing as true, never think to themselves, "Having realized great awakening in the ultimate sense, I shall completely liberate beings from cyclic existence." Yet, for the sake of training those to be trained, they manifest various births such as gods and humans, and possess many activities that accomplish the benefit and happiness of beings. Although these do not exist in the ultimate sense, they manifest them conventionally like an illusion, and they practice in a manner that does not conceptually grasp those various manifestations as true. Thus it is said.To demonstrate the second type of conceptual grasping that relies on the imputation of a person, the meaning of the two verses beginning with "For example, a Buddha" is as follows: Even though those who perform emanations, such as the supreme emanation body, perform all the activities of a Buddha, such as teaching the Dharma, not even the slightest pride or arrogance arises in that emanation thinking, "I am the one performing the Buddha's activities," because there is no conceptual thought whatsoever. Likewise, a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the perfection of wisdom, which does not conceptually grasp the apprehended and the apprehender as true, even though they realize that all phenomena are empty of truth and of a single taste, conventionally performs all activities, such as the three of perfecting, ripening, and purifying, just like an emanation or an illusion, and manifests various activities.To demonstrate another example, it is explained: Just as a skilled master carpenter creates mechanical figures of men and women from wood, and those figures perform all kinds of activities such as walking and sitting, yet they do not conceptually think, "I have done this," because they lack a mind; in that same way, a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the perfection of wisdom—having realized that all phenomena, though non-existent in the ultimate sense, appear conventionally like an illusion—and who has attained stability, performs all activities to accomplish the welfare of beings while abiding in non-conceptual wisdom that is free from the manifest conceptualization of grasping at the apprehended and the apprehender, just like a wish-fulfilling jewel or a wish-granting tree. This concludes the commentary on the twenty-sixth chapter, the chapter on the illusion-like, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, the profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent arising.Interconnected Meaning: Regarding the second, the interconnected meaning: to demonstrate how, by having abandoned the four conceptualizations that are to be abandoned, one is praised by the Buddhas and cannot be overcome by the four māras, the meaning of the three verses beginning with "Thus, skilled in conduct" is as follows: By having abandoned the four conceptualizations of grasping at the apprehended and the apprehender as truly existent, as explained in that way, those who are skilled in the conduct of realizing that all phenomena are empty of true existence are honored and prostrated to by many hosts of gods, such as Brahmā and Indra, who bow their bodies with respect while joining their palms together. Furthermore, not only that, but all the Buddhas residing in the world systems of the ten directions also proclaim a continuous garland of praise, extolling the marvelous qualities of that great being, the bodhisattva.Therefore, to demonstrate that they have transcended the domain of Māra, it is explained: If all the sentient beings in fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to become Māras, and each of those Māras were to emanate as many Māras again from every single hair on their bodies, and they were to seek an opportunity against that bodhisattva who has attained non-conceptual wisdom, even then, all of them together would be unable to cause even the slightest obstruction, such as the moving of a single hair, to that one who is skilled in means.Having thus demonstrated that they have transcended the Māra of the divine child, it is explained in order to show that they have transcended the four Māras without exception. Through four causes, a bodhisattva who is skilled in means and possesses the power of having realized emptiness directly is difficult for the four Māras, such as the Māra of the divine child, to overcome, and cannot be shaken from the path of the Great Vehicle. What are those four causes? They are: abiding in the wisdom that realizes that phenomena are empty by nature; great compassion that does not abandon the fulfillment of the welfare of sentient beings; a firm vow to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings by attaining unsurpassed enlightenment, and to act without turning back, just as one has spoken; and having accumulated vast collections of merit and wisdom, such as making offerings to the Buddhas, whereby one is cherished by the Victors and enters into the blessings of the Sugatas. Thus, if one possesses these four causes, one cannot be harmed by the four Māras and is able to defeat all Māras. This is what is meant.In explaining the three causes—teaching the path of awakening to others as an antidote to those four conceptualizations, which is the cause of the path of seeing and the peak of the path; entrusting the words and meanings of the perfection of wisdom; and striving to accomplish the cause of uninterruptedness oneself—six verses are spoken, beginning with "The Mother of the Tathāgatas." The meaning is this: when a bodhisattva, for the sake of attaining great awakening, correctly teaches the path of seeing and so forth to others, and when they explain or write down this perfection of wisdom, which is the Mother that gives birth to the Tathāgatas, if a bodhisattva, with great joy, aspires from the heart and gives it to others, and if they themselves sincerely practice or strive to accomplish this path, then that bodhisattva, whose continuum is softened by love and compassion and who is certain, should be known as one who has entered the path of omniscience. Regarding the manner in which, although the great awakening comprised by the path of seeing and the peak of the path exhausts defilements, in the ultimate sense it is non-abiding because there is no exhaustion and no birth: bodhisattvas do not abide in the ultimate sense even in the suchness that is the mode of existence of the phenomena of the dharmadhātu, and they abide without any grasping at anything whatsoever. Just as clouds in the sky do not depend on anything, they abide in suchness, which is free from all elaborations, without abiding in any phenomenon through grasping at truth.Just as a mantra-holder, without having a dwelling, house, or similar base in which to reside, travels through the sky, when they desire a place to stay, through the power of the mantra, they arrive at the time to be born in that very sky; and, not being born from the earth or similar elements, they manifest and bless into appearance a delightful pleasure grove, complete with pleasing flowers, trees, and the like, just as they desire. In that same way, a bodhisattva who has practiced the conduct of a conqueror’s child—such as establishing sentient beings in ripening and liberation—through the blessing of the mantra of the supreme, non-conceptual perfection of wisdom, and who is skilled in the manner of accomplishing the benefit of others and possesses a clear intellect that realizes the meaning of the nature of reality, does not perceive the phenomena of the path that are to be entered as truly existent for the sake of realization, nor do they perceive the qualities of a buddha that are to be attained, or the means of attaining them, as truly existent objects of rejection. Furthermore, by way of having abandoned the cognitive obscurations and conceptualizations that grasp at a truly existent person—such as the one who explains the dharma—and the conceptualizations that view the one desiring the dharma as the very object to whom the dharma is explained, as a truly existent "person" (pudgala) that is merely imputed, they do not perceive them; rather, they realize all phenomena as empty of true existence. This is the abiding of those bodhisattvas who, in conventional terms, desire to pacify the suffering of sentient beings and who delight in the qualities of the Mahayana path and its fruition, such as the ten powers. Therefore, the reason their manner of abiding is greatly superior to that of the shravakas and pratyekabuddhas is that, apart from the abiding of the Tathagata himself—who has abandoned the two obscurations and abides in supreme meditative absorptions such as the eight liberations and the totalities—this abiding of the bodhisattva is the supreme among all the various types of abiding of other shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, which are possessed of the joy and happiness of the stainless, where all suffering and its causes are completely pacified through meditative absorption; and because there is nothing higher than that, it is the supreme, unsurpassable abiding.Even though they abide in a meditative concentration that pacifies all conceptual proliferation, they do not fall into the extreme of peace where the performance of benefit for others is severed. For example, just as birds dwell in the supportless sky yet do not fall to the ground, and just as fish dwell in the water yet do not suffocate or die, in that same way, Bodhisattvas who have attained skill in means, through the power of meditative concentration, have transcended the level of ordinary beings, have given rise to the path of seeing and the realization of the truths within their mental continuum, and even though they abide one-pointedly in the emptiness that is free from conceptual proliferation, they do not pass into a nirvana where the heart of peace is snatched away and the benefit of others is severed, because they possess the supreme power of compassion and previous aspirations.Therefore, the way in which one who wishes to attain the state of the three bodies must train in the perfection of wisdom is as follows: one who wishes to attain the supreme of all the qualities that sentient beings possess—that is, one who wishes to attain the dharmakāya; one who wishes to touch the most marvelous and wondrous primordial wisdom of the Buddha, which is the supreme of all qualities; and one who, having become a Buddha oneself, wishes to bestow upon sentient beings the gift of the Dharma that is supreme, excellent, and holy through inconceivable emanations—such a person should rely upon this supreme abode of the Victors and their spiritual children, who accomplish the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings without exception. This is what is said. This is the commentary on the twenty-seventh chapter, the chapter on the essence, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.The nature of the path of seeing. Having thus explained the incidental meaning, the second, the nature of the path of seeing, is the meaning of the four verses beginning with "This training..." The training in the perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the great enlightenment itself as the path of seeing, is the supreme of all the countless trainings of the bodhisattva that the guides, the perfect Buddhas, have fully proclaimed; there is nothing superior to this, so there is nothing beyond it. Therefore, any wise person who wishes to go to the stage of a Buddha, who has reached the far shore of all trainings, must train in this perfection of wisdom, the path of the Great Vehicle, which is the training of the Buddha. This path of seeing is the treasury of the twelve hundred qualities and so forth, the repository of the thirty-six aspects—comprising the six perfections within each of the six, such as generosity—and the way in which one is born into the lineage of the Buddha and all the qualities of the ten stages of ultimate reality arise from it. This is explained through two examples: this path of seeing, such as the patience of knowing the truth regarding suffering, is the great and supreme treasury of Dharma, as it is the source of the twelve hundred qualities, such as seeing the face of the Buddha. It is the marvelous and holy treasury of Dharma, vast with the wealth of qualities such as the thirty-six perfections—generosity and so forth—as well as dharanis, meditative concentrations, and the factors of enlightenment. Being born into the lineage from which the Buddha himself arises, it is certain that one will attain the state of a Buddha. Progressing through the ten stages, such as the first stage, the Joyous, one reaches the culmination of all qualities, which is the treasury where all the temporary and ultimate happiness and joy of beings arise and abide. Although all the protectors of the world, the Buddhas and Bhagavats of the ten directions—those of the past who have already passed, those of the future, and those currently present—arose from practicing this path of the perfection of wisdom, the natural perfection of wisdom, the dharmadhātu, never becomes exhausted; it remains free from increase or decrease. Therefore, to show through an example that this is the cause of all qualities, it is explained: just as all trees, fruits, flowers, forests, and so forth arise perfectly from the earth and emerge upon it, yet even though trees and the like are produced again and again, the earth is not exhausted through cessation, nor does it increase from stage to stage, nor does it deviate from its state of being, nor does it suffer loss. The earth does not conceptualize, "I have produced the trees and forests," and even though it produces fruits again and again, it feels no weariness or dissatisfaction; it arises from the gathering of causes, conditions, and dependent relationships, and there is no self of a person who acts as a creator.In the same way, whatever happiness and virtuous qualities there are of the bodhisattvas who are the sons of the Buddhas, the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, the gods such as Brahmā and Indra, and all wandering beings, they all arise from the cultivation of the path of seeing of the supreme perfection of wisdom; for by practicing the path of the Great Vehicle, one attains complete and perfect buddhahood, and from the teaching of that Dharma, all high status and definite goodness arise. Thus, although all happiness and excellence of both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa arise in dependence upon the perfection of wisdom, that wisdom itself, in the ultimate sense, never diminishes nor does it increase. So it is said.Since it is not sufficient to merely meditate on emptiness in meditative equipoise, one must also become familiar with the twelve links of dependent origination in their forward and reverse orders during the post-meditation state. To explain this very method, the three verses beginning with "The lowest of sentient beings" were spoken. The meaning is as follows: In the world, depending on body and resources, there are various classes of sentient beings—the lowest, who are in the miserable realms; the intermediate, such as humans; and the highest, who are the gods. The Sugata has taught that all of these do not arise from a Primal Being, Ishvara, or a permanent Time, but rather arise from the ignorance of grasping at a self. Due to the power of this ignorance—which is the opponent and the discordant factor of the wisdom of pristine awareness—one grasps at a personal self. Consequently, karma is accumulated, and when conditions such as the nourishment provided by craving and grasping are gathered, the fruits of birth, aging, and death are established. Thus, this great machine of the suffering of cyclic existence, consisting of the twelve links of dependent origination of contaminated phenomena, arises again and again. Even so, that machine of ignorance in the continuum of sentient beings is not exhausted by the arising of its fruits, nor does it increase; it remains just as it is.The Buddha’s pristine awareness, the path of meditation that accords with its nature, the entry point of the path of seeing, the path of preparation that is the method for its arising, and the path of accumulation that is its root—all of these arise from the supreme perfection of wisdom that realizes selflessness. By repeatedly familiarizing oneself with that very pristine awareness of selflessness and accumulating a vast collection of merit, ignorance is ceased, and since one does not accumulate the karma that projects cyclic existence, the machine of suffering does not arise. Furthermore, when the conditions of method—such as meditating on love and compassion as taught by a spiritual friend—are gathered, the machine of pristine awareness, consisting of the ten stages and five paths of the Great Vehicle, arises. Its root, the perfection of wisdom that realizes the nature of reality, is never exhausted, nor does it increase in the ultimate sense; it remains as a dependent origination that is like an illusion in conventional terms.As it is said in the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra*:If one thoroughly knows all phenomenaThat have arisen in dependence upon causes,Then one’s treasury is inexhaustible;The treasury of Dharma is inconceivable.The Protector of the world has clearly taughtThat these four things are inexhaustible:Sentient beings, space, the bodhisattva mind,And likewise, the qualities of the Buddha.If these were substantial entities,They would eventually be exhausted;But because they are non-existent, they are inexhaustible;Therefore, they are taught to be inexhaustible.Thus, any bodhisattva who investigates and searches with reasoning into this dependent origination of all phenomena of cyclic existence and nirvana—which are merely conventional—and finds nothing at all, thereby fully understands that they are unborn by their own nature and unceasing, meaning they are without exhaustion. Knowing such a profound meaning of the perfection of wisdom is to have mastered the profound essence of the treasury of the Buddha’s speech and to have seen the Dharmakāya. As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*:This dependent origination is the profound and precious treasury of the Victors' speech;Whoever sees this correctlySees the Buddha, the supreme among those who realize suchness.In this way, by knowing and familiarizing oneself with the meaning of the profound nature of reality, emptiness, and by abiding in the path of meditation such as the meditative absorption of the "leap-over" (*thod rgal*), just as the sun, which is free of clouds and radiates intense light, dispels all darkness without exception, one destroys the dense darkness of the obscurations of ignorance along with its latent tendencies, and attains the supreme, self-arisen pristine awareness of a Buddha. This is just as it was prophesied that the sixty monks would become the Tathāgata named Puṣpakūṭa. This is the commentary on the twenty-eighth chapter, the chapter on Puṣpakūṭa, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of Fortunate Ones, which Clarifies the Reality of Dependent Origination*, a commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā*.The sixth, the peak training of the path of meditation, is taught in the *Ornament* as follows: "The nine meditative absorptions including cessation, up to the nine other opposing factors." There are three parts to this. The first is the definition: the realization that follows the Mahāyāna path, which abides in the lineage of the direct antidote to the seeds of the obstructions to be abandoned by meditation, is the definition of the peak training of the path of meditation. The second, its divisions, consists of the nine uninterrupted paths that are the direct antidotes to the nine cycles of conceptualization to be abandoned by meditation, and the nine paths of liberation of the path of meditation. The third, its extent, is from the first bhūmi up to the tenth bhūmi.In explaining such a peak training of the path of meditation, three verses are spoken, beginning with "Possessing great power." Regarding this, in order to show two of the four conceptualizations of subject and object—which are the things to be abandoned—it is said that a bodhisattva on the path of meditation, who possesses the great power of qualities such as having abandoned the two conceptualizations of subject and object that are obstructions to omniscience, abides in the four primary meditative absorptions of dhyāna and also trains in the samādhi of the "leap-over" (thong rgal). At that time, they do not abide by way of clinging to the subject and object as truly existent, nor do they abide by way of tasting the bliss of meditative absorption, because they have realized directly that the object is devoid of true existence.However, these four—the limbs of the first primary meditative absorption of dhyāna, including samādhi and joy and bliss—become the basis for attaining the qualities of abandonment and realization of the supreme, unsurpassable, perfect awakening, because all paths of seeing and meditation rely upon the primary meditative absorptions. Although Buddhajñāna applies this and what follows to the peak training of the uninterrupted path, according to the master, the way in which one abandons the two conceptualizations of subject and object that are obstructions to omniscience, trains in infinite samādhis, and accomplishes the welfare of others by taking on various births, is as follows: A bodhisattva who has attained the supreme wisdom that realizes the nature of reality, while abiding in the four dhyānas of the path of meditation, also enters into and experiences the four supreme formless samādhis and the meditative absorption of cessation, yet does not cling to them as truly existent. Since these formless dhyānas become the favorable conditions for clairvoyance, miraculous powers, and so forth, they are conditions that help in attaining the supreme state of a perfect Buddha; thus, one trains in them. One does not train in them like a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, who abides in the bliss of peace after having exhausted the defilements or outflows, because the bodhisattva lacks the mind that seeks peace for one's own sake.This method is the wondrous and marvelous quality of bodhisattvas who possess infinite qualities, such as having abandoned the one hundred and eight conceptualizations of subject and object that are obstructions to omniscience. What is this? It is that, having abided in samādhis such as the four dhyānas, they realize that there is not even the slightest sign of true existence in them. If those who abide in the path of meditation, having attained the eight dhyānas and formless absorptions, should have their bodies disintegrate, they do not take birth in the higher realms due to the exhaustion of the limbs of the causal dhyāna of meditative absorption. Instead, they take birth in realms where they desire to accomplish the welfare of others, such as ripening sentient beings, just as they wish or intend.The Uninterrupted Peak Training. The seventh, the uninterrupted peak training, is as stated in the Ornament: "The three-thousand-fold world, the inferior śrāvakas, and so on... up to... the uninterrupted concentration." Regarding this, there are three sections: definition, classification, and the boundary. The first is: the ultimate yoga of a bodhisattva, which is seized by wisdom that has transcended the path of accumulation of the Great Vehicle—which is a meditation encompassing the three knowledges—and which directly produces the omniscience that is its own result; this is the definition of the uninterrupted peak training. That and the wisdom of the end of the continuum are synonymous. The second, its classification, consists of the four momentary trainings. The third, the boundary, exists only at the end of the continuum.To explain the uninterrupted peak training, which, like a lotus in water, remains in existence yet is not stained by the faults of existence: for example, if a person from Jambudvīpa who had never before gone to the divine realms or the beautiful cities of the gods—which are perfect and supreme—were to later travel there by means of miraculous powers and so forth, and upon seeing those delightful places such as the mansions and pleasure groves held by the gods, were to feel no attachment to them, and then, upon returning to this Jambudvīpa, were to feel nauseated by their own home and dwellings, seeing them as unpleasant and thus not becoming attached to them; just so, the bodhisattva explains the basis and support of the path’s qualities, such as the wisdom realizing the lack of true existence and love, compassion, and so forth. By exerting themselves in the yoga of uninterrupted concentration and abiding in concentrations such as the four dhyānas and the eight liberations, they see the supreme and excellent qualities of a buddha. Because they see them, they do not crave the dhyānas, the formless concentrations, or the joys of those states. By the power of that, they abandon rebirth and, as for the phrase "back into the desire realm," this does not mean only the lower realm, but rather that they abide in the desire realm as they wish. They have no attachment to any phenomena of the three realms; even though they abide in cyclic existence, they are not stained by the faults of cyclic existence, just as a lotus born from water is not stained by the water, and thus they do not abide in the phenomena of the childish.
